items.q: What is a React Server Component and how does it differ from a Client Component?
items.a: An RSC runs only on the server: its code never reaches the browser, it can fetch data and use server resources, but it can't use state or effects. A Client Component ('use client') ships to the browser and owns interactivity, state, and event handlers.

items.q: Why do Server Components reduce client bundle size?
items.a: Their code and imported dependencies execute on the server and are never bundled for the browser; only the rendered output and any Client Components reach the client.

items.q: Can a Server Component use useState or useEffect?
items.a: No. Server Components have no client lifecycle, so those hooks aren't allowed. Move interactive parts into a Client Component marked 'use client'.

items.q: What problem does the React Compiler solve?
items.a: It removes the need to manually place useMemo/useCallback/React.memo by analyzing components at build time and inserting memoization automatically, reducing unnecessary re-renders.

items.q: What are the Rules of Hooks?
items.a: Call hooks only at the top level (not in loops, conditions, or nested functions) and only from React functions. This keeps hook call order stable across renders so React can track state correctly.

items.q: How does useReducer differ from useState?
items.a: useState is best for simple values; useReducer centralizes complex state transitions in a reducer function, making multi-action updates more predictable and testable.

items.q: How do you avoid prop drilling in React?
items.a: Use the Context API to provide a value at an ancestor and consume it anywhere below with useContext, or adopt a state library. This avoids threading props through intermediate components that don't need them.

items.q: When should you NOT use Context?
items.a: For frequently changing or large state, since every consumer re-renders when the context value changes. Prefer local state, memoized selectors, or a dedicated store (Redux/Zustand/Query) for hot paths.

items.q: Why use a server-state library like React Query over useEffect?
items.a: It gives caching, deduping, retries, background refetch, and stale-while-revalidate out of the box, eliminating brittle manual fetch-in-useEffect patterns and race conditions.

items.q: How does React.memo differ from useMemo?
items.a: React.memo wraps a component to skip re-render when its props are shallowly equal; useMemo caches a computed value inside a component between renders. One memoizes a component, the other a value.

items.q: How do React.lazy and Suspense improve performance?
items.a: React.lazy loads a component as a separate chunk only when rendered; Suspense shows a fallback while it loads. This code-splits the bundle so users download less up front.

items.q: What causes unnecessary re-renders and how do you find them?
items.a: New object/function props each render, context changes, or parent re-renders. Use the React Profiler and memoization (memo/useMemo/useCallback) plus stable references to cut them.

items.q: What do React 19 Actions solve?
items.a: They standardize async mutations bound to transitions, automatically handling pending status, errors, and optimistic state so you stop hand-managing loading flags and try/catch in every handler.

items.q: What does useOptimistic do?
items.a: It renders an immediate optimistic value while an async action is in flight and automatically reverts to the real state if the action fails -- e.g. showing a sent message before the server confirms.

items.q: What is the new use() hook?
items.a: use() reads a resource like a promise or context, and unlike other hooks it can be called conditionally and in loops -- letting components suspend on a promise or read context inline.

items.q: What's the difference between useTransition and useDeferredValue?
items.a: useTransition wraps the state setter at the call site, so you decide which update is a transition and get an isPending flag; useDeferredValue wraps a value at the consumer, letting that value lag behind while urgent updates render. Same goal, different placement.

items.q: How does React decide update priority?
items.a: Updates from direct user interaction (click, input, focus) are urgent and rendered synchronously; updates in startTransition or read through useDeferredValue are non-urgent and can be interrupted to handle urgent work, then resumed.

items.q: Give a real use case for useTransition.
items.a: Filtering a large list as the user types: keep the input update urgent and wrap the expensive filter render in startTransition so typing stays smooth while the list catches up.

items.q: What do error boundaries catch and not catch?
items.a: They catch errors during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of the child tree. They do NOT catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout/promises), SSR, or errors thrown in the boundary itself.
items.topic: Error Boundaries & Error Handling in React 19

items.q: Is there a hooks-based error boundary in React 19?
items.a: No. Error boundaries remain class components (getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch); most teams use the react-error-boundary library, or the new createRoot options onUncaughtError, onCaughtError, and onRecoverableError.
items.topic: Error Boundaries & Error Handling in React 19

items.q: How do you handle errors in event handlers then?
items.a: Use regular try/catch inside the handler and set state to show an error UI -- error boundaries won't catch those, so handle them explicitly.
items.topic: Error Boundaries & Error Handling in React 19

items.q: useRef vs useState - when do you use each?
items.a: useRef holds a mutable value that persists across renders WITHOUT triggering a re-render (DOM nodes, timers, previous values); useState triggers a re-render when it changes. Use refs for non-visual mutable data, state for values that drive the UI.

items.q: What changed about refs in React 19?
items.a: ref is now a regular prop on function components, so forwardRef is deprecated -- you can read ref directly from props. useImperativeHandle still customizes what methods a parent can call through that ref.

items.q: What are portals and why use them?
items.a: createPortal renders children into a DOM node outside the parent's hierarchy -- ideal for modals, tooltips, and popovers that must escape overflow:hidden or z-index stacking -- while preserving React context and event propagation.

items.q: Why write a custom hook?
items.a: To reuse stateful logic (e.g. useFetch, useDebounce) across components via composition, avoiding the wrapper hell of HOCs and render props. It must follow the Rules of Hooks.

items.q: Controlled vs uncontrolled components - difference?
items.a: Controlled: React state is the single source of truth, value set by state and updated via onChange -- easy validation and conditional logic. Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value, read on demand via a ref -- less code, used for simple forms or file inputs.

items.q: How do React 19 form Actions simplify forms?
items.a: You pass an async function to <form action={fn}>; React runs it in a transition, and useFormStatus exposes pending state -- removing boilerplate onSubmit handlers and manual loading flags.

items.q: When is an uncontrolled input the better choice?
items.a: For file inputs (which are inherently uncontrolled), simple forms where you only need the value on submit, or integrating non-React widgets -- reading via a ref avoids unnecessary re-renders per keystroke.

items.q: What is reconciliation and how does React's diffing stay near O(n)?
items.a: Reconciliation compares the new and previous virtual DOM trees to compute minimal DOM updates. A naive tree diff is O(n^3); React uses heuristics -- different element types replace the subtree, same types diff attributes and recurse, and keys match list children -- to run in roughly O(n).

items.q: Why are keys important and what's the index-key bug?
items.a: Keys give list items a stable identity so React can detect insertions, moves, and removals correctly. Using the array index as a key breaks this when the list reorders or items are inserted/removed -- React mismatches items, causing wrong state, lost input, or subtle render bugs.

items.q: What happens when an element's type changes between renders?
items.a: React tears down the old subtree (unmounting its components and state) and mounts a fresh one -- it does not try to diff across different types, which is why changing a wrapper type resets the child state.

items.q: What is React Fiber?
items.a: The reimplemented reconciliation engine (React 16+) that splits rendering into units of work that can be paused, prioritized, and resumed -- the foundation for concurrent features like Suspense and transitions.

items.q: How does the useEffect dependency array work?
items.a:
Omitting it runs the effect after every render; an empty array [] runs it once after mount; listing values runs it whenever any of them change between renders (compared by reference/Object.is).

 Q. What is the cleanup function and when does it run?

 A. The function returned from an effect; React runs it before re-running the effect and when the component unmounts. Use it to clear timers, unsubscribe, and remove listeners so you don't leak or double-subscribe.

items.q: What's a common useEffect bug and how do you avoid it?
items.a: Stale closures from missing dependencies, or infinite loops from depending on a value the effect updates / an unstable object. Fix by including all used values, memoizing objects, or deriving during render instead of in an effect.

items.q: When should you NOT use useEffect?
items.a: For values you can compute during render (derived state), for event-specific logic (put it in the handler), and for transforming data for rendering -- effects are for synchronizing with external systems, not for in-render computation.

items.q: useMemo vs useCallback - what's the difference?
items.a: useMemo returns a memoized value (the result of calling a function); useCallback returns a memoized function itself. useCallback(fn, deps) is essentially useMemo(() => fn, deps).

items.q: Does memoization always improve performance?
items.a: No. It has overhead (storing and comparing deps) and adds complexity; misused it can slow things down. Profile first and apply it to proven hot paths or to stabilize references for memoized children.

items.q: How does the React 19 Compiler change this?
items.a: It auto-memoizes components and values at build time, so much manual useMemo/useCallback becomes unnecessary -- adopt the compiler before hand-optimizing.

items.q: What is a Higher-Order Component (HOC)?
items.a: A function that takes a component and returns a new component with added props or behavior (e.g. withAuth). It's a composition pattern for cross-cutting logic, largely superseded by custom hooks but still common in libraries.
items.topic: Component Patterns: HOCs, Render Props & Composition

items.q: HOCs/render props vs custom hooks - which and why?
items.a: Custom hooks reuse stateful logic without adding wrapper components, avoiding the deeply nested 'wrapper hell' HOCs and render props create. Prefer hooks for new code; understand HOCs/render props for existing code and component libraries.
items.topic: Component Patterns: HOCs, Render Props & Composition

items.q: What is the render props pattern?
items.a: A component takes a function as a prop (often children) and calls it with data, letting the caller control rendering. It shares logic flexibly but can nest awkwardly; hooks usually read cleaner now.
items.topic: Component Patterns: HOCs, Render Props & Composition

items.q: Why must list items have a stable, unique key?
items.a: Keys let React match items across renders to correctly update, move, or remove them. Using the array index breaks on reorder/insert (wrong item state, lost input); use a stable id from the data.

items.q: What's a common bug with && conditional rendering?
items.a: Using a number on the left -- count && <List/> renders a literal 0 when count is 0, since 0 is falsy but still a renderable value. Coerce to boolean (count > 0 && ...) to avoid the stray 0.

items.q: What are the ways to conditionally render in React?
items.a: Ternary in JSX for either/or, && for render-or-nothing, early return for guard clauses, and mapping with conditions for lists. Choose for readability; avoid deeply nested ternaries.

items.q: How does client-side routing work in a SPA?
items.a: The router intercepts navigation, matches the URL to a route, swaps the rendered component, and updates the address bar via the History API -- all without a full page reload, while keeping back/forward working.

items.q: How do you navigate programmatically and read URL params?
items.a: Use useNavigate() to push routes in code (e.g. after a form submit) and useParams()/useSearchParams() to read dynamic segments and query strings from the current URL.

items.q: What are nested routes and why use them?
items.a: Routes rendered inside a parent layout via an outlet, so shared chrome (nav, sidebar) persists while the child changes -- mapping the UI hierarchy to the URL hierarchy and enabling per-section layouts.

items.q: What does useEffectEvent solve?
items.a: It extracts non-reactive logic from an Effect into a stable Effect Event you can call inside the Effect. This lets the Effect read the latest props/state without adding them to the dependency array -- avoiding both stale closures and unnecessary re-runs.

items.q: What is the Activity API (React 19.2) for?
items.a: Activity renders parts of the UI as 'background activity' -- hidden with display:none while preserving their state and properly cleaning up Effects -- so you can pre-render or keep hidden views (like inactive tabs) ready without unmounting them.

items.q: What are View Transitions in React 19.2?
items.a: A built-in way to animate elements that update inside a Transition or during navigation, leveraging the browser's View Transition API -- covering many cases that previously required an animation library.

items.q: This component re-renders when its parent updates even though props look unchanged - why?
items.a: Because by default a child re-renders when its parent does. If the child is wrapped in React.memo, it still re-renders when a prop's reference changes -- inline objects/arrays/functions get a new reference each render, so memo sees them as 'changed'. Stabilize them (useMemo/useCallback) or pass primitives.

items.q: Why don't React.memo and useCallback always prevent re-renders?
items.a: memo does a shallow prop comparison; if any prop is a new reference (a fresh object/array/inline function) it still re-renders. useCallback/useMemo must wrap those props with correct dependencies, or the reference changes anyway. Missing/unstable deps defeat the optimization.

items.q: How does the React Compiler change this in React 19?
items.a: It auto-memoizes components and values at build time, stabilizing references and skipping needless re-renders without manual useMemo/useCallback -- so much of this hand-tuning becomes unnecessary once the compiler is enabled.

items.q: What causes a hydration mismatch and how do you debug it?
items.a: The server HTML differs from the client's first render -- from browser-only APIs (window, localStorage), non-deterministic values (Date.now, Math.random), invalid nesting, or locale/timezone differences. Debug by finding code that differs server vs client; React's dev warnings name the mismatched element.

items.q: How do you fix a hydration error from browser-only code?
items.a: Defer it to the client: run it in useEffect (which only fires after hydration), gate rendering on a mounted state flag, or load the component with a dynamic import using ssr:false so it never renders on the server.

items.q: When is suppressHydrationWarning appropriate?
items.a: Only for unavoidable, intentional mismatches on a single element (e.g. a timestamp), as a last resort. It silences the warning for that node without fixing underlying mismatches, so use it narrowly, not to mask real bugs.

items.q: Implement a useDebounce hook.
items.a: useState for the debounced value; useEffect with [value, delay] that does const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay) and returns () => clearTimeout(id). The cleanup clears the prior timer each change, so the value only updates after the user pauses for `delay` ms.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build a useDebounce Hook

items.q: Why does the cleanup function matter in useDebounce?
items.a: Each time value changes, the effect re-runs; cleanup clears the previous pending timer so it never fires. Without it, every keystroke would eventually update the value, defeating debouncing and firing many API calls.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build a useDebounce Hook

items.q: How would you build useThrottle instead, and when use it?
items.a: Throttle runs at most once per interval: track the last-run timestamp (a ref) and only update if enough time has passed, else schedule a trailing update. Use throttle for continuous events (scroll, mousemove); debounce for 'settle then act' (search input).
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build a useDebounce Hook

items.q: How do you implement an Accordion where only one panel is open?
items.a: Keep the open index in state (number | null). Each header button calls setOpen(open === i ? null : i) to toggle; render a panel's body only when open === i. For multi-open, store a Set of open indices instead and add/remove on toggle.

items.q: How would you make the Accordion accessible?
items.a: Use real <button> headers (keyboard + focus for free), set aria-expanded on each, aria-controls pointing to the panel id, and the panel's role/region with aria-labelledby. Support Enter/Space (native to button) and manage focus order.

items.q: What's the state model difference between single-open and multi-open?
items.a: Single-open: one value (the open index or id, nullable). Multi-open: a collection (Set/array of open ids) you add to or remove from on toggle. Choosing the right shape upfront is what the interviewer is checking.

items.q: Implement a useFetch hook returning data, loading, and error.
items.a: useState for data/loading/error; useEffect on [url]: set loading, fetch, then on success set data (else error), finally clear loading. In cleanup, set an ignore flag (or abort) so a late response from a previous url doesn't overwrite current state.

items.q: How do you prevent a stale fetch from overwriting state?
items.a: Track an ignore flag scoped to the effect run; the cleanup sets it true. Only apply the response if not ignored -- so when url changes, the previous request's late response is discarded. AbortController is the alternative.

items.q: How would you add caching to useFetch?
items.a: Keep a module-level (or context) cache keyed by url; return cached data immediately if present and optionally revalidate in the background -- essentially what React Query/SWR do, which is the usual 'don't reinvent this in production' follow-up.

items.q: How do you model tic-tac-toe state and detect a winner?
items.a: State: an array of 9 cells (null|'X'|'O') and the current player. calculateWinner checks the 8 lines (3 rows, 3 cols, 2 diagonals); if any line has three equal non-null marks, that's the winner. Block moves on filled cells or after a winner; detect a draw when the board fills with no winner.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build a Tic-Tac-Toe Game

items.q: How would you generalize to an N x N board needing M in a row?
items.a: Replace the hardcoded lines with a directional scan: from each filled cell, count consecutive same marks in four directions (horizontal, vertical, two diagonals); a count >= M wins. This scales beyond the fixed 3x3 line list.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build a Tic-Tac-Toe Game

items.q: How do you add 'time travel' through move history?
items.a: Store an array of past board states (or moves); render a list of moves and let clicking one set the current board to that snapshot. Keep history immutable -- push new states rather than mutating -- so jumping back is just selecting an index.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build a Tic-Tac-Toe Game

items.q: How do you build an accessible modal dialog?
items.a: Render it in a portal with role='dialog' and aria-modal='true'; on open, move focus into the dialog and trap it (cycle Tab within); close on Escape and overlay click; on close, restore focus to the trigger; mark background content inert/aria-hidden. Controlled open state drives it.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Modal Dialog & Accessible Components

items.q: Why render a modal through a portal?
items.a: So it escapes the parent's overflow:hidden and z-index stacking and mounts at the document body level, while still belonging to the React tree (events bubble, context flows). This avoids clipping and stacking bugs.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Modal Dialog & Accessible Components

items.q: What keyboard interactions must an accessible modal support?
items.a: Focus moves into the dialog on open and is trapped (Tab/Shift+Tab cycle within), Escape closes it, and focus returns to the triggering element on close -- matching ARIA dialog expectations so keyboard and screen-reader users aren't stranded.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Modal Dialog & Accessible Components

items.q: How do you implement infinite scroll in React?
items.a: Observe a sentinel element at the list's end with IntersectionObserver (preferred over scroll listeners); when it intersects, fetch the next page (cursor/offset) and append. Guard with an 'isLoading' flag to avoid duplicate fetches, and stop when the API signals no more pages.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Infinite Scroll & List Virtualization

items.q: Why add list virtualization to a long list?
items.a: Rendering thousands of DOM nodes is slow and memory-heavy. Virtualization ('windowing') renders only rows in/near the viewport and recycles them as you scroll, keeping the DOM small and scrolling smooth regardless of dataset size.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Infinite Scroll & List Virtualization

items.q: IntersectionObserver vs a scroll event handler - why prefer the observer?
items.a: IntersectionObserver fires asynchronously off the main thread when a target enters the viewport, avoiding the jank and throttling complexity of high-frequency scroll handlers -- cleaner and more performant for triggering loads.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Infinite Scroll & List Virtualization

items.q: What makes autocomplete such a comprehensive interview question?
items.a: It exercises nearly everything: DOM and event handling, async data fetching, debouncing, accessibility (combobox ARIA + keyboard), CSS positioning, caching, and race-condition handling -- and it naturally extends into a system-design discussion about performance and APIs.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build an Autocomplete / Typeahead

items.q: How do you handle race conditions in an autocomplete?
items.a: Each keystroke can fire a request that resolves out of order; ignore stale responses by tracking the latest query (or an AbortController per request) and only applying a response if it matches the current input -- so an older slow response can't overwrite newer suggestions.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build an Autocomplete / Typeahead

items.q: What accessibility is expected for an autocomplete?
items.a: The WAI-ARIA combobox pattern: appropriate roles, aria-expanded, aria-controls, and aria- activedescendant for the highlighted option, plus keyboard support (Up/Down to move, Enter to select, Escape to close) so it works without a mouse.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Build an Autocomplete / Typeahead

items.q: How do you choose a React state-management approach in 2026?
items.a: Match tool to state type: React Query/TanStack for server data (caching/refetch/invalidation), useState/useReducer + Context for local/UI state, and a lightweight store (Zustand/Jotai) or Redux Toolkit for shared client state. Don't pick by popularity -- pick by how complex and how frequently the state changes.
items.topic: State Management Libraries: RTK, Zustand, Jotai & React Query

items.q: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit - when each?
items.a: Zustand: minimal API, tiny bundle (~1-3KB), no providers, fine-grained subscriptions -- great for small-to-medium apps and UI state. Redux Toolkit: opinionated, scalable, with devtools/time-travel, middleware, normalization, and RTK Query -- best for large, multi-team enterprise apps where structure and debugging outweigh bundle size.
items.topic: State Management Libraries: RTK, Zustand, Jotai & React Query

items.q: Why separate server state from client state?
items.a: Server data needs caching, background refetching, and invalidation -- exactly what React Query/SWR provide -- while client UI state (modals, toggles) just needs simple shared storage. Conflating them (e.g. caching API data in Redux by hand) causes stale data and re-render bugs; splitting them keeps each simpler.
items.topic: State Management Libraries: RTK, Zustand, Jotai & React Query

items.q: How do you build a file explorer / tree view in React?
items.a: Model the data as nested nodes; render a recursive Node component that shows the item and, if it's an expandable folder, renders its children via the same component. Track expanded folders (a Set of ids or per-node state), toggle on click, and indent by depth.

items.q: Why is recursion the natural fit, and what's the base case?
items.a: A tree is self-similar -- folders contain nodes that are themselves files or folders -- so a component that renders itself for children maps cleanly onto it. The base case is a file (leaf): render it and stop; folders recurse into children only when expanded.

items.q: How would you handle very large trees performantly?
items.a: Lazy-load children only when a folder is expanded (don't render the whole tree upfront), and virtualize the visible rows so the DOM stays small. Memoize nodes so toggling one branch doesn't re- render unrelated ones.

items.q: How do you implement drag-and-drop for a Kanban board?
items.a: Use the HTML Drag and Drop API (draggable items firing dragstart, columns handling dragover/drop) or a library like dnd-kit. On drop, immutably move the card from the source column/index to the target, updating both lists' order. Track the dragged item's id during the operation.

items.q: Why prefer dnd-kit over the raw HTML DnD API or react-beautiful-dnd?
items.a: dnd-kit is modern, lightweight, and built with accessibility and keyboard support in mind; the raw HTML DnD API is clunky and inconsistent across browsers, and react-beautiful-dnd is effectively unmaintained. dnd-kit handles sensors, collisions, and a11y for you.

items.q: What accessibility concerns does drag-and-drop raise?
items.a: Pointer-only DnD excludes keyboard and screen-reader users; an accessible board offers keyboard moves (pick up, move, drop) and ARIA live announcements of changes. dnd-kit provides keyboard sensors and announcements to support this.

items.q: What is the use() hook and how does it differ from other hooks?
items.a: use() reads a resource (a Promise or Context) during render and, unlike other hooks, may be called conditionally or in loops. With a Promise it suspends until resolution (works with Suspense); with Context it reads like useContext but without the call-position restriction.
items.topic: The use() Hook: Reading Promises & Context

items.q: What's the Server/Client pattern with use() and promises?
items.a: A Server Component can start data fetching and pass the unawaited Promise as a prop to a Client Component, which calls use(promise) to read it -- suspending until it resolves. This streams data without the client initiating the fetch or managing loading state manually.
items.topic: The use() Hook: Reading Promises & Context

items.q: Does use() replace useEffect for data fetching?
items.a: No. use() consumes a resource (often a promise created elsewhere, e.g. on the server or memoized) and integrates with Suspense; it's not for triggering effects or holding state. You still use state/effects for interactivity and side effects, and frameworks/loaders to create the promises.
items.topic: The use() Hook: Reading Promises & Context

items.q: What problem does useSyncExternalStore solve?
items.a: Safely subscribing to a store outside React while preventing 'tearing' -- where concurrent rendering could show different parts of the UI inconsistent values from the same store mid-render. It guarantees all components read a consistent snapshot, which a naive useState+useEffect subscription can't in concurrent mode.

items.q: What arguments does useSyncExternalStore take?
items.a: subscribe(callback): registers the callback to run on store changes and returns an unsubscribe function; getSnapshot(): returns the current store value (must be referentially stable when unchanged); and optionally getServerSnapshot() for SSR. React re-renders when notified and the snapshot differs.

items.q: Who uses useSyncExternalStore in practice?
items.a: State libraries (Zustand, Redux's react-redux, Jotai) use it internally to integrate with React's concurrent renderer correctly. App code uses it directly to subscribe to browser state (navigator.onLine, matchMedia) without tearing.

items.q: What is the compound components pattern?
items.a: Multiple components that work together as one unit, sharing implicit state through context (e.g. Tabs/Tab/TabPanel). The parent owns state and provides it via context; children consume it -- giving a flexible, expressive API where the consumer arranges the markup without prop-drilling.

items.q: Why use compound components over a single configurable component?
items.a: They give a more flexible, readable API: the consumer composes children freely (like HTML's select/option) instead of passing large config-prop objects. It avoids prop explosion and lets each part be placed/styled independently while sharing state.

items.q: How do compound components share state without prop drilling?
items.a: The parent creates a context and provides the shared state/handlers; each child component reads that context (often via a custom hook) instead of receiving props through intermediate elements -- keeping the public API clean while coordinating behavior internally.

items.q: What does useFormStatus do and where must it be used?
items.a: It reads the parent form's submission status (pending, data, method, action) so a child like a submit button can show a pending state without prop drilling or context. It only works in a component rendered INSIDE the <form>; called in the same component as the form, it sees no status.

items.q: What problem does useId solve?
items.a: It produces deterministic IDs identical on server and client, preventing hydration mismatches that arise from Math.random() or incremental counters. Use it to connect labels to inputs and for ARIA attributes in SSR apps.

items.q: Why must you not use useId for list keys?
items.a: useId returns one stable ID per component instance, not a unique value per iteration, so using it as a list key gives duplicate/incorrect keys. Keys should come from stable data identifiers (e.g. item.id); useId is for element ids/ARIA, not list identity.

items.q: How do you diagnose a React performance problem?
items.a: Measure first with the React DevTools Profiler: record interactions, read the flamegraph to find which components render, how long commits take, and why they rendered. Then fix the hot spots -- memoization, state locality, virtualization, code-splitting -- rather than optimizing blindly.
items.topic: Performance Profiling with the React DevTools Profiler

items.q: What does the Profiler tell you that guesswork can't?
items.a: Exactly which components re-rendered in a commit, the time each took, and the trigger (props/state/hooks/parent render). This pinpoints unnecessary re-renders and expensive subtrees so you optimize the actual bottleneck instead of guessing.
items.topic: Performance Profiling with the React DevTools Profiler

items.q: Common causes of excess re-renders the Profiler surfaces?
items.a: Unstable prop references (inline objects/arrays/functions) defeating React.memo, frequently- changing Context values re-rendering all consumers, and effects with overly broad dependency arrays running too often. Fixes: stabilize references, split/segment context, narrow deps.
items.topic: Performance Profiling with the React DevTools Profiler

items.q: What changed about caching defaults in Next.js 16?
items.a: Caching is now opt-in. Previously fetches were cached by default; in 16 everything runs at request time unless you explicitly mark it with 'use cache'.

items.q: What problem does Partial Prerendering solve?
items.a: It removes the per-route static-vs-dynamic tradeoff by serving a prerendered static shell immediately and streaming dynamic content into the same response.

items.q: How do you invalidate cached data in the new model?
items.a: Tag cached entries with cacheTag and purge them with updateTag, so you invalidate exactly the data that changed instead of rebuilding everything.

items.q: Explain SSR vs SSG vs ISR.
items.a: SSR renders HTML on each request (fresh, slower); SSG prebuilds at build time (fast, static); ISR serves static pages and regenerates them in the background after a set interval, combining speed with periodic freshness.

items.q: When would you choose SSR over SSG?
items.a: Choose SSR when content is personalized or changes per request (dashboards, auth-gated pages); choose SSG for stable content (docs, marketing) where speed and CDN caching matter most.

items.q: What does ISR's revalidate setting control?
items.a: How long a statically generated page is served before Next.js regenerates it in the background on the next request, trading absolute freshness for static performance.

items.q: What are Server Actions and why use them?
items.a: Server Actions are 'use server' functions that run on the server and can be invoked from client forms or handlers to mutate data. They remove boilerplate API routes and keep secrets server-side while supporting progressive enhancement.

items.q: How do you fetch data in a Server Component?
items.a: Make the component async and await your data source (DB or fetch) directly; the work runs on the server and only the rendered result ships to the client.

items.q: When do you still need a Route Handler?
items.a: For custom public API endpoints, webhooks, non-UI responses (files, streaming), or third-party integrations that need a stable URL rather than an in-app action.

items.q: What is Next.js middleware used for?
items.a: Code that runs before a request is completed -- used for authentication checks, redirects, rewrites, locale routing, and headers, often at the edge for low latency.

items.q: How does the App Router handle layouts and loading states?
items.a: Nested layout.tsx files wrap segments and persist across navigation; loading.tsx provides instant Suspense fallbacks; error.tsx isolates errors to a segment.

items.q: How does next/image optimize images?
items.a: It serves correctly sized, modern-format images, lazy-loads offscreen ones, and reserves space to prevent layout shift, improving Core Web Vitals automatically.

items.q: How does streaming work in the App Router?
items.a: The server renders the RSC tree and streams it in chunks; Suspense boundaries flush a ready shell first, then push slower parts as their data resolves, so users see content progressively instead of waiting for everything.
items.topic: App Router Internals: Streaming & RSC Payload

items.q: Why does the App Router send an RSC payload instead of HTML?
items.a: The serialized RSC payload lets React reconcile server output with existing client state during navigation without a full document reload, enabling partial rendering and persisted layouts.
items.topic: App Router Internals: Streaming & RSC Payload

items.q: How does client-side navigation stay fast?
items.a: The router prefetches route segments visible in the viewport and reuses persisted layouts, so only the changed segment is fetched and rendered on navigation.
items.topic: App Router Internals: Streaming & RSC Payload

items.q: How does the Metadata API improve SEO in Next.js?
items.a: You export static metadata or an async generateMetadata per route to set title, description, Open Graph, Twitter, and canonical tags -- colocated with the route and resolved on the server, so crawlers reliably get correct tags.

items.q: How do you generate dynamic Open Graph images?
items.a: Add an opengraph-image file (or use next/og's ImageResponse) in a route segment; Next.js generates a per-page social preview image at request/build time without an external service.

items.q: Why use next/font over a <link> to Google Fonts?
items.a: next/font self-hosts the font at build time, removing an external request and preventing layout shift by reserving space and inlining font CSS -- improving privacy and Core Web Vitals.

items.q: Where should you enforce auth in a Next.js app?
items.a: On the server: middleware for fast route-level gating, plus verification in Server Components/Route Handlers and inside Server Actions before any data access. Client checks are for UX only -- never the security boundary.

items.q: Why store sessions in httpOnly cookies rather than localStorage?
items.a: httpOnly cookies aren't readable by JavaScript, mitigating XSS token theft, and are sent automatically with requests. localStorage tokens are exposed to any script on the page.

items.q: How do you protect a Server Action?
items.a: Treat it like an API endpoint: re-check authentication and authorization inside the action before mutating, since it can be invoked directly -- don't rely on the calling component being gated.

items.q: How do you choose a rendering strategy for a given page?
items.a: Match freshness and personalization needs to cost: SSG/PPR for stable content (best LCP, cacheable), SSR for per-request/personalized data (fresher, higher TTFB), and reserve heavy client rendering for interactive widgets. Often mix them per route with PPR.
items.topic: Rendering Strategy Tradeoffs & Core Web Vitals

items.q: What are the Core Web Vitals and what replaced FID?
items.a: LCP (loading -- largest contentful paint), INP (responsiveness -- interaction to next paint, which replaced First Input Delay in 2024), and CLS (visual stability -- cumulative layout shift). Good scores correlate with UX and SEO.
items.topic: Rendering Strategy Tradeoffs & Core Web Vitals

items.q: A page has poor LCP - how do you diagnose and fix it in Next.js?
items.a: Find the LCP element (often a hero image), then prioritize it (next/image priority), serve modern formats and correct sizes, preconnect to origins, reduce render-blocking JS/CSS, and prefer server rendering of the shell so the main content paints fast.
items.topic: Rendering Strategy Tradeoffs & Core Web Vitals

items.q: Node.js runtime vs Edge runtime in Next.js?
items.a: Node runtime gives full Node APIs and libraries for general server work; Edge runtime is a smaller Web-API environment that runs globally with very fast cold starts, ideal for middleware and latency- sensitive logic -- but can't use Node-only APIs.

items.q: How are environment variables exposed safely?
items.a: Variables are server-only by default; only those prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ are inlined into the client bundle. Never put secrets in NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars since they ship to the browser.

items.q: What deployment options does Next.js support?
items.a: Vercel (zero-config native), a self-hosted Node server (next start), a Docker container, or static export (output: 'export') for fully static sites without a server -- chosen by infra and rendering needs.

items.q: What do loading.tsx and error.tsx do in the App Router?
items.a: loading.tsx auto-wraps a segment in Suspense, showing a fallback while it loads; error.tsx is a client component that catches errors thrown while rendering that segment and shows a recoverable error UI with a reset() to retry.

items.q: How do you trigger and render a 404 in Next.js?
items.a: Call notFound() in a server component/route to throw the not-found state, and provide not- found.tsx to render the 404 UI for that segment or unmatched routes.

items.q: Why are these scoped per segment?
items.a: Because the App Router nests boundaries: a loading or error state wraps only its segment, so a slow or failing part shows a localized fallback while the rest of the page stays interactive.

items.q: How do you structure i18n routing in Next.js?
items.a: Use a locale segment in the path (/en/..., /fr/...), detect the preferred locale in middleware (from the Accept-Language header or a cookie) and redirect, then load the matching message catalog per request so content renders translated on the server.

items.q: What's the difference between internationalization and localization?
items.a: Internationalization (i18n) is designing the app so it CAN support multiple locales (externalized strings, locale-aware formatting); localization (l10n) is the actual adaptation for a specific locale -- translations, formats, and cultural conventions.

items.q: How do you format dates, numbers, and currency per locale?
items.a: Use the built-in Intl APIs (Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat) with the active locale, rather than hardcoding formats -- they handle separators, currency symbols, and conventions correctly.

items.q: What replaced middleware.ts in Next.js 16, and why?
items.a:
proxy.ts -- a more explicit, Node.js-native request-handling file. The rename clarifies intent and improves predictability, security, and maintainability over the older middleware approach.

 Q. What performance gains did Next.js 16.2 deliver?

 A. Roughly 87% faster dev server startup vs 16.1 (~4x), ~50% faster server-side rendering, 20x faster ImageResponse for complex images, and 200+ Turbopack fixes -- on top of Turbopack being the default bundler.
items.topic: Next.js 16.2: DevTools MCP, proxy.ts & Latest Perf

items.q: What is the Next.js DevTools MCP?
items.a: A Model Context Protocol integration that brings AI-assisted, context-aware debugging into Next.js DevTools, helping teams diagnose issues faster with richer insight into the running app.
items.topic: Next.js 16.2: DevTools MCP, proxy.ts & Latest Perf

items.q: How do you pass data between routes in the Next.js App Router?
items.a: Use URL search params for shareable/bookmarkable state (searchParams prop or useSearchParams), route (path) params for identifiers, and server-side fetching on the destination for shared data. Reserve client state/context for ephemeral UI state -- avoid pushing large payloads through navigation.
items.topic: Data Passing, Search Params & SEO Patterns

items.q: Why prefer search params over client state for some data?
items.a: Search params live in the URL, so the state is shareable, bookmarkable, survives refresh, and is server-readable for SSR/SEO -- unlike in-memory client state that's lost on reload and invisible to the server.
items.topic: Data Passing, Search Params & SEO Patterns

items.q: How is SEO metadata handled in the App Router?
items.a: Via the Metadata API: export a static metadata object or an async generateMetadata per route to set title, description, Open Graph, and canonical tags on the server -- replacing manual <Head> management and ensuring crawlers get correct tags.
items.topic: Data Passing, Search Params & SEO Patterns

items.q: How do you prevent leaking private data from Server Components?
items.a: Use a Data Access Layer that performs authorization and returns minimal DTOs (only public fields), mark server-only modules with the server-only package so client imports fail at build time, and never pass raw DB records to Client Components.

items.q: What does the 'server-only' package do?
items.a: It causes a build-time error if a module meant for the server (secrets, DB access, proprietary logic) is imported into a Client Component -- preventing accidental 'environment poisoning' where server code/secrets ship to the browser.

items.q: Where do you enforce authorization in Next.js, and why not the client?
items.a: On the server: middleware for route gating plus per-request checks in Server Components/Actions/Route Handlers. Client checks only control UI and are trivially bypassed, so they're never the security boundary.

items.q: How do you prevent stale results in an autocomplete?
items.a: Cancel the in-flight request when a newer query starts -- use an AbortController per request and abort the previous one (or track a request id and ignore out-of-order responses) so a slow earlier response can't overwrite newer suggestions.
items.topic: Building an Autocomplete / Typeahead in Next.js

items.q: Where should the suggestion API call live in Next.js?
items.a: Behind a Route Handler or Server Action that proxies the upstream API, so API keys stay server-side and you can add caching/rate-limiting -- the client calls your endpoint, not the third party directly.
items.topic: Building an Autocomplete / Typeahead in Next.js

items.q: What accessibility and UX states does an autocomplete need?
items.a: Combobox semantics (role, aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant), keyboard up/down/enter/escape handling, and explicit loading, empty ('no results'), and error states -- not just the happy path.
items.topic: Building an Autocomplete / Typeahead in Next.js

items.q: How would you architect a secure dashboard in Next.js?
items.a: Fetch data in Server Components (server-side, secrets stay server), enforce auth in middleware before the route renders, and use Client Components only for interactive elements (charts, filters, form actions). This minimizes client JS and keeps sensitive logic off the browser.
items.topic: Building Production Features: Patterns from Interview Prep Sites

items.q: What production issues commonly surface in Next.js apps?
items.a: Stale data from misconfigured revalidation/caching, environment-variable mismatches between local and prod, and API timeouts or rate limits -- often visible only under real traffic. Logs and monitoring are how you diagnose them.
items.topic: Building Production Features: Patterns from Interview Prep Sites

items.q: How do you keep routing scalable in a large App Router app?
items.a: Use nested layouts to share chrome without duplication, route groups to organize sections, and dynamic segments for parameterized routes -- keeping URLs clean and the folder structure mirroring the UI hierarchy.
items.topic: Building Production Features: Patterns from Interview Prep Sites

items.q: How do you implement sorting, filtering, and pagination for a large table in Next.js?
items.a: Push sort/filter/page into URL search params and fetch the current page server-side (server pagination) so you never load the whole dataset. For small data, do it client-side with derived state. Debounce the filter input and render loading/empty/error states.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Data Table with Sort, Filter & Pagination

items.q: Why drive table state through URL search params?
items.a: So the table's sort/filter/page is shareable, bookmarkable, survives refresh, and is readable on the server for SSR -- versus client-only state that's lost on reload and invisible to server rendering.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Data Table with Sort, Filter & Pagination

items.q: What are the accessibility and UX must-haves for a data table?
items.a: Semantic table markup (thead/th with scope, caption), sortable headers exposing aria-sort, keyboard-operable controls, and explicit loading, empty ('no results'), and error states rather than a blank grid.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Data Table with Sort, Filter & Pagination

items.q: How do you implement a basic image carousel?
items.a: Keep the active index in state; prev/next handlers update it with wraparound ((i + n) % total); render the current image (or translate a track) and dot indicators reflecting the index. Add a transition for the slide animation.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Image Carousel & Media Components

items.q: How do you add autoplay correctly, and why is cleanup critical?
items.a: Start an interval in useEffect that advances the index, return a cleanup that clears it, and pause on hover/focus. Without cleanup the interval leaks and stacks across renders/unmounts, causing erratic advancing and memory leaks.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Image Carousel & Media Components

items.q: How does next/image improve a carousel's performance?
items.a: It serves correctly sized, modern-format images, lazy-loads offscreen slides, and reserves space to prevent layout shift -- improving LCP/CLS versus raw tags, which matters when a carousel holds many images.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Image Carousel & Media Components

items.q: What are parallel routes and when do you use them?
items.a: Parallel routes render multiple independent page sections in one layout at the same time via named slots (folders like @analytics, @team), each with its own loading and error handling. Use them for dashboards or split views where sections load and fail independently.

items.q: What problem do intercepting routes solve?
items.a: They let you load a route within the current page's context instead of a full navigation -- e.g. opening a photo in a modal overlay when clicked from a feed, while a direct link or refresh to that URL shows the full standalone page. You keep shareable URLs and modal UX simultaneously.

items.q: How do the intercepting-route folder conventions work?
items.a: Prefixes mirror relative paths: (.) intercepts a route at the same level, (..) one level up, (..)(..) two levels up, and (...) from the root. The matched segment renders in place (e.g. in a @modal slot) rather than navigating away.

items.q: How do you compute the days grid for a calendar month?
items.a: From the selected year/month: get the weekday of the first day (to know how many leading blanks), the number of days in the month, and fill a grid of weeks. new Date(year, month+1, 0).getDate() gives days in month; new Date(year, month, 1).getDay() gives the starting weekday offset.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Calendar / Date Picker Component

items.q: What edge cases must a date picker handle?
items.a: Leap years (Feb 29), configurable week start (Sun vs Mon), min/max selectable dates, disabled dates, month/year boundary navigation, and timezone pitfalls -- work with local date parts (year/month/day) rather than UTC timestamps to avoid off-by-one-day bugs.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Calendar / Date Picker Component

items.q: How do you make a calendar accessible?
items.a: Use a grid role with appropriate roles for cells, aria-label each day (full date), mark the selected and today's date with aria-selected/aria-current, and support keyboard navigation (arrows move days, Enter selects) so it's operable without a mouse.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Calendar / Date Picker Component

items.q: What are Route Handlers and how do they differ from the old API routes?
items.a:
route.ts files in the App Router exporting method-named functions (GET/POST/...) that take a Web Request and return a Web Response -- replacing pages/api. They use Web standard APIs, support both runtimes and streaming, and integrate with App Router caching.

 Q. When do you use a Route Handler vs a Server Action?

 A. Route Handlers are addressable HTTP endpoints -- for webhooks, public APIs, proxying third-party services, or anything external must call by URL. Server Actions are RPC-style functions invoked from your own components for mutations, without a manual endpoint. Use handlers for URL-addressable APIs, actions for in-app mutations.
items.topic: Route Handlers: Building APIs in the App Router

items.q: How does caching work for a GET Route Handler?
items.a: A GET handler can be statically cached by default in some setups; you control it with route segment config (e.g. dynamic = 'force-dynamic' to always run, or revalidate for ISR-like behavior). Methods other than GET are never cached. Be explicit about caching for data freshness.
items.topic: Route Handlers: Building APIs in the App Router

items.q: What are the Core Web Vitals and their targets?
items.a: LCP (largest contentful paint, loading - good < 2.5s), INP (interaction to next paint, responsiveness - good < 200ms, replaced FID in 2024), and CLS (cumulative layout shift, visual stability - good < 0.1). They quantify real user experience and influence SEO ranking.
items.topic: Web Performance: Core Web Vitals & Optimization Techniques

items.q: How do you prevent layout shift (CLS)?
items.a: Reserve space for images/embeds/ads by setting explicit width/height or aspect-ratio, avoid inserting content above existing content after load, use font-display strategies to avoid invisible-text reflow, and prefer transform-based animations over ones that change layout.
items.topic: Web Performance: Core Web Vitals & Optimization Techniques

items.q: How do you improve INP (responsiveness)?
items.a: Keep the main thread free: break up long JavaScript tasks (yield with scheduler/setTimeout), defer or offload non-critical work (Web Workers), minimize hydration cost, and avoid heavy synchronous handlers -- so the UI can respond to interactions quickly.
items.topic: Web Performance: Core Web Vitals & Optimization Techniques

items.q: What is the Cache Components model in Next.js 16?
items.a: With cacheComponents enabled, nothing is cached implicitly; you explicitly mark cacheable components/functions/pages with the 'use cache' directive. It combines with Partial Pre-Rendering so a static shell serves instantly while dynamic parts stream -- making caching explicit and predictable instead of the older implicit defaults.

items.q: How do you control cache freshness and invalidation under 'use cache'?
items.a: Use cacheLife() to set the lifetime/SWR behavior of a cached unit (presets or custom), and revalidateTag() to invalidate by tag -- note revalidateTag now needs a cacheLife to enable stale-while- revalidate. The older route-segment revalidate config is deprecated when cacheComponents is on.

items.q: What is Partial Pre-Rendering (PPR) and why does it matter?
items.a: PPR pre-renders a static shell of a page and serves it instantly, then streams the dynamic parts ('holes') as they resolve -- combining static speed with dynamic data. On suitable pages it can cut initial load substantially versus a fully dynamic render.

items.q: What changed with the bundler in Next.js 16?
items.a:
Turbopack is now the stable, default bundler for both dev and production -- roughly 5-10x faster Fast Refresh and 2-5x faster builds. Webpack isn't removed but is no longer default; fall back with next dev --webpack / next build --webpack only if you have unmigrated Webpack-specific config.

 Q. Is the React Compiler safe to enable, and what does it do?

 A. React Compiler 1.0 is stable. Enabled via reactCompiler: true, it auto-memoizes to cut needless re- renders, removing most manual useMemo/useCallback. It only transforms code following the Rules of React and skips (with a warning) components with render side effects or direct mutation, so it won't silently miscompile -- but test in CI as it adds build time.
items.topic: Next.js 16 Migration: Turbopack Default & React Compiler 1.0

items.q: What are the key breaking changes migrating from Next.js 15 to 16?
items.a: middleware.ts becomes proxy.ts (network-level, Node runtime by default; auth/business logic moves into route handlers/layouts/actions), parallel route slots now require default.js, request APIs (cookies/headers/params) are async and must be awaited, Turbopack is default, and there are container memory-behavior changes. Official codemods handle most of it.
items.topic: Next.js 16 Migration: Turbopack Default & React Compiler 1.0

items.q: What is a Pod and why not run containers directly?
items.a: A Pod is the smallest schedulable unit: one or more tightly-coupled containers sharing network and storage. Kubernetes schedules, restarts, and scales Pods, giving self-healing and a consistent unit.

items.q: How does a Deployment differ from a ReplicaSet?
items.a: A ReplicaSet keeps a fixed number of identical Pods running. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to add declarative updates, rolling releases, and rollbacks.

items.q: What is the role of etcd?
items.a: etcd is the distributed key-value store that holds the cluster's entire state as the single source of truth; the API server reads and writes it.

items.q: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
items.a: Both automate testing and building; Continuous Delivery stops at a release-ready artifact requiring a manual approval to ship, while Continuous Deployment automatically releases every passing change to production.

items.q: What stages belong in a typical CI pipeline?
items.a: Checkout, install, lint, unit and integration tests, build/package (often a container image), security scan, and publish the artifact -- failing fast at the earliest broken stage.

items.q: How do you achieve safe rollbacks?
items.a: Deploy immutable versioned artifacts with strategies like blue-green or canary, keep the previous version available, and automate reverting traffic when health checks fail.

items.q: What's the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
items.a: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS; a container shares the host kernel and isolates only the process and filesystem. Containers are smaller, start faster, and pack more densely, but share the host kernel.

items.q: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
items.a: An image is an immutable, layered template built from a Dockerfile; a container is a running (or stopped) instance of that image with a writable layer on top.

items.q: Why use multi-stage Docker builds?
items.a: To compile or build in one stage with full tooling, then copy only the artifacts into a minimal final image -- shrinking image size and attack surface.

items.q: When would you choose CloudFormation over Terraform?
items.a: CloudFormation suits AWS-only, compliance-heavy setups with deep native integration and AWS- managed state; Terraform suits multi-cloud, modular reuse, and teams who value HCL's expressiveness and a large module registry.
items.topic: Infrastructure as Code: Terraform vs CloudFormation

items.q: What is Terraform state and why does it matter?
items.a: State maps your config to real resources so Terraform knows what to create, change, or destroy. It's stored remotely (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB lock) to enable team collaboration and prevent concurrent corruption.
items.topic: Infrastructure as Code: Terraform vs CloudFormation

items.q: How do you test/validate IaC before applying?
items.a: Lint (tflint/cfn-lint), scan for misconfigurations (tfsec, Checkov, cfn_nag), run terraform plan or change sets to preview, and apply in a non-prod environment first.
items.topic: Infrastructure as Code: Terraform vs CloudFormation

items.q: What are the three pillars of observability?
items.a: Logs (timestamped discrete events), metrics (numeric aggregates over time like CPU or request rate), and traces (the end-to-end path and timing of a request across services). Together they explain what happened and why.

items.q: How does monitoring differ from observability?
items.a: Monitoring tracks predefined signals and alerts when they cross thresholds (known unknowns); observability lets you explore and diagnose novel problems you didn't anticipate (unknown unknowns) from rich telemetry.

items.q: What are SLO, SLI, and error budget?
items.a: An SLI is a measured indicator (e.g. success rate); an SLO is the target for it (e.g. 99.9%); the error budget is the allowed shortfall, guiding how aggressively you can ship versus stabilize.

items.q: Trunk-based development vs GitFlow - when each?
items.a: Trunk-based (short-lived branches, frequent merges to main) suits continuous delivery and fast feedback; GitFlow (long-lived develop/release branches) suits scheduled, versioned releases. Most CI/CD-heavy teams favor trunk-based.

items.q: What's the difference between merge and rebase?
items.a: Merge keeps both histories and adds a merge commit; rebase replays your commits onto a new base for a clean linear history but rewrites commit hashes -- avoid rebasing shared/public branches.

items.q: How do feature flags help deployment?
items.a: They decouple deploy from release: code ships dark and is toggled on later, enabling gradual rollouts, A/B tests, and instant rollback without redeploying.

items.q: How should secrets be managed in a CI/CD pipeline?
items.a: Store them in a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) and inject at runtime with least- privilege access and rotation -- never commit them or bake them into images. Use the CI's encrypted secret store for pipeline credentials.

items.q: What is 'shift left' in security?
items.a: Moving security checks earlier -- into development and CI (dependency scanning, SAST, image scanning, secret detection) -- so issues are caught before production rather than after deployment.

items.q: How do you reduce supply-chain risk in dependencies?
items.a: Pin versions with lockfiles, scan with SCA tools (Snyk, Dependabot, Trivy), verify integrity, generate an SBOM, and sign artifacts so you can trust and trace what ships.

items.q: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling - compare them.
items.a: Rolling: gradually replace instances (available, but mixed versions). Blue-green: two full environments, switch traffic at once for instant rollback. Canary: send a small % to the new version, watch metrics, then ramp. Choose by rollback speed, cost, and risk tolerance.

items.q: How does a canary release reduce risk?
items.a: By exposing the new version to a small slice of traffic first and monitoring error rates/latency, you catch regressions affecting few users and can roll back before a full rollout.

items.q: What makes safe deployments possible regardless of strategy?
items.a: Clear health checks, automated rollback on failed checks, immutable versioned artifacts, and feature flags to decouple deploy from release so you can disable a feature without redeploying.

items.q: What's the difference between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing?
items.a: L4 balances on TCP/UDP (IP/port) -- fast, protocol-agnostic; L7 balances on application data (HTTP path, host, headers) -- enabling content-based routing, TLS termination, and smarter rules at some overhead.
items.topic: Networking Fundamentals: DNS, Load Balancing & HTTP

items.q: How does DNS resolution work at a high level?
items.a: A resolver walks from root to TLD to the authoritative nameserver to get the domain's record (e.g. an A record's IP), caching by TTL. DNS can also route traffic via policies (latency, geo, failover).
items.topic: Networking Fundamentals: DNS, Load Balancing & HTTP

items.q: What does TLS/HTTPS provide?
items.a: Encryption (confidentiality), integrity, and server authentication via certificates, so traffic can't be read or tampered with in transit. TLS termination often happens at the load balancer or reverse proxy.
items.topic: Networking Fundamentals: DNS, Load Balancing & HTTP

items.q: Microservices vs monolith - tradeoffs?
items.a: Monolith: simpler to develop, test, and deploy initially, but couples scaling and releases. Microservices: independent deploy/scale and team autonomy, at the cost of network complexity, distributed data, and heavier observability needs. Choose by scale, team size, and domain boundaries -- don't default to micro.

items.q: How do microservices communicate?
items.a: Synchronously via REST or gRPC for request/response, and asynchronously via message queues or event streams (SQS, Kafka) for decoupling. Async improves resilience; sync is simpler but couples availability.

items.q: What is a circuit breaker and why use it?
items.a: A pattern that stops calling a failing downstream service after a threshold, returning fast/fallback responses to prevent cascading failures and giving the service time to recover.

items.q: Horizontal vs vertical scaling - tradeoffs?
items.a: Vertical (bigger machine) is simple but capped and a single point of failure; horizontal (more machines behind a balancer) scales elastically and adds redundancy but requires stateless services and coordination. Most cloud designs prefer horizontal.

items.q: Where can you cache in a typical web architecture?
items.a: Browser/client cache, CDN edge cache (static assets), a reverse-proxy cache, an application cache like Redis (hot data/sessions), and database result/query caches -- each cutting work closer to the user.

items.q: Why is cache invalidation hard?
items.a: Stale data must be refreshed at the right time without serving wrong results or thundering-herd refetches. Strategies (TTLs, tag/key invalidation, write-through) trade freshness, complexity, and load -- there's no free correct-and-fast option.

items.q: What is platform engineering and how does it relate to DevOps?
items.a: A discipline where a platform team builds an Internal Developer Platform with self-service golden paths, reducing developers' cognitive load. It builds on DevOps culture -- DevOps is the philosophy; the IDP is the productized tooling that scales it across teams.

items.q: What is an Internal Developer Platform (IDP)?
items.a: A self-service layer (often with a portal like Backstage) giving developers templated, guardrailed paths to provision environments, pipelines, and services without filing tickets or mastering infra -- standardizing how teams ship.

items.q: What is a 'golden path' / paved road?
items.a: A recommended, well-supported, pre-configured way to build and deploy a service -- templates and defaults that bake in best practices and security, so the easy path is also the correct one.

items.q: What is GitOps?
items.a: An operating model where Git is the source of truth for desired system state; an agent (Argo CD, Flux) continuously reconciles the live environment to match the repo. Deployments become reviewed Git commits, giving audit trail, consistency, and rollback by revert.

items.q: How does GitOps enable easy rollback and self-healing?
items.a: Because desired state is versioned in Git, rolling back is reverting to a previous commit; the agent reconciles the cluster to it. The same reconciliation detects drift (manual changes) and self-heals by restoring the declared state.

items.q: Push-based CD vs pull-based GitOps - difference?
items.a: Push: the pipeline pushes changes into the cluster (needs cluster credentials in CI). Pull: an in- cluster agent pulls the desired state from Git and applies it, improving security and continuous drift correction.

items.q: How do you approach a frontend system design question?
items.a: Clarify requirements/scale first, then reason through rendering strategy per page, state architecture (global UI vs server state), component boundaries and design system, data fetching/caching, and cross-cutting concerns (performance, a11y, security) -- narrating tradeoffs rather than jumping to one 'right' answer.

items.q: How do you separate global UI state from server state?
items.a: Keep server state (fetched, cacheable, shared) in a data layer like React Query/SWR with caching and revalidation; keep ephemeral global UI state (theme, modals, selection) in context or a light store. Conflating them causes stale data and re-render issues.

items.q: What cross-cutting concerns matter in frontend architecture?
items.a: Performance (code-splitting, lazy loading, web vitals), accessibility, security (XSS/CSP, safe data handling), error/loading boundaries, observability, and how the codebase scales as teams and features grow.

items.q: What is the RADIO framework for frontend system design?
items.a: Requirements (clarify scope, users, scale), Architecture (components and how they interact), Data model, Interface (component props + network/API contracts), and Optimizations (performance, accessibility, edge cases) -- a structured way to drive the discussion and cover what interviewers grade.

items.q: How would you design an infinite-scrolling feed?
items.a: Cursor/offset pagination from the API, IntersectionObserver to load the next page near the bottom, list virtualization to keep the DOM small, image lazy-loading, optimistic UI for actions (like), and handling loading/error/empty states -- discussing tradeoffs of each.

items.q: What are key optimizations to raise in a typeahead design?
items.a: Debounced input, cancelable/abortable requests to avoid stale results, client/result caching, list virtualization for large result sets, accessible combobox semantics, and graceful loading/empty/error states.

items.q: What are the most common DSA patterns to know?
items.a: Two pointers, sliding window, hashing (O(n) lookup), BFS/DFS (trees/graphs), binary search (sorted data or answer space), and dynamic programming (memoization/tabulation). Recognizing which pattern fits a problem is the core skill interviewers test.

items.q: How do you analyze time and space complexity?
items.a: Express how runtime/memory grow with input size n in Big-O, counting dominant operations (nested loops -> O(n^2), halving -> O(log n), single pass -> O(n)). State both time and space, and the worst case, then discuss tradeoffs (e.g. a hash map trades space for time).

items.q: How should you approach a DSA problem in an interview?
items.a: Clarify inputs/constraints/edge cases, state a brute-force then optimize, identify the pattern/data structure, talk through the approach and complexity before coding, then implement and test with examples -- communication is graded alongside correctness.

items.q: What do the main HTTP methods and their idempotency mean?
items.a: GET (read, safe + idempotent), POST (create, not idempotent), PUT (replace, idempotent), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove, idempotent). Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as once -- important for safe retries.
items.topic: API Design & Testing: REST, Status Codes & Contracts

items.q: Which status codes should an API use and when?
items.a: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 4xx client errors (400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 429 too many requests), 5xx server errors (500, 503). Consistent, correct codes make the API predictable and testable.
items.topic: API Design & Testing: REST, Status Codes & Contracts

items.q: What is contract testing and why does it matter for microservices?
items.a: It verifies that a service (producer) and its consumers agree on the request/response shape (e.g. with Pact), catching breaking API changes before deploy -- crucial when independently-deployed services must stay compatible.
items.topic: API Design & Testing: REST, Status Codes & Contracts

items.q: How would you design a front-end autocomplete component (system design)?
items.a: Walk RADIO: requirements (latency, scale), architecture (input -> debounce -> cache -> API -> results), data model and API (query/limit, response shape), interface (combobox a11y), and optimizations: debounce, per-query caching, race-condition handling, list virtualization, and result ranking. Discuss tradeoffs of each.
items.topic: Front-End System Design: Autocomplete & News Feed (Deep Dive)

items.q: What are the key design considerations for an infinite news feed?
items.a: Cursor-based pagination, infinite scroll via IntersectionObserver, list virtualization to cap DOM size, normalized client cache for feed items, optimistic UI for actions (like/comment), image lazy-loading, and a freshness strategy (poll vs websockets) -- plus loading/error/empty states.
items.topic: Front-End System Design: Autocomplete & News Feed (Deep Dive)

items.q: Polling vs websockets for feed freshness - how to choose?
items.a: Polling (periodic fetch) is simple and fine for low-frequency updates; websockets give real-time push for high-frequency/interactive feeds at the cost of connection management and server complexity. Choose by update frequency and interactivity needs.
items.topic: Front-End System Design: Autocomplete & News Feed (Deep Dive)

items.q: How do you recognize a dynamic programming problem?
items.a: It has overlapping subproblems (the same sub-results recur) and optimal substructure (the optimal solution builds from optimal sub-solutions). Signals: 'count the ways', 'min/max cost', 'can you reach'. Solve top-down with memoization or bottom-up with tabulation, caching subproblem answers.

items.q: What is backtracking and when do you use it?
items.a: A recursive enumerate-and-prune technique: try a choice, recurse, and undo it if it can't lead to a valid/optimal solution. Use it for generating permutations, combinations, subsets, and constraint problems like N-Queens or Sudoku -- pruning invalid branches early to cut the search space.

items.q: Top-down memoization vs bottom-up tabulation?
items.a: Top-down: natural recursion plus a cache of computed subproblems (lazy, only computes needed states). Bottom-up: iteratively fill a table from base cases up (no recursion overhead, easy to reason about space). Same complexity; choose by clarity and whether all states are needed.

items.q: How do you merge overlapping intervals?
items.a: Sort intervals by start time, then scan once keeping a current merged interval: if the next interval's start <= current end, they overlap -- extend current end to max(current end, next end); otherwise push current and start a new one. O(n log n) from the sort.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Merge Intervals & Sweep Line

items.q: What other problems use the interval / sweep-line pattern?
items.a: Insert interval into a sorted list, remove minimum intervals to make the rest non-overlapping (greedy by end time), meeting rooms (minimum rooms via sweeping start/end events), and interval- list intersections -- all variations of sort-then-sweep.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Merge Intervals & Sweep Line

items.q: Why sort by start time first?
items.a: Sorting guarantees that when you scan, any interval that could overlap the current one comes adjacent, so a single linear pass suffices to detect and merge overlaps -- without sorting you'd need to compare every pair (O(n^2)).
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Merge Intervals & Sweep Line

items.q: Merge vs rebase - what's the difference and when use each?
items.a: Merge combines branches and records a merge commit, preserving true history; rebase replays your commits onto another base for a clean linear history. Use merge for shared/public branches (don't rewrite shared history); rebase locally to tidy your branch before merging.

items.q: git reset vs git revert - when do you use each?
items.a: reset moves the branch pointer (--soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstages, --hard discards) and rewrites history -- safe only locally. revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous one without rewriting history -- the safe choice for shared/public branches.

items.q: What does interactive rebase let you do?
items.a: git rebase -i lets you reorder, squash/fixup, edit, or drop commits before merging -- producing a clean, meaningful history (e.g. squashing 'wip' commits into one). Done on your own branch before sharing, not on public history.

items.q: How do fast and slow pointers detect a linked-list cycle?
items.a: Advance one pointer by 1 and another by 2 each step; if there's a cycle they eventually meet (the fast pointer laps the slow one), otherwise fast reaches the end. To find the cycle start, reset one pointer to head and advance both by 1 until they meet again. O(n) time, O(1) space.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Fast & Slow Pointers and Prefix Sums

items.q: How do prefix sums make range queries O(1)?
items.a: Precompute prefix[i] = sum of the first i elements; then any range sum [i, j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i] in O(1) after O(n) setup. With a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies you count subarrays summing to k in a single pass.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Fast & Slow Pointers and Prefix Sums

items.q: Why use fast/slow pointers over a hash set for cycle detection?
items.a: Both find a cycle, but fast/slow uses O(1) extra space versus O(n) for a hash set of visited nodes. When the interviewer asks for constant space, Floyd's algorithm is the expected answer, and it also locates the cycle's start and the list's middle.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Fast & Slow Pointers and Prefix Sums

items.q: How would you design a scalable web crawler?
items.a: Seed a URL frontier (priority + politeness queue); a pool of fetchers pulls URLs, downloads pages, a parser extracts links back into the frontier, and content is stored. Add URL/content dedup (hashes, Bloom filter for seen URLs), robots.txt + per-domain rate limiting (politeness), trap detection, and re- crawl scheduling for freshness -- all distributed acros...

items.q: Why use a Bloom filter in a web crawler?
items.a: To check 'have we seen this URL?' across billions of URLs using minimal memory. A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic set: no false negatives, small false-positive rate -- acceptable for skipping likely-seen URLs without storing them all, which an exact set couldn't fit in memory.

items.q: What is crawler 'politeness' and how do you enforce it?
items.a: Not overloading any single server: honor robots.txt rules, limit concurrent requests and rate per domain, and space out repeat visits. The URL frontier is designed so URLs from the same host aren't fetched too frequently, often via per-host queues with delays.

items.q: How do you treat a matrix as a graph for traversal problems?
items.a: Each cell is a node; its up/down/left/right (and sometimes diagonal) neighbors are edges. Use BFS for shortest path / level expansion (e.g. rotting oranges, shortest path in a grid) and DFS for connected regions (number of islands, flood fill), with a visited set or in-place marking and careful bounds checks.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Matrix/Grid Traversal & String Algorithms

items.q: How do you rotate an NxN matrix 90 degrees in place?
items.a: Transpose it (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]) then reverse each row - this rotates clockwise in O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space. Reversing columns instead (or transposing the other diagonal) gives counter-clockwise.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Matrix/Grid Traversal & String Algorithms

items.q: What does the KMP algorithm improve over naive string matching?
items.a: Naive matching re-scans after each mismatch (O(n*m)). KMP precomputes a prefix/failure function so on a mismatch it skips ahead using already-matched characters, never re-examining text it has passed - O(n+m). Rabin-Karp instead uses a rolling hash, good for multiple-pattern or streaming search.
items.topic: DSA Patterns: Matrix/Grid Traversal & String Algorithms

items.q: How would you design a video streaming service like YouTube/Netflix?
items.a: Upload originals to object storage; a transcoding pipeline (queue + worker fleet) produces multiple bitrates/resolutions segmented for HLS/DASH. Serve segments via a CDN from edge locations (the key to low latency and bandwidth cost). Store metadata in databases, and run recommendations and view-count aggregation as separate services. The player adapts bitr...

items.q: What is adaptive bitrate streaming and why does it matter?
