items.a: The video is encoded at several bitrates and chopped into short segments (HLS/DASH); the player monitors bandwidth and switches to a higher/lower-quality segment per chunk. This avoids buffering on poor connections and uses full quality on good ones, improving perceived performance.

items.q: Why is the CDN the most important component for streaming?
items.a: Video is huge and latency-sensitive; serving every byte from origin would be slow and prohibitively expensive. A CDN caches segments at edge locations close to users, cutting latency and origin/bandwidth load dramatically - it's the dominant factor in streaming cost and performance.

items.q: How do you design an LFU cache with O(1) operations?
items.a: Maintain a key->node map, a frequency->doubly-linked-list map (nodes at each use-count, ordered by recency), and a running minFreq. get/put move a node to the next frequency bucket; eviction removes the LRU node from the minFreq bucket. The hash maps plus DLLs give O(1) get and put.
items.topic: DSA: Designing Data Structures (LFU, O(1) getRandom, Min Stack)

items.q: How do you support insert, delete, and getRandom all in O(1)?
items.a: Store values in a dynamic array (for O(1) random index) and a value->index hash map (for O(1) locate). To delete, swap the target with the last array element, update that element's index in the map, then pop the array end -- avoiding an O(n) shift.
items.topic: DSA: Designing Data Structures (LFU, O(1) getRandom, Min Stack)

items.q: How does a Min Stack return the minimum in O(1)?
items.a: Alongside each pushed value, store the minimum so far (or keep a parallel stack of minima). Push records min(value, currentMin); pop removes both; getMin reads the top min in O(1). Trades O(n) extra space for constant-time min queries.
items.topic: DSA: Designing Data Structures (LFU, O(1) getRandom, Min Stack)

items.q: How do you prevent double charging in a payment system?
items.a: Enforce idempotency: the client generates an idempotency key per payment intent; the payment service deduplicates on it so retries (from timeouts/network errors) map to the same single charge. Combined with a ledger and PSP idempotent APIs, a retry never creates a second payment.
items.topic: System Design: Payment System (Ledgers, Idempotency & Reconciliation)

items.q: Why is reconciliation necessary even with idempotent APIs?
items.a: Because you can't assume the external system (PSP/bank) is always right or in sync -- replication lag, partial failures, or discrepancies happen. Nightly reconciliation compares your ledger against the PSP's settlement files and flags mismatches for investigation, ensuring the books are correct.
items.topic: System Design: Payment System (Ledgers, Idempotency & Reconciliation)

items.q: Why use a double-entry ledger for payments?
items.a: It's the authoritative, auditable record of money movement: every transaction is recorded as balanced debits and credits, making it tamper-evident and easy to verify (sums must balance). It's the source of truth that reconciliation and reporting build on, prioritizing correctness for financial data.
items.topic: System Design: Payment System (Ledgers, Idempotency & Reconciliation)

items.q: How would you design real-time ad-click aggregation?
items.a: Ingest clicks via a distributed log (Kafka), aggregate in a stream processor (Flink/Spark) over time windows, and write results to a fast OLAP/time-series store for dashboards. Use event IDs for dedup, watermarks for late events, and idempotent writes. Discuss exactly-once semantics and hot-key/skew handling.
items.topic: System Design: Real-Time Analytics & Ad-Click Aggregation

items.q: What is the difference between Lambda and Kappa architectures?
items.a: Lambda runs parallel batch and speed (stream) layers -- the batch layer recomputes accurate results while the stream layer gives low-latency approximate ones, merged at query time (complex, duplicated logic). Kappa uses a single stream-processing pipeline (reprocess by replaying the log) -- simpler, now often preferred.
items.topic: System Design: Real-Time Analytics & Ad-Click Aggregation

items.q: How do you handle late or out-of-order events in streaming aggregation?
items.a: Use event-time windows with watermarks: a watermark estimates that events up to a time have arrived, allowing windows to close while tolerating bounded lateness; very late events go to a side output or trigger a correction. This keeps aggregates accurate despite network reordering.
items.topic: System Design: Real-Time Analytics & Ad-Click Aggregation

items.q: Why does RTL discourage testing implementation details?
items.a: Tests tied to internal state or structure break on harmless refactors. Testing observable behavior keeps tests resilient and meaningful, failing only when user-facing behavior actually changes.

items.q: What is the recommended query priority?
items.a: Prefer what users rely on: getByRole (with name) first, then label, placeholder, and text queries, and getByTestId only as a last-resort escape hatch.

items.q: When do you use findBy vs getBy vs queryBy?
items.a: getBy throws if not found (must exist now); queryBy returns null (assert absence); findBy returns a promise and retries (for async content).

items.q: How do you test something that appears asynchronously?
items.a: Use a findBy query or wrap the assertion in waitFor; both retry until the condition holds or it times out, so you don't assert before the async update renders.

items.q: What does waitFor do and when do you use it?
items.a: waitFor repeatedly runs a callback until it stops throwing (or times out). Use it to await a side effect or assertion that becomes true after async work, not for simple element queries (prefer findBy).

items.q: How do you avoid act() warnings?
items.a: Drive interactions with await user-event, await findBy/waitFor for resulting updates, and ensure all state updates are wrapped/awaited so React has flushed them before assertions.

items.q: How do you test a component that needs context or a router?
items.a: Wrap it in the required providers during render -- often via a custom render() that injects theme, router, and query-client providers -- so the component behaves as it would in the app.

items.q: Why use MSW instead of mocking fetch directly?
items.a: MSW intercepts requests at the network level, so your code uses its real fetching logic and you get realistic responses and error cases, making tests closer to production behavior.

items.q: What's the risk of over-mocking?
items.a: Mocks that replace too much can pass while the real integration is broken, giving false confidence. Mock external boundaries (network, time) and keep internal behavior real.

items.q: Why are role-based queries also an accessibility check?
items.a: getByRole resolves elements via the accessibility tree using roles and accessible names. If a control lacks a proper role or label, the query fails -- so writing role-based tests naturally exposes missing a11y semantics.

items.q: How do you query an element that has no visible text?
items.a: Give it an accessible name (aria-label, aria-labelledby, or an associated <label>) and query by role with that name; if you can't name it, that's usually an accessibility bug to fix.

items.q: What does jest-dom add to assertions?
items.a: Custom matchers like toBeInTheDocument, toBeVisible, toBeDisabled, and toHaveAccessibleName that make intent-revealing, accessibility-aware assertions on DOM nodes.

items.q: What is Cypress and what testing types does it support?
items.a: An open-source front-end testing framework for modern web apps, supporting end-to-end, integration, and component testing with an integrated runner -- known for developer experience and in-browser execution.

items.q: What is time-travel debugging in Cypress?
items.a: The runner snapshots the DOM at each command so you can hover over steps and see exactly what the app looked like at that point, making failures easy to diagnose without re-running.

items.q: Cypress vs Playwright - when do you pick each?
items.a: Cypress shines for simpler, frontend-focused suites with great DX and visual debugging; Playwright suits cross-browser coverage, true free parallelism, multi-tab/cross-origin, and large CI suites. Pick by browser needs, scale, and cost.

items.q: How does Cypress reduce test flakiness?
items.a: It automatically retries commands and assertions until they pass or time out, so you rarely add manual waits; cy.intercept stubs network calls for deterministic responses.

items.q: Why prefer user-event over fireEvent?
items.a: user-event simulates the full event sequence a real user produces (e.g. typing fires focus, keydown, input, keyup) rather than one synthetic event, so tests better reflect real behavior and catch more bugs.

items.q: Why is user-event asynchronous now?
items.a: Because it models realistic timing of interaction events; you call userEvent.setup() and await actions like type/click so all resulting state updates flush before assertions, avoiding act warnings.

items.q: How do you simulate typing into an input?
items.a: const user = userEvent.setup(); await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox'), 'hello') -- this fires the realistic key/input event sequence rather than directly setting value.

items.q: What does cy.intercept do and why is it useful?
items.a: It intercepts network requests to stub responses, spy on calls, or simulate errors/delays. This makes tests deterministic and lets you exercise error and edge-case states without depending on a real backend.

items.q: How do fixtures help Cypress tests?
items.a: Fixtures store reusable static response data (JSON) you load with cy.fixture and serve via cy.intercept, keeping tests consistent and decoupled from live data.

items.q: How do you run Cypress reliably in CI?
items.a: Run headless in the pipeline, capture screenshots/video on failure for debugging, seed deterministic data, and parallelize across machines (often via Cypress Cloud) to keep suite time manageable.

items.q: How do you debug why a query isn't finding an element?
items.a: Use screen.debug() to print the rendered DOM, logRoles(container) or screen.getByRole errors to see available roles/names, and screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL() to get suggested queries -- then pick the accessible query that matches.

items.q: What are the most common causes of act() warnings?
items.a: State updates happening after the test thinks it's done -- usually un-awaited async user-event or findBy calls. Await all interactions and async queries so React flushes updates before assertions.

items.q: Why avoid overusing getByTestId?
items.a: Test IDs don't reflect how users or assistive tech find elements, so they miss accessibility issues and couple tests to implementation. Prefer role/label/text queries; use test IDs only as a last resort.

items.q: What is Cypress component testing and how does it differ from E2E?
items.a: It mounts an individual component in a real browser with cy.mount, testing it in isolation with real rendering -- faster and more focused than full E2E flows, and more realistic than jsdom-based unit tests.

items.q: Why use data-cy selectors instead of CSS classes or text?
items.a: data-cy attributes are dedicated test hooks decoupled from styling and copy, so tests don't break when classes or visible text change -- the Cypress-recommended stable selector strategy.

items.q: Why avoid cy.wait with a fixed time?
items.a: Fixed waits are flaky and slow -- they either wait too long or not enough. Instead assert on a visible state change or wait on an intercepted request alias (cy.wait('@getUsers')) so timing is deterministic.

items.q: What is the 'testing trophy' and how does it differ from the pyramid?
items.a: It recommends the largest investment in integration tests (good confidence-to-cost ratio), with fewer E2E and unit tests and a base of static analysis (types, lint). The classic pyramid instead puts most weight on unit tests.

items.q: Why does RTL prefer integration-style tests?
items.a: Rendering a feature with its real children and context catches integration/wiring bugs and reflects real usage, giving more confidence per test than isolated unit tests of internals -- while remaining faster and more stable than full E2E.

items.q: How do you decide what to mock?
items.a: Mock only genuine boundaries you don't control or that are slow/non-deterministic -- network, time, randomness. Keep internal components and logic real so the test exercises actual behavior.

items.q: How do you parallelize Cypress in CI?
items.a: Split the spec files across multiple CI machines running in parallel; Cypress Cloud can load-balance specs by past timing for even distribution. This cuts total wall-clock time for large suites.
items.topic: Cypress at Scale: CI, Parallelization & Flake Control

items.q: How should test retries be used responsibly?
items.a: Configure limited retries to absorb transient flakiness and keep CI green, but treat retried tests as a signal -- investigate and fix the root cause rather than masking real instability permanently.
items.topic: Cypress at Scale: CI, Parallelization & Flake Control

items.q: What are Cypress's architectural limits at scale?
items.a: Running inside the browser limits multi-tab, multi-origin, and some cross-domain scenarios, and reliable parallelism often needs the paid Cloud. For broad cross-browser and heavy parallel needs teams often pick Playwright.
items.topic: Cypress at Scale: CI, Parallelization & Flake Control

items.q: How do you test form validation with RTL?
items.a: Render the form, use user-event to enter invalid then valid input, submit via the button, and assert the validation/error message appears and clears. Query inputs by label and errors by role/text so tests mirror real use.

items.q: How do you assert a form submits the correct data?
items.a: Pass a mock submit handler (jest.fn) or mock the network with MSW, fill fields via user-event, submit, then assert the handler was called with the expected payload.

items.q: Why query inputs by label instead of placeholder or test id?
items.a: getByLabelText reflects how users and assistive tech associate labels with inputs, so it also verifies accessibility; placeholders aren't labels and test ids bypass the accessibility tree.

items.q: What is cy.request used for?
items.a:
Making real HTTP requests independent of the UI -- to test API endpoints directly, seed or reset data, and set up state quickly before exercising the interface, avoiding slow UI-driven setup.

 Q. Why and how do you write custom Cypress commands?

 A. To encapsulate repeated flows (login, seeding) via Cypress.Commands.add, keeping specs DRY and readable. e.g. an apiLogin command that cy.requests the auth endpoint and stores the token -- far faster than UI login each test.

items.q: Why seed data via API rather than the UI in tests?
items.a: UI setup is slow and brittle; seeding through cy.request or tasks is fast and deterministic, so each test starts from a known state without depending on unrelated UI flows.

items.q: How do you test a component's loading then loaded states?
items.a: Assert the loading indicator appears (getBy/findBy), then await the resolved content with findBy*/waitFor. Mock the network (MSW) so you control when it resolves and can assert each state deterministically.

items.q: How do you test an error state from a failed request?
items.a: Stub the request to reject/return an error (via MSW), render, then await the error UI with findByText/role. This verifies the component handles failure, not just the happy path.

items.q: Why avoid fixed setTimeout waits in async tests?
items.a: They're flaky and slow -- too short causes false failures, too long wastes time. RTL's findBy/waitFor retry until the condition holds or times out, giving deterministic results across environments.

items.q: What is visual regression testing and why use it?
items.a: Capturing a baseline image of the UI and comparing later runs to flag unintended visual changes (layout, color, spacing) that functional tests don't catch -- useful for design-sensitive components.

items.q: How do you check accessibility in Cypress?
items.a: Use cypress-axe: cy.injectAxe() then cy.checkA11y() runs axe-core against the rendered page and fails on WCAG violations (missing labels, contrast, roles), bringing a11y checks into CI.

items.q: Why automate accessibility checks in tests?
items.a: To catch regressions (missing alt text, unlabeled controls, contrast issues) continuously rather than in occasional manual audits, making accessibility a maintained baseline, not an afterthought.

items.q: How do you test a component that uses routing?
items.a: Render it inside a router (MemoryRouter with initialEntries to control the starting URL), interact, then assert the visible result of navigation -- e.g. the target page's content appears -- rather than inspecting router internals.

items.q: Why use MemoryRouter in tests?
items.a: It keeps routing state in memory (no real browser URL), lets you set the initial route via initialEntries, and runs fast and deterministically -- ideal for unit/integration tests of navigation.

items.q: What should a navigation test actually assert?
items.a: The user-visible outcome: after clicking a link or triggering navigate, the expected page content renders. Avoid asserting on history objects or router calls, which couples the test to implementation.

items.q: Component testing vs E2E in Cypress - when each?
items.a: Component tests (cy.mount) for fast, isolated checks of a component's rendering/behavior; E2E for critical end-to-end user journeys that need full-stack confidence. Favor more component tests and reserve E2E for key flows to keep suites fast and stable.
items.topic: Cypress: Choosing Test Levels (Component vs E2E)

items.q: Why not test everything with E2E?
items.a: E2E is slow and more brittle (network, timing, full environment). Relying on it for everything yields long, flaky suites. Push detail down to component/unit tests and keep E2E focused on must-work paths.
items.topic: Cypress: Choosing Test Levels (Component vs E2E)

items.q: How do you decide the right test level for a case?
items.a: Pick the lowest level that gives the confidence you need: pure logic - unit; a component's behavior - component test; a critical multi-page flow - E2E. Match cost and confidence to the risk.
items.topic: Cypress: Choosing Test Levels (Component vs E2E)

items.q: What is the modern 2026 React testing stack?
items.a:
Vite for the build, Vitest as the test runner (fast ESM/TS, Jest-compatible API), RTL for rendering and queries, and TypeScript for types. Create React App is deprecated, so new projects scaffold with Vite.

 Q. How hard is migrating RTL tests from Jest to Vitest?

 A. Mostly mechanical: Vitest's API mirrors Jest (describe/it/expect), with vi replacing jest for mocks/timers, and config moves into Vite. RTL queries and user-event stay identical, so component tests need little change.
items.topic: Modern Stack: RTL with Vite & Vitest (2026)

items.q: Does RTL change when you switch runners?
items.a: No -- RTL is the rendering/query layer (getByRole, user-event) and is runner-agnostic. You can run the same RTL tests under Jest or Vitest; only the runner config and mock API differ.
items.topic: Modern Stack: RTL with Vite & Vitest (2026)

items.q: How do you test a custom hook?
items.a: Use renderHook from @testing-library/react: it runs the hook and exposes result.current. Trigger state changes inside act (await for async), use rerender to test prop reactivity, and assert on the returned values -- no throwaway component needed.

items.q: How do you test a hook that needs context (e.g. React Query)?
items.a: Pass a wrapper option to renderHook that provides the needed context providers (QueryClientProvider, router, theme), so the hook runs in a realistic environment.

items.q: What should custom-hook tests assert?
items.a: The hook's observable contract -- returned values, state transitions, and effects' outcomes -- not internal variables. This keeps tests resilient to refactors, consistent with testing behavior over implementation.

items.q: How do you test accessibility in RTL with jest-axe?
items.a: Render the component, pass its container to await axe(container) from jest-axe, then expect(results).toHaveNoViolations(). It runs axe-core to flag WCAG issues like missing labels, bad contrast, and invalid ARIA in CI.

items.q: What can't automated a11y testing catch?
items.a: Roughly half of real issues -- it can't judge meaningful focus order quality, logical reading flow, sensible alt-text wording, or full keyboard/screen-reader UX. Automated checks catch structural violations; manual testing covers the rest.

items.q: Why combine jest-axe with role-based queries?
items.a: Role queries push you toward accessible markup as you write tests; jest-axe adds a broad automated audit. Together they make accessibility a continuous, enforced baseline rather than a one- off review.

items.q: How do you test a useDebounce hook?
items.a: renderHook to run it, enable fake timers, update the input value, advance time by less than the delay (assert unchanged), then past the delay (assert updated). Fake timers make the time-based behavior deterministic without real waiting.
items.topic: Testing a Custom Hook & a Coding-Challenge Component

items.q: How would you test the Accordion's 'only one open' behavior?
items.a: Render it, click the first header and assert its panel is visible, click the second and assert the second is visible while the first is now hidden -- verifying single-open behavior through what the user sees, via user-event and role/text queries.
items.topic: Testing a Custom Hook & a Coding-Challenge Component

items.q: Why use fake timers when testing debounced logic?
items.a: Real delays make tests slow and flaky. Fake timers (jest.useFakeTimers/vi) let you advance time precisely and deterministically, so you can assert behavior right before and after the debounce threshold.
items.topic: Testing a Custom Hook & a Coding-Challenge Component

items.q: What's the recommended 2026 JS testing stack?
items.a: Vitest for unit/integration on new projects (fast, Vite-native), Jest for existing/Webpack and React Native, and Playwright for end-to-end (broad browser coverage, free parallelism). RTL stays as the component rendering/query layer. A common 'split strategy' is Vitest below the browser + Playwright in it.
items.topic: 2026 Testing Landscape: Vitest, Playwright & the Split Strategy

items.q: Why has Playwright overtaken Cypress for new E2E projects?
items.a: True multi-browser support including WebKit/Safari, built-in free parallelism (no paid cloud needed), browser-level network interception, mobile emulation, and auto-waiting -- reflected in higher satisfaction scores. Cypress still wins on interactive in-browser debugging UX.
items.topic: 2026 Testing Landscape: Vitest, Playwright & the Split Strategy

items.q: When is Jest still the right choice over Vitest?
items.a: For existing Jest/Webpack codebases (migration not yet worth it), React Native (its officially supported runner), and teams wanting the largest ecosystem/community. The APIs are compatible, so migrating later is low-risk.
items.topic: 2026 Testing Landscape: Vitest, Playwright & the Split Strategy

items.q: How do you test that a modal closes on Escape and overlay click?
items.a: Render it open, then await user.keyboard('{Escape}') and assert onClose was called (or the dialog left the DOM); separately click the overlay and assert the same. Query the dialog by role='dialog' so the test also checks correct semantics.

items.q: How do you test a Tabs component's behavior?
items.a: Click each tab via user-event and assert the associated panel is visible while others are not, and that the clicked tab has aria-selected='true'. Querying by role (tab/tabpanel) validates accessibility alongside behavior.

items.q: Why test keyboard interactions for these components?
items.a: Because accessible components must work for keyboard/screen-reader users -- Escape to close, Tab to move, arrow keys for tabs. Testing only mouse clicks misses the a11y contract interviewers expect for dialogs and tabs.

items.q: How do you test an infinite-scroll component?
items.a: Mock the paged API (MSW), render and assert page one renders, then trigger the load mechanism -- typically by mocking IntersectionObserver and invoking its callback (or firing the scroll handler) -- and assert the next page's items are appended. Assert the loading and end states too.
items.topic: Testing Async Lists, Infinite Scroll & Carousels

items.q: How do you test a carousel's autoplay without slow tests?
items.a: Use fake timers: render, advance time past the autoplay interval, and assert the active slide changed; then unmount and assert no further timers fire (the interval was cleaned up), avoiding leaks and act warnings.
items.topic: Testing Async Lists, Infinite Scroll & Carousels

items.q: How do you test a debounced autocomplete?
items.a: Type with user-event, advance fake timers past the debounce, then await findBy for the suggestions (mock the network with MSW); assert keyboard navigation (arrow/enter) selects an option. This verifies debounce, async, and a11y behavior together.
items.topic: Testing Async Lists, Infinite Scroll & Carousels

items.q: What is MSW and why use it over mocking fetch directly?
items.a: Mock Service Worker intercepts requests at the network layer (service worker in browser, interceptor in Node), so your code makes real fetch/axios calls and MSW returns mocked responses from defined handlers. This tests the real fetching path, reuses handlers across tests/Storybook/dev, and avoids brittle per-call fetch stubs.
items.topic: Mocking the Network with MSW (Mock Service Worker)

items.q: How do you structure MSW in a test suite?
items.a: Define request handlers (endpoints and their mock responses), start the MSW server in global setup (beforeAll), reset handlers between tests (afterEach) for isolation, and close it afterAll. Override handlers per test to simulate errors, delays, or specific payloads.
items.topic: Mocking the Network with MSW (Mock Service Worker)

items.q: How do you test error and loading states with MSW?
items.a: Override a handler for that test to return an error status or a delayed response, then assert the component shows the error or loading UI. Because the real fetch path runs, you verify actual error handling, not a shortcut mock.
items.topic: Mocking the Network with MSW (Mock Service Worker)

items.q: How do you test drag-and-drop components reliably?
items.a: Test the keyboard-accessible path (if the library offers one, e.g. dnd-kit): focus the item, use user- event keyboard to pick up/move/drop, and assert the resulting order/placement. jsdom doesn't fully implement native drag events, so simulating raw drag is brittle -- assert outcomes, not drag internals.

items.q: How do you test a collapsible tree / file explorer?
items.a: Render it, click a folder and assert its children become visible, click again and assert they're hidden, and check nesting via accessible structure (roles/labels). Test what the user sees (expanded items) rather than internal expanded-state variables.

items.q: Why assert outcomes instead of internal interaction state?
items.a: Because tests pinned to internal state (e.g. an isDragging flag) break on refactors and don't prove the user-visible result. Asserting the final order/visibility verifies the behavior that actually matters and stays resilient.

items.q: How do you test a component that uses Suspense?
items.a: Back its data with a controllable mocked promise; render and assert the Suspense fallback appears, then resolve the promise and await the loaded content with findBy*. Controlling when the promise resolves lets you deterministically assert both the pending and resolved states.

items.q: How do you test that an error boundary catches an error?
items.a: Render a child component that throws (e.g. on a prop/state) inside the boundary, and assert the boundary's fallback UI renders instead of the crash. Expected console.error from React can be temporarily silenced so it doesn't pollute output.

items.q: How do you test loading/error/success with a data library and MSW?
items.a: Mock the endpoint with MSW (success, then error/delay variants per test), render, and assert the loading UI, then the resolved data via findBy, and the error UI when the handler returns an error -- exercising the real fetch path through the library.

items.q: How does Cypress reduce flaky tests?
items.a: Built-in retry-ability: commands and assertions automatically retry until they pass or hit a timeout, so you rarely need manual waits/sleeps. Combined with running in a real browser and automatic waiting for elements/requests, this makes tests far less flaky than naive sleep-based scripts.
items.topic: Cypress E2E: Selectors, Network Stubbing & Custom Commands

items.q: How do you stub network requests in Cypress, and why?
items.a: cy.intercept() intercepts matching requests to return a fixture, force an error/delay, or spy and assert they were called -- making tests deterministic and independent of a live backend. cy.fixture() supplies mock JSON. This isolates the frontend and lets you test error/empty states reliably.
items.topic: Cypress E2E: Selectors, Network Stubbing & Custom Commands

items.q: What are best practices for selectors and reuse in Cypress?
items.a: Select by dedicated test attributes (data-cy/data-testid) rather than brittle CSS classes or text that changes; and extract repeated flows (login, seeding) into custom commands via Cypress.Commands.add so specs stay DRY and readable.
items.topic: Cypress E2E: Selectors, Network Stubbing & Custom Commands

items.q: How do you test optimistic UI with rollback?
items.a: Trigger the action and assert the optimistic value shows immediately; then in one test resolve the action and assert the confirmed state, and in another make it reject and assert the UI reverts to the previous value and shows the error. This proves the rollback path, not just the happy path.

items.q: Why is rollback the critical case for optimistic UI tests?
items.a: Because the common bug ('silent-failure trap') is that an action error doesn't revert the optimistic state, leaving the UI lying about success. A test that forces the action to fail and asserts the revert + error is what catches this; happy-path tests alone miss it.

items.q: How do you assert the pending state of a Server Action form?
items.a: Render the form, submit it, and while the mocked action is in flight assert the submit button shows its pending state (e.g. disabled / 'Adding...' text driven by useFormStatus), then resolve and assert it returns to idle. Control the action's timing so the pending window is observable.

items.q: What's the difference between jest.fn(), jest.spyOn, and jest.mock()?
items.a:
jest.fn() makes a standalone mock function; jest.spyOn wraps a real method so you can watch or override it while the original stays available; jest.mock replaces an entire module with mocks.

 Q. Why and how do you reset mocks between tests?

 A. To stop state leaking across tests. clearMocks wipes recorded calls, resetMocks also resets implementations, and restoreMocks restores spied originals; configure them or call them in beforeEach.

items.q: How do you test asynchronous code in Jest?
items.a: Return or await a promise, use async/await in the test, or use resolves/rejects matchers; for timers use jest.useFakeTimers and advance them.

items.q: What's the difference between toBe and toEqual?
items.a: toBe checks reference/primitive identity via Object.is; toEqual recursively compares values, so it's the right matcher for objects and arrays whose contents match but references differ.

items.q: What are the pros and cons of snapshot tests?
items.a: Pros: fast to write, catch unintended UI/output changes. Cons: can become large, get blindly updated, and test implementation detail if overused -- keep snapshots small and reviewed.

items.q: What do the four coverage metrics mean?
items.a: Statements (lines of logic run), branches (each if/else path taken), functions (each function called), and lines (source lines executed) -- together showing how thoroughly tests exercise the code.

items.q: What's the difference between beforeEach and beforeAll?
items.a: beforeAll runs once before all tests in a file (expensive shared setup); beforeEach runs before every test (fresh, isolated state). Pair with afterEach/afterAll for cleanup.

items.q: When do you use the jsdom vs node test environment?
items.a: Use jsdom for code touching the DOM/browser APIs (React components); use node for server, utility, or Node-API code, which is faster and avoids loading a fake DOM.

items.q: How do you control time in tests?
items.a: Use jest.useFakeTimers() and advance with jest.advanceTimersByTime or runAllTimers to test debounces, intervals, and timeouts deterministically without real waiting.

items.q: Jest vs Vitest - how do you choose?
items.a: Vitest fits Vite-based projects needing fast ESM/TS and quick cold starts; Jest fits broad ecosystems, mature tooling, and is the supported runner for React Native. Decide by your build toolchain, ESM requirements, and ecosystem needs.
items.topic: Jest vs Vitest & Modern Runner Choices

items.q: What did Jest 30 improve?
items.a: A new resolver delivering significantly faster runs and lower memory on large TypeScript codebases, plus raised platform baselines (newer Node/TS, jsdom v26) and new matchers.
items.topic: Jest vs Vitest & Modern Runner Choices

items.q: Why can ESM be tricky in Jest historically?
items.a: Jest's traditional CommonJS-based transform needed extra config (transforms, transformIgnorePatterns) for native ESM packages, whereas Vite-native runners handle ESM out of the box.
items.topic: Jest vs Vitest & Modern Runner Choices

items.q: How do you test a custom React hook in Jest?
items.a: Use renderHook from @testing-library/react to run the hook in a test component, wrap state- changing calls in act, and assert on result.current -- no need to build a throwaway component manually.

items.q: How do you test debounced or timer-based code?
items.a: Enable jest.useFakeTimers(), trigger the action, then advance time with jest.advanceTimersByTime() to deterministically fire the debounce/timeout without real waiting.

items.q: How do you assert a promise rejects in Jest?
items.a: await expect(fn()).rejects.toThrow(...) or wrap in try/catch; the resolves/rejects matchers let you assert async outcomes cleanly without manual .then chains.

items.q: How do you partially mock a module in Jest?
items.a: Use jest.mock with a factory that spreads jest.requireActual('module') and overrides only the exports you need -- keeping real behavior for the rest while stubbing specific functions.

items.q: How do you mock an ES module's default and named exports?
items.a: jest.mock('mod', () => ({ __esModule: true, default: jest.fn(), namedFn: jest.fn() })) -- the __esModule flag tells Jest to treat default correctly alongside named exports.

items.q: What should you mock and what should you not?
items.a: Mock external boundaries -- HTTP clients, databases, filesystem, randomness, time -- to keep tests deterministic. Don't mock the code under test or pure internal logic, or you stop testing real behavior.

items.q: Is 100% code coverage a good goal? Why or why not?
items.a: No -- coverage measures lines executed, not whether assertions are meaningful. You can hit 100% with weak tests. Aim for high coverage of important paths with strong assertions; chasing the last few percent often tests trivial code at high cost.
items.topic: Coverage Strategy, Flaky Tests & CI Integration

items.q: What causes flaky tests and how do you fix them?
items.a: Timing/async races, shared mutable state between tests, real timers/network, and ordering dependence. Fix by awaiting async work, using fake timers, isolating state (resetMocks/fresh fixtures), mocking external calls, and quarantining flaky tests until fixed.
items.topic: Coverage Strategy, Flaky Tests & CI Integration

items.q: How do you keep a large Jest suite fast in CI?
items.a: Run in parallel/sharded across machines, use --onlyChanged or test path filtering on PRs, cache dependencies, fail fast, and separate fast unit tests from slower integration runs.
items.topic: Coverage Strategy, Flaky Tests & CI Integration

items.q: What does it.each do and why use it?
items.a: It runs the same test body over a table of inputs/expected values, so you cover many cases without copy-paste and each case reports independently -- great for boundary and equivalence testing.

items.q: How do you write a custom Jest matcher?
items.a: Use expect.extend({ matcherName(received, expected) { return { pass, message } } }); pass drives success/failure and message gives a readable error. Useful for repeated domain assertions.

items.q: What does jest-dom provide?
items.a: DOM-specific matchers like toBeInTheDocument, toBeVisible, toHaveValue, and toHaveAccessibleName that make assertions on rendered nodes expressive and intent-revealing.

items.q: What's the difference between a mock, stub, spy, and fake?
items.a: Stub: returns canned data. Spy: records calls (optionally wrapping the real fn). Mock: preset behavior plus assertions about how it was used. Fake: a real but lightweight implementation (e.g. in- memory store). Pick by whether you need to control output, observe calls, or substitute behavior.
items.topic: Test Doubles: Mocks, Stubs, Spies & Fakes

items.q: When do you assert on a mock's calls vs its return?
items.a: Assert on calls (toHaveBeenCalledWith) when the interaction is the behavior under test (did it notify the API correctly); assert on returns/output when the result matters. Avoid over-asserting internal calls that make tests brittle.
items.topic: Test Doubles: Mocks, Stubs, Spies & Fakes

items.q: What's the risk of over-mocking?
items.a: Tests pass while real integration is broken, and they become brittle to refactors. Mock only true boundaries (network, time); keep internal logic real so tests reflect actual behavior.
items.topic: Test Doubles: Mocks, Stubs, Spies & Fakes

items.q: What does Jest watch mode do?
items.a: It reruns tests affected by your latest changes and offers interactive filtering -- by filename, test- name pattern, or only-failed -- giving fast feedback during development without re-running the whole suite.
items.topic: Debugging Tests, Watch Mode & Performance Flags

items.q: When would you use --runInBand?
items.a: To run tests serially in one process -- for debugging (predictable order, easier breakpoints), or in constrained CI where parallel workers exhaust memory. It's slower but avoids worker-related flakiness.
items.topic: Debugging Tests, Watch Mode & Performance Flags

items.q: How do you debug a single failing test?
items.a: Filter to it with -t 'name' or run its file directly, add a breakpoint and run node --inspect-brk against Jest, or use --detectOpenHandles if it hangs from a leaked async resource.
items.topic: Debugging Tests, Watch Mode & Performance Flags

items.q: What's current in Jest 30?
items.a:
A faster module resolver and lower memory on large TS codebases, jsdom upgraded to v26, raised Node/TypeScript baselines, and new matchers -- narrowing the speed gap with Vite-native runners.

 Q. Jest or Vitest in 2026 - how do you decide?

 A. Vitest for Vite-based projects needing native ESM and fast cold starts; Jest for mature ecosystems, non-Vite setups, and React Native (its officially supported runner). Decide by build toolchain and ESM needs, not hype.
items.topic: Jest in 2026: ESM, Jest 30 & the Vitest Question

items.q: Why is ESM still a consideration with Jest?
items.a: Jest's CommonJS roots mean native-ESM packages can need transform/config work (transformIgnorePatterns, flags), whereas Vite-native runners handle ESM out of the box -- a common migration pain point.
items.topic: Jest in 2026: ESM, Jest 30 & the Vitest Question

items.q: How do you assert that code throws or rejects in Jest?
items.a: Sync: expect(() => fn()).toThrow(ErrorOrMessage). Async: await expect(promise).rejects.toThrow(...). You can match the error type or message to confirm the right failure, not just any throw.

items.q: How do you test that your code handles a dependency failure?
items.a: Mock the dependency to fail -- e.g. mockRejectedValue for a fetch or a thrown error from a stubbed module -- then assert your code catches it and produces the expected fallback/error state.

items.q: What edge cases deserve tests?
items.a: Empty/null/undefined inputs, boundary values (0, max, off-by-one), invalid/malformed data, and concurrent or failure conditions -- the places real bugs hide, beyond the happy path.

items.q: How should you balance unit, integration, and E2E tests?
items.a: Favor integration tests (best confidence-to-cost), with fewer focused unit tests for complex logic and a thin layer of E2E for critical paths, over a base of static checks (types/lint) -- the 'testing trophy' shape. Avoid an all-unit pyramid that misses wiring bugs.
items.topic: Integration Testing & Test Organization at Scale

items.q: How do you keep a large test suite maintainable?
items.a: Colocate or mirror tests with source, share setup via setup files, name tests by behavior, keep them independent and deterministic (no shared mutable state, mock only boundaries), and separate fast unit runs from slower integration in CI.
items.topic: Integration Testing & Test Organization at Scale

items.q: What makes a good test name?
items.a: It describes the behavior and condition, e.g. 'returns 401 when the token is missing' -- so a failure tells you what broke without reading the body. Avoid vague names like 'works' or 'test1'.
items.topic: Integration Testing & Test Organization at Scale

items.q: How do you test a Promise.all implementation?
items.a: Cover the contract: multiple resolved promises resolve to results in input order; if any rejects, the whole thing rejects with that reason; an empty array resolves to []. Use await expect(...).resolves/.rejects and assert ordering and failure behavior.
items.topic: Testing Implementations: Polyfills, Promises & Edge Cases

items.q: How do you thoroughly test a map/filter polyfill?
items.a: Compare against expected output for: a normal array, an empty array, correct index passed to the callback, and that it returns a new array without mutating the input. it.each keeps the many cases concise.
items.topic: Testing Implementations: Polyfills, Promises & Edge Cases

items.q: Why test edge cases for utility implementations?
items.a: Utilities are reused everywhere, so a boundary bug (empty input, index handling, mutation) propagates widely. Interviewers check that you test the contract and boundaries, signaling production- quality thinking.
items.topic: Testing Implementations: Polyfills, Promises & Edge Cases

items.q: How hard is migrating from Jest to Vitest?
items.a: Low-risk: the APIs are largely compatible (describe/it/expect; vi.* replaces jest.* for mocks and timers), config moves into the Vite config, and RTL tests are mostly unchanged. The main work is mocking/config differences and ESM handling.
items.topic: Migrating Jest to Vitest & Choosing a Runner

items.q: When should you migrate, and when stay on Jest?
items.a: Migrate at a natural inflection (refactor, framework upgrade, or when Jest startup on a big monorepo hurts) for Vite projects. Stay on Jest for Webpack-based apps, React Native, or when you depend on Jest-only plugins/ecosystem.
items.topic: Migrating Jest to Vitest & Choosing a Runner

items.q: What concretely changes in test code when moving to Vitest?
items.a: Mostly imports/globals: jest.fn/spyOn/useFakeTimers become vi.fn/spyOn/useFakeTimers, configure globals or import from 'vitest', and move setup into Vite config. Assertions and RTL queries stay the same.
items.topic: Migrating Jest to Vitest & Choosing a Runner

items.q: How do you test a Promise.all polyfill thoroughly?
items.a: Cover the contract: multiple resolved promises -> results in input order; one rejects -> the combined promise rejects with that reason (fail-fast); empty input -> resolves to []. Use await expect(...).resolves/.rejects, and fake timers to control resolution timing.

items.q: How do you verify a memoize implementation caches correctly?
items.a: Wrap a jest.fn, call the memoized version twice with the same args and assert the underlying fn ran once (toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)) while both calls returned the right value; call with new args and assert it recomputes. Tests behavior, not the cache internals.

items.q: Why test the contract rather than the implementation?
items.a: So any correct rewrite still passes -- tests pinned to internal cache shape or call order break on harmless refactors. Asserting observable behavior (results, call counts, errors) keeps tests resilient and meaningful.

items.q: How do you test debounced or throttled code with Jest?
items.a: Enable jest.useFakeTimers(), invoke the debounced function, advance time with jest.advanceTimersByTime(delay), and assert the wrapped function ran the expected number of times -- verifying it fired only after the delay (debounce) or at most once per interval (throttle), deterministically.

items.q: What's the difference between runAllTimers and runOnlyPendingTimers?
items.a: runAllTimers flushes every queued timer, but can infinite-loop if a timer schedules another; runOnlyPendingTimers runs just those currently pending, which is safer for code like recurring intervals or self-rescheduling timeouts.

items.q: How do you test a timer that triggers async work?
items.a: Combine fake timers with promise flushing -- advance timers (advanceTimersByTimeAsync where available) and await microtasks so the async callback's promise resolves before you assert. Otherwise the assertion runs before the async effect completes.

items.q: How do you test a reducer?
items.a: Call it with a starting state and an action and assert the returned state (toEqual the expected new state). Also assert immutability -- the returned object is new and the original state is unchanged -- since reducers must be pure and not mutate.

items.q: Why is pure logic the highest-value thing to unit test?
items.a: It's deterministic and rendering-free, so tests are fast, stable, and pinpoint failures precisely. Reducers, selectors, and utilities concentrate business logic; testing them directly gives strong coverage of behavior without the cost and flakiness of full UI tests.

items.q: How do you test a Zustand or Redux store?
items.a: For Zustand, call the store's actions (or set) and assert getState() reflects the change; reset state between tests. For Redux Toolkit, dispatch actions to the store (or test the slice reducer directly) and assert the resulting state -- both are pure-logic assertions.

items.q: What is property-based testing and how does it differ from example tests?
items.a: You assert a general property that should hold for all inputs (e.g. a round-trip identity), and the framework (fast-check) generates many randomized inputs to try to falsify it, shrinking any failure to a minimal counterexample -- versus example tests that check specific hand-picked cases.

items.q: What kinds of properties are useful to test?
items.a: Round-trip (decode(encode(x)) === x), invariants (sort output is ordered and a permutation of input), idempotence (f(f(x)) === f(x)), and consistency with a reference/oracle. These catch edge cases (empty, unicode, extremes) that example tests often miss.

items.q: When is property-based testing most worthwhile?
items.a: For pure functions with clear invariants -- parsers/serializers, data transforms, math/utilities, and algorithms. It's less suited to UI or side-effect-heavy code. Pair it with example tests for specific known cases and regressions.

items.q: What is the GIL and why does it matter?
items.a: The Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to run Python bytecode at once. It simplifies memory management but blocks CPU-bound multithreading from using multiple cores.

items.q: When do threads still help despite the GIL?
items.a: For I/O-bound work: while one thread waits on network or disk the GIL is released and others run, so threads improve I/O concurrency.

items.q: What changed with free-threading in Python 3.14?
items.a: The no-GIL build is now officially supported (still optional), allowing true parallel CPU-bound threading, with some single-thread overhead and C-extension updates needed.

items.q: What's the difference between a list and a tuple?
items.a: Lists are mutable and used for homogeneous, changing sequences; tuples are immutable and often used for fixed records and as dict keys. Immutability makes tuples hashable.

items.q: Why is a mutable default argument dangerous?
items.a: The default is created once at function definition and shared across calls, so mutating it leaks state between calls. Use None and create a fresh object inside the function.

items.q: How does a generator expression differ from a list comprehension?
items.a: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory; a generator expression yields items lazily one at a time, saving memory for large or streamed data.

items.q: What is a decorator and how does it work?
items.a: A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a new function wrapping it, applied with @. It runs code before/after the original -- used for logging, caching, auth, and timing -- leveraging closures.

items.q: How do generators save memory?
items.a: They yield items one at a time and keep only current state, so you can iterate huge or infinite sequences without building the whole collection in memory.

items.q: What problem do context managers solve?
items.a: They guarantee resource setup and cleanup (files, locks, connections) via with, running teardown even if an exception occurs, preventing leaks.

items.q: What is the difference between __str__ and __repr__?
items.a: __str__ is the readable, user-facing string (print); __repr__ is the unambiguous, developer-facing representation (debugging/REPL), ideally something that could recreate the object. repr() falls back when __str__ is absent.

items.q: How does Python resolve multiple inheritance?
items.a: Via the Method Resolution Order (MRO) using C3 linearization, a deterministic order you can inspect with Class.__mro__; super() follows this order so each class is initialized once.

items.q: What does the @property decorator do?
items.a: It exposes a method as a read-only (or get/set) attribute, letting you add validation or computation behind attribute-style access without changing the calling code.

items.q: Do Python type hints affect runtime behavior?
items.a: No by default -- they're for static checkers (mypy/pyright), IDEs, and docs. Runtime validation requires tools like Pydantic, which read the annotations to validate and coerce data.

items.q: What does Pydantic add over plain type hints?
items.a: Runtime validation, parsing, and coercion against typed models, with clear errors -- turning annotations into enforced data contracts (the basis of FastAPI request/response models).

items.q: Why have ruff and uv become popular?
items.a: They're Rust-based and dramatically faster: ruff replaces multiple lint/format tools in one, and uv replaces pip/virtualenv workflows, cutting CI and local setup time substantially.

items.q: What's the difference between 'is' and '=='?
items.a: is compares identity (whether two names point to the same object in memory); == compares value equality via __eq__. Use == for value checks; reserve is for None and true identity tests.

items.q: How does CPython manage memory?
items.a: Primarily reference counting -- an object is freed when its count hits zero -- plus a generational cyclic garbage collector to reclaim reference cycles that counting alone can't free.

items.q: When do you need copy.deepcopy?
items.a: When duplicating a nested mutable structure where inner objects must also be independent; a shallow copy shares the inner references, so mutating a nested element would affect both copies.

items.q: What's the difference between an iterable and an iterator?
items.a: An iterable has __iter__ and can produce an iterator (e.g. a list); an iterator has __next__, holds iteration state, and yields items until StopIteration. for loops call iter() on the iterable to get an iterator.

items.q: How do generators differ from returning a list?
items.a: A generator yields values lazily one at a time, keeping only current state -- so it handles huge or infinite sequences with minimal memory, whereas a list materializes everything up front.

items.q: What does 'yield from' do?
items.a: It delegates iteration to a sub-iterable/generator, yielding all its values and transparently passing through sent values and return value -- useful for composing generators.

items.q: threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio - when each?
items.a: I/O-bound with blocking libraries -> threading; very high-concurrency I/O -> asyncio (event loop, async/await); CPU-bound -> multiprocessing for real parallelism across cores (or a free-threaded build). Match the tool to whether you're I/O- or CPU-bound.

items.q: Why doesn't threading speed up CPU-bound Python (standard build)?
items.a: The GIL allows only one thread to execute bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound threads contend rather than run in parallel. Use multiprocessing or a free-threaded build for CPU parallelism.

items.q: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
items.a: Concurrency is structuring work so multiple tasks make progress (interleaved), e.g. asyncio on one thread; parallelism is tasks literally running at the same instant on multiple cores, e.g. multiprocessing.

items.q: What's the difference between EAFP and LBYL?
items.a: EAFP ('easier to ask forgiveness than permission') tries the operation and catches exceptions; LBYL ('look before you leap') checks preconditions first. Python idiomatically prefers EAFP, which avoids race conditions between check and use.

items.q: What do else and finally add to try/except?
items.a: else runs only if no exception occurred (keeping the try block minimal); finally always runs for cleanup (closing files, releasing locks) whether or not an exception was raised.

items.q: Why avoid a bare 'except:'?
items.a: It catches everything -- including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit -- hiding bugs and making debugging hard. Catch specific exception types so unexpected errors still surface.

items.q: What does if __name__ == '__main__' do?
items.a:
It runs the guarded block only when the file is executed directly, not when imported. This lets a module act both as an importable library and as a runnable script without side effects on import.

 Q. Absolute vs relative imports - which to prefer?

 A. Absolute imports (from pkg.mod import x) are clearer and more robust, recommended for most code; relative imports (from .mod import x) are concise within a package but can confuse and break if the package moves.

items.q: How do you avoid circular imports?
items.a: Restructure so modules don't mutually depend, move shared code to a third module, or defer the import inside the function that needs it so it resolves at call time rather than import time.

items.q: Why use the logging module instead of print?
items.a: logging gives levels, configurable handlers/formatters, per-module loggers, and runtime control (e.g. DEBUG in dev, WARNING in prod) without code changes -- print can't be filtered, routed, or leveled, and clutters output.

items.q: What are Python's logging levels and when use each?
items.a: DEBUG (diagnostic detail), INFO (normal events), WARNING (something unexpected but handled), ERROR (a failure in an operation), CRITICAL (severe, app-threatening). Set the threshold per environment to control verbosity.

items.q: How do you debug interactively in Python?
items.a: Insert breakpoint() (or import pdb; pdb.set_trace()) to drop into the debugger, then step, inspect variables, and continue -- far more powerful than scattering print statements.

items.q: What's significant about Python 3.14's free-threading?
items.a: The no-GIL build is now officially supported (still optional), allowing true parallel CPU-bound multithreading across cores -- with some single-thread overhead and C-extension updates needed. It's the biggest concurrency shift in years.

items.q: Why have uv and ruff become 2026 defaults?
items.a: Both are Rust-based and dramatically faster: uv replaces pip/virtualenv workflows (often 10-100x faster installs) and ruff replaces several lint/format tools in one, cutting CI and local setup time substantially.

items.q: What are t-strings (PEP 750)?
items.a: Template strings added in 3.14 that let you safely process interpolated values before they're rendered (e.g. for escaping/sanitization), giving more control than f-strings for custom string handling.

items.q: List comprehension vs generator expression - when each?
items.a: Use a list comprehension when you need the full list in memory (indexing, reuse); use a generator expression for large or streamed data where you iterate once -- it yields lazily and uses minimal memory.

items.q: What does the walrus operator (:=) do?
items.a: It assigns within an expression, e.g. while (line := f.readline()):, letting you capture and test a value in one place -- reducing duplication, though overuse hurts readability.

items.q: Name a few Pythonic idioms interviewers look for.
items.a: Truthiness (if items: not if len(items) > 0), enumerate for index+value, zip to pair sequences, unpacking with *, dict/set comprehensions, and context managers (with) for resources.

items.q: Why is pytest preferred over unittest?
items.a: Less boilerplate (plain assert with detailed failure introspection, no class hierarchy required), powerful reusable fixtures with scopes, easy parametrization, and a large plugin ecosystem (coverage, mock, async) -- making tests more concise and readable.
items.topic: Testing in Python: pytest, Fixtures & Mocking

items.q: What are pytest fixtures and fixture scopes?
items.a: Fixtures provide reusable setup/teardown injected into tests via arguments (@pytest.fixture). Scopes control lifetime: function (default, per test), module, class, or session (once for the whole run) -- balancing isolation against setup cost.
items.topic: Testing in Python: pytest, Fixtures & Mocking

items.q: How do you mock a dependency in a pytest test?
items.a: Use unittest.mock.patch (or pytest-mock's mocker) to replace the dependency with a MagicMock for the test's duration, set return_value/side_effect, and assert calls -- isolating the unit from network, DB, or time.
items.topic: Testing in Python: pytest, Fixtures & Mocking

items.q: How do you check if two strings are anagrams in Python?
items.a:
Compare character counts: return Counter(a) == Counter(b) (O(n)), or sorted(a) == sorted(b) (O(n log n)). Counter is cleaner and faster; mention normalizing case/spaces if required.

 Q. Explain the two-pointer technique with an example.

 A. Use two indices moving toward each other or in tandem to solve in O(n) without extra space -- e.g. checking a palindrome (compare ends inward) or finding a pair summing to a target in a sorted array (move pointers based on the sum).
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Strings, Collections & Two Pointers

items.q: When do you reach for Counter or defaultdict?
items.a: Counter for frequency counts and multiset comparisons (anagrams, top-k); defaultdict to group items without key-existence checks (e.g. grouping words by length). Both make counting/grouping concise and O(n).
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Strings, Collections & Two Pointers

items.q: Which Python standard-library tools speed up DSA solutions?
items.a: collections.Counter (frequencies), defaultdict (grouping without key checks), deque (O(1) push/pop both ends for BFS/sliding window), heapq (min-heap for top-k/Dijkstra), and bisect (binary search). They let you focus on the algorithm, not reimplementing structures.
items.topic: DSA in Python: Idiomatic Patterns for Coding Rounds

items.q: How do you implement memoization cleanly in Python?
items.a: Use functools.lru_cache (or cache) as a decorator on a pure recursive function, or a dict you check/populate. lru_cache turns exponential recursion (e.g. naive Fibonacci) into linear with one line.
items.topic: DSA in Python: Idiomatic Patterns for Coding Rounds

items.q: Why is deque preferred over a list for a BFS queue?
items.a: list.pop(0) is O(n) because it shifts all elements; collections.deque gives O(1) appends and pops at both ends, keeping BFS and sliding-window solutions efficient.
items.topic: DSA in Python: Idiomatic Patterns for Coding Rounds

items.q: How do you implement an LRU cache with O(1) operations?
items.a: Combine a hash map (key -> node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency: get moves the node to the front and returns it; put inserts/updates at the front and evicts the tail when over capacity. In Python, collections.OrderedDict with move_to_end gives this concisely.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: LRU Cache, Sliding Window & Top-K

items.q: Explain the sliding window technique with an example.
items.a: Maintain a moving window (two indices) over a sequence, expanding/contracting to satisfy a constraint -- e.g. longest substring without repeating characters: advance the right edge, shrink from the left when a duplicate appears, tracking the max length. O(n) instead of O(n^2).
items.topic: Coding Challenges: LRU Cache, Sliding Window & Top-K

items.q: How do you find the top-K elements efficiently?
items.a: Maintain a min-heap of size k (heapq): push elements and pop the smallest when size exceeds k, leaving the k largest -- O(n log k). For top-k frequent, combine Counter with a heap or use heapq.nlargest.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: LRU Cache, Sliding Window & Top-K

items.q: BFS vs DFS - how do they differ and when use each?
items.a: BFS explores level by level using a queue (deque) -- best for shortest path in unweighted graphs and level-order tree traversal. DFS goes deep first via recursion/stack -- best for cycle detection, topological sort, and exploring all paths. Both are O(V+E) with a visited set.

items.q: How do you represent a graph and avoid infinite loops in traversal?
items.a: Use an adjacency list (dict mapping node -> list of neighbors). Track a visited set (or marked state) and skip already-visited nodes, so cycles don't cause infinite traversal. For weighted shortest paths, use a heap (Dijkstra).

items.q: What must every recursive solution have, and what's a Python caveat?
items.a: A base case that stops recursion and a recursive step combining subproblem results. In Python, deep recursion can hit the default recursion limit (~1000), so very deep trees/graphs may need an iterative (stack/queue) approach or sys.setrecursionlimit.

items.q: What is a monotonic stack and what does it solve?
items.a: A stack kept entirely increasing or decreasing; you pop elements that violate the order as you push. It solves next-greater/next-smaller-element, daily temperatures, and largest rectangle in histogram in O(n) -- far better than the O(n^2) brute force.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Heaps, Stacks & the Monotonic Stack

items.q: When do you reach for a heap (priority queue)?
items.a: When you repeatedly need the smallest/largest element: top-K elements, merging K sorted lists, a running median (two heaps), or shortest paths (Dijkstra). Python's heapq is a min-heap giving O(log n) push/pop and O(1) peek of the minimum.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Heaps, Stacks & the Monotonic Stack

items.q: How do you implement a max-heap with Python's heapq?
items.a: heapq is a min-heap, so push negated values (and negate on pop), or store tuples with an inverted key. For top-K largest, either a min-heap of size k or heapq.nlargest(k, iterable) works.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Heaps, Stacks & the Monotonic Stack

items.q: What is Union-Find and when do you use it?
items.a: A Disjoint Set Union structure with find (which root/component an element is in) and union (merge two components). With path compression and union by rank it's near-O(1) amortized. Use it for connectivity, cycle detection in undirected graphs, and Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.

items.q: What is a Trie and what problems does it solve?
items.a: A prefix tree where each node is a character and root-to-node paths spell prefixes. It gives O(L) insert/search by word length and excels at autocomplete, prefix matching, spell-check, and word- dictionary problems -- faster than scanning all words.

items.q: What do path compression and union by rank do for Union-Find?
items.a: Path compression flattens the tree during find so future lookups are direct; union by rank/size attaches the smaller tree under the larger to keep it shallow. Together they make operations near- constant (inverse-Ackermann) amortized time.

items.q: What is 'binary search on the answer' and when do you use it?
items.a: When the answer is a number in a monotonic range and you can write a feasibility check (can we do it with value X?), you binary-search the answer space instead of an array -- e.g. minimum ship capacity in D days, or minimum eating speed. If feasible(X) is monotonic in X, halve the range using it. O(log(range) * checkCost).
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Binary Search & Its Variants

items.q: How do you find the first or last occurrence of a value?
items.a: Use a lower-bound/upper-bound binary search: for the first occurrence, when arr[mid] >= target move hi left and record; for the last, when arr[mid] <= target move lo right and record. Python's bisect_left/bisect_right implement these directly.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Binary Search & Its Variants

items.q: How do you binary-search a rotated sorted array?
items.a: At each step one half is sorted: find which half (compare arr[lo] to arr[mid]); if the target lies within the sorted half's range, search there, else search the other half. Still O(log n). Handle duplicates as a separate edge case.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Binary Search & Its Variants

items.q: How does XOR find the single number among duplicates?
items.a:
XOR all elements: identical numbers cancel (a^a=0) and x^0=x, so the result is the lone unpaired value. O(n) time, O(1) space -- a classic bit-manipulation trick interviewers love. Variants handle two singles by partitioning on a differing bit.

 Q. When is a greedy algorithm correct versus needing DP?

 A. Greedy works when the problem has the greedy-choice property (a local optimum leads to a global optimum) and optimal substructure -- e.g. interval scheduling by earliest finish time. If local choices can trap you in a suboptimal solution (local optima don't compose), you need DP or another method. You should justify why the greedy choice is safe.

items.q: What does n & (n-1) do and where is it used?
items.a: It clears the lowest set bit of n. Repeatedly applying it counts set bits (Brian Kernighan's algorithm), and n & (n-1) == 0 checks whether n is a power of two (single set bit). Useful for bit counting and power-of-two checks in O(set bits).

items.q: What is topological sort and when do you use it?
items.a: An ordering of a DAG's nodes where every directed edge goes from earlier to later -- used for dependency/prerequisite resolution (course schedule, build order, task scheduling). It only exists if the graph is acyclic; detecting you can't produce a full ordering means there's a cycle.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Topological Sort & Course Schedule

items.q: Explain Kahn's algorithm for topological sort.
items.a: BFS-based: compute in-degrees, enqueue all nodes with in-degree 0, then repeatedly dequeue a node (add to order) and decrement its neighbors' in-degrees, enqueuing any that hit 0. If the order contains all nodes, it's valid; if fewer, a cycle prevents completion. O(V+E).
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Topological Sort & Course Schedule

items.q: How does topological sort detect a cycle?
items.a: If, after processing, the produced ordering has fewer nodes than the graph (Kahn's: some nodes never reach in-degree 0), a cycle exists. In DFS-based topo sort, encountering a node currently on the recursion stack (gray) indicates a back edge and thus a cycle.
items.topic: Coding Challenges: Topological Sort & Course Schedule

items.q: When do you use BFS vs Dijkstra for shortest paths?
items.a:
BFS for unweighted graphs (or uniform edge cost) - each BFS level is one more hop, so the first time you reach a node is the shortest path, O(V+E). Dijkstra for weighted graphs with non-negative weights, using a min-heap to always expand the closest node, O((V+E) log V).

 Q. How does Dijkstra's algorithm work?

 A. Maintain tentative distances (start=0, others=infinity) and a min-heap keyed by distance. Pop the closest unsettled node, and for each neighbor relax: if dist[u]+weight < dist[v], update and push. Once popped, a node's distance is final (relies on non-negative weights). Continue until the heap empties or the target is settled.

items.q: Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges, and what do you use instead?
items.a: Dijkstra assumes once a node is popped its distance is final, which negative edges can violate (a later path could be cheaper). Use Bellman-Ford (O(V*E)), which relaxes all edges V-1 times and can also detect negative cycles.

items.q: How do you reverse a linked list?
items.a: Iteratively walk the list keeping prev, curr, next: save next, point curr.next to prev, advance prev=curr and curr=next; return prev as the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space. Recursively, reverse the rest then set head.next.next = head and head.next = None.

items.q: How do you remove the nth node from the end in one pass?
items.a: Use two pointers from a dummy head: advance the first n+1 steps, then move both until the first hits the end -- the second now sits just before the target, so set second.next = second.next.next. The dummy node handles removing the head cleanly. O(n), single pass.

items.q: Why use a dummy/sentinel head node?
items.a: It removes special-casing for operations at the head (insertion, deletion, merging) -- you always have a node before the 'real' head to rewire, then return dummy.next. It makes pointer logic uniform and far less bug-prone.

items.q: Explain the JavaScript event loop.
items.a: A single thread executes the call stack; when it empties, the loop pulls work from queues. Microtasks (Promises) drain fully before the next macrotask (timers, I/O), keeping JS non-blocking.

items.q: Why does Promise.then run before setTimeout(fn, 0)?
items.a: Promise callbacks are microtasks, which run right after the current task and before any macrotask; setTimeout schedules a macrotask, so it runs later even with 0ms.

items.q: Is async/await different from Promises under the hood?
items.a: No. async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises; await pauses the function and resumes it as a microtask when the awaited Promise settles.

items.q: What is a closure and why is it useful?
items.a: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its defining scope after the outer function returns. It enables private state, memoization, currying, and stable event handlers.

items.q: What's the difference between let, const, and var?
items.a: var is function-scoped and hoisted (initialized undefined); let and const are block-scoped with a temporal dead zone; const additionally forbids reassignment of the binding.

items.q: How can closures cause memory leaks?
items.a: If a closure keeps references to large objects or DOM nodes longer than needed, they can't be garbage-collected; release references or scope them tightly to avoid leaks.

items.q: How is the value of 'this' determined?
items.a: By call site: as a plain call it's undefined/global (strict/non-strict); as obj.method() it's obj; with call/apply/bind it's the bound value; arrow functions capture 'this' lexically from their enclosing scope.

items.q: Explain the prototype chain.
items.a: Each object links to a prototype; property lookups walk this chain until found or reaching null. It enables inheritance and shared methods without copying them onto every instance.

items.q: What is hoisting and how do var, let, const differ?
items.a: Declarations are processed before execution. var is hoisted and initialized to undefined; let and const are hoisted but uninitialized (temporal dead zone) so early access throws; function declarations are fully available.

items.q: What is the difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled?
items.a: Promise.all rejects as soon as any promise rejects and otherwise resolves with all values; Promise.allSettled never rejects and returns each promise's status and value/reason, useful when partial failure is acceptable.

items.q: How do you handle errors with async/await?
items.a: Wrap awaited calls in try/catch; optionally centralize with a wrapper. Unhandled rejections can crash Node, so always catch or attach .catch to fire-and-forget promises.

items.q: What problem does Promise.race solve?
items.a: It settles with the first promise to finish -- handy for timeouts (race a request against a timer) or taking whichever of several sources responds first.

items.q: What's the difference between ES Modules and CommonJS?
items.a: ESM uses static import/export resolved at parse time (enabling tree-shaking and async loading); CommonJS uses dynamic require/module.exports resolved at runtime. ESM is the standard; Node supports both.

items.q: What is tree-shaking and what enables it?
items.a: Eliminating unused exports from the final bundle. It relies on ESM's static, statically-analyzable import/export structure so bundlers can prove code is unused and drop it.

items.q: Why is dynamic import() useful?
items.a: It loads a module on demand and returns a promise, enabling code-splitting and lazy-loading so the initial bundle stays small and features load when needed.

items.q: What's the difference between == and ===?
items.a: === checks type and value with no coercion; == coerces operands to a common type first, which causes surprising results. Best practice is to use === and convert types explicitly.

items.q: List the falsy values in JavaScript.
items.a: false, 0, -0, 0n, '' (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else -- including '0', '[]', and {} -- is truthy.

items.q: Why does NaN === NaN return false, and how do you check for NaN?
items.a: NaN is defined as not equal to anything including itself; use Number.isNaN(x) (or Object.is(x, NaN)) to detect it reliably.

items.q: Debounce vs throttle - what's the difference and when each?
items.a: Debounce waits until events stop for a delay then runs once (good for search input, resize end); throttle runs at most once per interval during continuous events (good for scroll, mousemove). Choose by whether you want the trailing result or steady sampling.

items.q: How would you implement a debounce function?
items.a: Return a function that clears a previous timer and sets a new setTimeout(delay); only when the delay elapses without another call does the wrapped function run -- using a closure to hold the timer id.

items.q: How do you keep heavy computation from freezing the UI?
items.a: Offload to a Web Worker, break work into chunks scheduled with setTimeout/requestIdleCallback, use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates, and memoize repeated results to avoid recomputation.

items.q: How does garbage collection work in JavaScript?
items.a: Mainly mark-and-sweep: the GC starts from roots (globals, the call stack), marks everything reachable, and reclaims unmarked (unreachable) objects. Reachability, not reference counting, determines liveness, so cycles are collected.

items.q: What commonly causes memory leaks in JS apps?
items.a: Uncleared timers/intervals and event listeners, references to detached DOM nodes, closures retaining large objects, and unbounded global caches/maps. They keep objects reachable so the GC can't free them.

items.q: When would you use WeakMap or WeakSet?
items.a: When you want to associate data with an object without preventing its garbage collection -- the weak reference lets the key be collected once nothing else references it, avoiding leaks (e.g. caching metadata per DOM node).

items.q: What's the difference between spread and rest?
items.a: Same ... syntax, opposite roles: spread expands an iterable/object into elements (copying/merging), while rest collects remaining items into an array/object (e.g. function args or the tail of a destructure).
items.topic: ES6+ Essentials: Destructuring, Spread & Optional Chaining

items.q: How does optional chaining differ from &&?
items.a: ?. short-circuits to undefined if a reference is null/undefined, avoiding errors on deep access (a?.b?.c). It's purpose-built for nullish access, clearer than chained && checks.
items.topic: ES6+ Essentials: Destructuring, Spread & Optional Chaining

items.q: ?? vs || for defaults - what's the difference?
items.a: || returns the right side for any falsy value (0, '', false); ?? only does so for null or undefined. Use ?? when 0 or '' are valid values you don't want replaced.
items.topic: ES6+ Essentials: Destructuring, Spread & Optional Chaining

items.q: Explain map, filter, and reduce.
items.a: map transforms each element into a new array of the same length; filter returns a subset matching a predicate; reduce folds the array into a single accumulated value (sum, object, etc.). All return new values without mutating the source.

items.q: How do you update state immutably?
items.a: Create new structures instead of mutating: spread for objects/arrays ({...obj, k:v}, [...arr, x]), and non-mutating methods (filter, map) for changes. This is required for React to detect changes by reference.

items.q: Which common array methods mutate the original?
items.a: sort, reverse, splice, push, pop, shift, unshift mutate in place; map, filter, slice, concat, and spread return new arrays. Mixing them up causes subtle shared-reference bugs.

items.q: What is event delegation and why use it?
items.a: Attaching a single listener to a common ancestor and using event.target to handle events from many children. It reduces listeners, works for dynamically added elements, and improves performance over per-element handlers.

items.q: Explain event bubbling vs capturing.
items.a: Events propagate down from the root to the target (capture phase), then back up to the root (bubble phase). Listeners default to the bubble phase; pass {capture:true} to handle during capture.

items.q: stopPropagation vs preventDefault?
items.a: stopPropagation halts the event from continuing to other elements in the propagation path; preventDefault cancels the browser's default action (e.g. following a link or submitting a form). They're independent.

items.q: What does the Temporal API fix about JavaScript dates?
items.a: It replaces the mutable, quirky Date object with an immutable, timezone-aware API (Instant, ZonedDateTime, Duration), eliminating classic Date bugs around time zones and mutation. It reached Stage 4 for ES2026; usable now via polyfill.

items.q: What is the 'using' keyword for?
