items.a: Explicit Resource Management: using declares a resource whose Symbol.dispose cleanup runs deterministically when the scope exits -- like try/finally for files, locks, or connections, without manual cleanup. Native in Node 22+.

items.q: Name a few other ES2026 additions.
items.a: Math.sumPrecise (accurate floating-point summation), Error.isError (reliable error-type check across realms), and Uint8Array base64/hex conversion helpers -- small but practical standard-library wins.

items.q: Explain microtask vs macrotask priority in the event loop.
items.a: After each macrotask, the engine drains the ENTIRE microtask queue (Promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) before rendering or running the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O). So microtasks always run before the next timer or paint.
items.topic: Event Loop Deep Dive: Microtasks & Starvation

items.q: What is microtask starvation?
items.a: When a microtask keeps enqueuing new microtasks, the queue never drains, so macrotasks and rendering are blocked indefinitely -- freezing the UI or crashing the app. A recursive Promise chain with no yield can cause it.
items.topic: Event Loop Deep Dive: Microtasks & Starvation

items.q: Why does an await resume before a setTimeout(0) scheduled earlier?
items.a: The awaited continuation is a microtask, which runs as soon as the current task finishes draining microtasks -- before any macrotask like setTimeout(0), even one queued earlier.
items.topic: Event Loop Deep Dive: Microtasks & Starvation

items.q: What is XSS and how do you prevent it?
items.a: Cross-site scripting injects attacker scripts that execute in users' browsers with page privileges. Prevent it by not rendering untrusted HTML (React escapes by default; avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML with raw input), sanitizing with DOMPurify when needed, setting a CSP, and using httpOnly/SameSite cookies.
items.topic: Web Security: XSS, CSP & Safe DOM

items.q: What does a Content Security Policy do?
items.a: It restricts which sources scripts, styles, and other resources can load from, so even injected markup can't run arbitrary or external scripts -- a strong defense-in-depth layer against XSS.
items.topic: Web Security: XSS, CSP & Safe DOM

items.q: Why store auth tokens in httpOnly cookies instead of localStorage?
items.a: httpOnly cookies aren't readable by JavaScript, so an XSS payload can't steal them; SameSite limits cross-site sending (CSRF). localStorage tokens are exposed to any script on the page.
items.topic: Web Security: XSS, CSP & Safe DOM

items.q: Implement debounce in JavaScript.
items.a: function debounce(fn, delay){ let t; return function(...args){ clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay); }; } -- the closure holds the timer; each call cancels the pending one, so fn runs only after calls stop for `delay`.

items.q: How does throttle differ from debounce in implementation?
items.a: Throttle runs fn at most once per interval: record the last run time (or a flag) and only invoke if enough time has passed since then (optionally scheduling a trailing call). Debounce instead waits for a pause and resets its timer on every call.

items.q: How would you write a polyfill for Array.prototype.map?
items.a: Add a function on the prototype that creates a result array, loops over the elements, and pushes callback(this[i], i, this) for each index present, returning the new array -- demonstrating you understand map returns a new array and passes (value, index, array).

items.q: How do you implement an Event Emitter's subscribe and emit?
items.a: Store listeners keyed by event name in a Map of arrays. subscribe(name, cb) pushes cb and returns { release: () => remove that exact cb }. emit(name, ...args) looks up the array, clones it (slice), and calls each listener with args. The clone protects the in-progress emission from handlers that add/remove listeners.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Implement an Event Emitter

items.q: Why use a Map instead of a plain object for listeners?
items.a: A plain object inherits prototype keys, so event names like 'toString' or 'valueOf' collide with built- ins. A Map (or Object.create(null)) avoids that, keeping event names isolated from inherited properties.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Implement an Event Emitter

items.q: Why clone the listener array before calling them in emit?
items.a: Because a listener might subscribe or unsubscribe during emission; iterating the live array would skip or double-call handlers. Cloning with slice() snapshots the listeners so the current emit is consistent.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Implement an Event Emitter

items.q: How do you implement deepClone, and when use structuredClone instead?
items.a: Recurse: return primitives as-is; for arrays/objects create a new container and clone each entry, tracking a visited Map to handle circular references. For most cases prefer the built-in structuredClone (preserves Date/Map/Set and cycles); write your own when you need functions, prototypes, or custom control.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Deep Clone, Flatten & Curry

items.q: How would you implement a flatten function?
items.a: Recurse over the array: for each element, if it's an array, flatten it and spread the result; otherwise push it. A depth parameter limits recursion (Array.prototype.flat(depth) is the native equivalent). reduce + recursion is the common pattern.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Deep Clone, Flatten & Curry

items.q: Explain currying and how to implement curry().
items.a: Currying turns f(a,b,c) into a chain f(a)(b)(c). Implement by collecting arguments: if enough args are gathered to satisfy fn.length, call fn; otherwise return a function that accumulates more args via closure. Tests closures and fn.arity understanding.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Deep Clone, Flatten & Curry

items.q: Implement Promise.all.
items.a: Return a new Promise; if the input is empty resolve to []. Track a results array and a counter. For each item, Promise.resolve(item).then(v => { results[i] = v; if (--remaining === 0) resolve(results); }, reject). Indexing by i preserves input order; the first rejection rejects the whole thing.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Implement Promise.all / any / allSettled

items.q: How do Promise.any and Promise.allSettled differ from Promise.all?
items.a: Promise.any resolves with the first fulfilled value and only rejects (with AggregateError) if all reject. Promise.allSettled never rejects -- it waits for every promise and resolves to an array of {status:'fulfilled',value} | {status:'rejected',reason}. Promise.all is fail-fast on first rejection.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Implement Promise.all / any / allSettled

items.q: What edge cases matter when implementing these?
items.a: Empty iterable (Promise.all resolves to [] immediately), non-promise values in the input (wrap with Promise.resolve), preserving result order by index (not completion order), and resolving only after the counter hits zero.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Implement Promise.all / any / allSettled

items.q: How do you implement Function.prototype.bind?
items.a: Return a new function that, when called, invokes the original with `this` set to the bound context and the bound + new args concatenated. e.g. fn.myBind(ctx, ...a) => (...b) => fn.apply(ctx, [...a, ...b]). Handle the new-operator case for completeness.

items.q: How does a memoize function work?
items.a: Wrap fn in a closure holding a cache (Map). On call, build a key from the arguments; if cached, return it; else call fn, store, and return. Single-arg memoize can key directly; variadic needs argument serialization. It trades memory for speed on pure functions.

items.q: What does the classNames utility do?
items.a: It conditionally joins class names: accepts strings, objects ({active: isActive}), and arrays, and returns a single space-separated string of the truthy ones -- avoiding manual template-string concatenation for conditional classes.

items.q: How do leading and trailing options change debounce behavior?
items.a: Trailing (default) invokes after calls stop for the delay. Leading invokes immediately on the first call, then suppresses until the quiet period. With both, it fires on the first call and once more at the end if there were further calls. maxWait forces an invoke if calls never pause.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: debounce/throttle with leading, trailing, cancel & flush

items.q: What do .cancel() and .flush() do on a debounced function?
items.a: cancel() discards any pending trailing invocation (clears the timer and stored args) so it never fires; flush() immediately invokes the pending call now instead of waiting out the delay. Implementing them shows you track pending state, not just a timer.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: debounce/throttle with leading, trailing, cancel & flush

items.q: How does throttle differ from debounce with these options?
items.a: Throttle guarantees the function runs at most once per interval during continuous calls (steady sampling), with leading/trailing controlling whether the first and/or last call in a window fires. Debounce instead waits for a pause and resets on every call.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: debounce/throttle with leading, trailing, cancel & flush

items.q: How do you make a custom object iterable?
items.a: Implement Symbol.iterator as a method returning an iterator -- an object with a next() that returns {value, done}. Then for...of, spread, and destructuring work on it. A generator method is the easiest way to produce that iterator.

items.q: What are generators and why use them?
items.a: Functions (function*) that produce values lazily: yield pauses execution and returns a value, resuming on the next call. They're ideal for lazy/infinite sequences, custom iteration, and memory- efficient pipelines -- computing values on demand instead of all upfront.

items.q: What are async generators for?
items.a: async function* with for await...of iterates over asynchronous sequences -- e.g. consuming paginated API responses or a stream chunk by chunk -- yielding promises that are awaited each step, cleanly modeling async data flows.

items.q: How do you position a tooltip relative to its target?
items.a: Read the trigger's getBoundingClientRect, then place the floating element at the desired side using those coordinates (account for scroll). For robustness, detect viewport overflow and flip/shift to keep it visible -- the problem Floating UI (formerly Popper) automates.

items.q: What makes tooltip positioning tricky?
items.a: Keeping it in the viewport: a top tooltip near the screen's top must flip to the bottom; one near an edge must shift horizontally. You also handle scroll/resize repositioning and stacking context -- naive absolute positioning breaks in these cases.

items.q: What accessibility does a tooltip need?
items.a: Link the trigger to the tooltip with aria-describedby, show it on keyboard focus as well as hover, ensure it's dismissible (Escape) and doesn't trap focus, and don't put essential interactive content in a hover-only tooltip. WAI-ARIA has a tooltip pattern to follow.

items.q: How does AbortController cancel a fetch?
items.a: Create a controller, pass controller.signal to fetch's options, and call controller.abort() to cancel -- the in-flight fetch rejects with an AbortError. You catch and ignore AbortError (it's expected) while still handling real errors.

items.q: How do you use AbortController to fix autocomplete race conditions?
items.a: Keep the current request's controller; when a new keystroke fires, abort the previous controller before starting the new request, so a slow earlier response is canceled and can't overwrite newer suggestions. Cleaner than tracking an 'ignore latest' flag.

items.q: What modern helpers build on AbortSignal?
items.a: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates a signal that auto-aborts after a timeout (easy fetch timeouts), and AbortSignal.any([...signals]) aborts when any input signal does (combine a user-cancel with a timeout). Many APIs (addEventListener, fetch) accept a signal to opt into cancellation.

items.q: What are Web Workers and when should you use one?
items.a: Background threads for running JS off the main thread so heavy work doesn't freeze the UI. Use them for CPU-intensive tasks -- parsing big files, image/data processing, crypto, heavy computation. You communicate via postMessage; workers can't touch the DOM.
items.topic: Web Workers: Offloading Work Off the Main Thread

items.q: How do workers communicate, and what are the data constraints?
items.a: Via postMessage and onmessage. Data is copied using structured clone (not shared), so large transfers have a cost unless you use Transferable objects (e.g. ArrayBuffer ownership transfer) or SharedArrayBuffer for shared memory. Workers have no DOM access.
items.topic: Web Workers: Offloading Work Off the Main Thread

items.q: Web Worker vs Service Worker - what's the difference?
items.a: A Web Worker offloads computation for a page. A Service Worker is a proxy between the app and network -- caching, offline support, push -- and underpins PWAs (and tools like MSW). Different purposes: one is for CPU work, the other for network/lifecycle control.
items.topic: Web Workers: Offloading Work Off the Main Thread

items.q: REST vs GraphQL - key differences and tradeoffs?
items.a: REST: multiple endpoints, HTTP-method/resource oriented, easy HTTP caching, but prone to over- /under-fetching. GraphQL: one endpoint, typed schema, client requests exactly the fields it needs (no over/under-fetch, nested in one round-trip), at the cost of server complexity, harder caching, and query-cost risks.

items.q: What are over-fetching and under-fetching?
items.a: Over-fetching: an endpoint returns more data than the client needs (wasted bytes). Under-fetching: an endpoint returns too little, so the client makes additional requests (extra round-trips). GraphQL addresses both by letting the client specify exactly which fields to return.

items.q: What new problems does GraphQL introduce?
items.a: Harder HTTP caching (single POST endpoint vs cacheable GET URLs), potential for expensive deeply- nested or N+1 queries (needs depth/complexity limiting and dataloaders), schema/versioning discipline, and more server-side setup. Client libraries add normalized caching to compensate.

items.q: What are generics and why use them?
items.a: Generics parameterize code over types so one implementation works for many types while preserving type safety, e.g. Array<T>, avoiding any.

items.q: What is type narrowing? Give an example.
items.a: Narrowing refines a broad type to a specific one in a branch. e.g. if (typeof x === 'string') treats x as string inside that block; in, instanceof, and custom predicates work similarly.

items.q: What does 'unknown' offer over 'any'?
items.a: unknown is type-safe: you can hold any value but must narrow it before use, so the compiler still protects you. any disables checking entirely.

items.q: What are utility types? Give examples.
items.a: Built-in generic types that transform other types: Partial<T> makes properties optional, Pick<T,K>/Omit<T,K> select or drop keys, Record<K,V> builds a map type, ReturnType<F> extracts a function's return type.

items.q: What's the difference between interface and type alias?
items.a: Both describe shapes; interfaces are extendable and support declaration merging and are idiomatic for object/class contracts, while type aliases are more flexible (unions, primitives, tuples, conditional types).

items.q: What are decorators used for in TypeScript?
items.a: They annotate or modify classes, methods, properties, or parameters at design time for cross- cutting concerns -- logging, validation, dependency injection -- and are central to frameworks like Angular and NestJS.

items.q: What is a discriminated union and why is it useful?
items.a: A union of object types sharing a literal discriminant field (e.g., kind). Switching on that field lets the compiler narrow to one variant and enforce exhaustive handling, catching missed cases.
items.topic: Advanced Types: Unions, Guards & Mapped Types

items.q: What is a user-defined type guard?
items.a: A function returning a type predicate (arg is Type); when it returns true, the compiler narrows the argument to that type in the caller, enabling safe access to type-specific members.
items.topic: Advanced Types: Unions, Guards & Mapped Types

items.q: What are mapped types used for?
items.a: To transform each property of a type programmatically -- making them optional, readonly, or remapped -- which is how utility types like Partial<T> and Readonly<T> are built.
items.topic: Advanced Types: Unions, Guards & Mapped Types

items.q: What problem does the satisfies operator solve?
items.a: It validates that a value conforms to a type without widening it, so you keep precise literal/inferred types (e.g. exact keys of a config) while still catching mismatches against the constraint.
items.topic: Modern TS: satisfies, const Type Params & Project Refs

items.q: What are const type parameters?
items.a: Declaring <const T> makes the compiler infer the narrowest literal types for arguments passed to a generic, preserving tuple/literal precision instead of widening to string[]/string.
items.topic: Modern TS: satisfies, const Type Params & Project Refs

items.q: How do project references help large codebases?
items.a: They split a codebase into independently buildable units with their own tsconfig, enabling incremental compilation and faster, cacheable builds across a monorepo.
items.topic: Modern TS: satisfies, const Type Params & Project Refs

items.q: What is a .d.ts declaration file for?
items.a: It describes the types of existing JavaScript (a library or global) without emitting code, letting TypeScript type-check usage of untyped or JS-only packages.

items.q: How do you add types for a library that ships none?
items.a: Install its @types package from DefinitelyTyped if available; otherwise write a local .d.ts with declare module 'lib' describing the API, or augment existing types.

items.q: What does esModuleInterop solve?
items.a: It smooths interop between CommonJS and ES module default imports, letting you write import x from 'cjs-lib' correctly instead of import * as x -- avoiding default-export mismatches.

items.q: What does 'T extends U' do in a generic?
items.a: It constrains the type parameter so only types assignable to U are allowed, letting the compiler assume U's members are present -- e.g. <T extends {id: string}> guarantees t.id exists.

items.q: How do you type a function that returns a property's exact type?
items.a: Use two parameters with a key constraint: function get<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]. The indexed access T[K] returns the precise type of that property.

items.q: What does the infer keyword do?
items.a: Inside a conditional type it captures a type for use in the true branch -- e.g. T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T unwraps a Promise's resolved type. It powers utilities like ReturnType and Awaited.

items.q: What is declaration merging in TypeScript?
items.a: Multiple declarations with the same name combining into one -- e.g. two interfaces of the same name merge their members. It underpins module augmentation, letting you extend existing library or global types.

items.q: How do you add a property to an existing type like Window?
items.a: Use declaration merging / module augmentation: declare global { interface Window { myFlag: boolean } } so the global Window type gains your property without editing the original declaration.

items.q: What is covariance vs contravariance, briefly?
items.a: Covariance preserves direction (a Dog[] is usable as Animal[]); contravariance reverses it (a function taking Animal is usable where one taking Dog is expected). TS applies contravariant parameter checks under strictFunctionTypes.

items.q: What does enabling 'strict' do in tsconfig?
items.a: It turns on a bundle of strict checks at once -- strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, and more -- catching whole classes of bugs at compile time. It's the recommended baseline.

items.q: What does strictNullChecks change?
items.a: null and undefined are no longer assignable to every type; you must explicitly allow and handle them (e.g. via unions or optional chaining), eliminating many 'cannot read property of undefined' bugs.

items.q: What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess do?
items.a: It adds undefined to the type of indexed access (arr[i], obj[key]), forcing you to handle the possibly- missing element -- preventing unsafe assumptions about array/object lookups.

items.q: Enum vs union of string literals - which and why?
items.a: Both model a fixed set. String-literal unions ('a' | 'b') are lighter (no runtime object), tree-shakeable, and simpler; enums give a named runtime object and reverse mappings. Many teams prefer literal unions unless they need the enum's runtime presence.

items.q: What is a tuple type and when is it useful?
items.a: A fixed-length array with a known type at each position, e.g. [string, number]. Useful for paired returns (like useState's [value, setter]) and fixed records where order carries meaning.

items.q: What are literal types?
items.a: Types that allow only an exact value -- 'GET', 42, true -- usually combined into unions to model finite, type-safe options the compiler can exhaustively check.

items.q: What are function overloads and when do you use them?
items.a: Multiple declared call signatures over a single implementation, so the compiler picks the right return type based on the arguments (e.g. a function returning string for one input shape and number for another). Use when one function genuinely behaves differently by input.

items.q: Index signature vs Record - which to use?
items.a: An index signature ({ [k: string]: V }) types arbitrary dynamic keys; Record<K, V> is cleaner and lets you constrain keys to a known union. Prefer Record for known key sets; index signatures for truly open-ended maps.

items.q: What's the risk of an index signature?
items.a: It permits any key, so typos and missing keys aren't caught and access may be wrongly assumed defined. noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to results; a Record with a key union is safer when keys are known.

items.q: What is TypeScript 7.0 / Project Corsa?
items.a: A native rewrite of the TypeScript compiler and language service in Go, delivering around 10x faster type-checking, ~8x faster project load, and lower memory -- the same type system, just far faster at scale.

items.q: How does TS 6.0 relate to TS 7.0?
items.a: 6.0 (March 2026) is the last JavaScript-based release -- a transition that removes deprecations and aligns config defaults so codebases are ready for the native 7.0 engine. Use 6.0 to clean up, then switch engines.

items.q: Can you use the native compiler today, and is it safe?
items.a: Yes -- via @typescript/native-preview and the tsgo binary. It's type-check complete (finds essentially the same errors as 5.9/6.0), so teams use tsgo --noEmit for fast CI checks while keeping tsc for emit during migration.

items.q: any vs unknown vs never - explain each.
items.a: any disables type checking (anything goes, unsafe). unknown is type-safe: holds any value but must be narrowed before use. never is the bottom type with no possible values -- for code that never returns and for exhaustiveness checks. Prefer unknown over any; use never to catch unhandled cases.
items.topic: Type Safety in Practice: any vs unknown vs never

items.q: How do you use never for exhaustiveness checking?
items.a: In a switch over a union, assign the value to a never in the default case (const _x: never = value). If a new union member is added and unhandled, it won't be assignable to never and the build fails -- forcing you to handle it.
items.topic: Type Safety in Practice: any vs unknown vs never

items.q: Why is unknown safer than any for external data?
items.a: Because you must narrow unknown (typeof/guards) before using it, the compiler keeps protecting you; any silently allows any operation, so malformed API data flows through and fails at runtime instead of compile time.
items.topic: Type Safety in Practice: any vs unknown vs never

items.q: How do you safely type data from an API?
items.a: Declare the expected type, but validate the response at runtime with a schema library (zod, io-ts) because TypeScript types are erased and can't check network data. Parse-then-use: the validated result carries the static type safely.
items.topic: Typing APIs, Generics in Practice & Error Handling

items.q: How can you model errors with types instead of throwing?
items.a: Use a Result/Either type -- a discriminated union like { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }. Callers must handle both branches, making failure explicit and type-checked rather than an unchecked throw.
items.topic: Typing APIs, Generics in Practice & Error Handling

items.q: Why isn't a type annotation enough for external data?
items.a: Types vanish at compile time (type erasure), so the runtime can still receive a malformed payload that doesn't match the annotation. Runtime validation is required to actually guarantee the shape.
items.topic: Typing APIs, Generics in Practice & Error Handling

items.q: How do you type a generic debounce so it preserves argument types?
items.a: Constrain the function type and reuse its parameters: debounce<T extends (...a: any[]) => void>(fn: T, ms: number): (...args: Parameters<T>) => void. Parameters<T> extracts fn's argument tuple so callers get full type-checking on the debounced version.
items.topic: Typing Utility Functions: Generic debounce & Polyfills

items.q: What do Parameters<T> and ReturnType<T> do?
items.a: Built-in utility types that extract a function type's argument tuple and its return type respectively -- letting you build wrappers (debounce, memoize, decorators) that stay typed to the original function's signature.
items.topic: Typing Utility Functions: Generic debounce & Polyfills

items.q: How would you type a generic map polyfill?
items.a: function map<T, U>(arr: T[], fn: (item: T, index: number) => U): U[] -- two type parameters relate input element type T to output U, so the result array's type is inferred from the callback's return.
items.topic: Typing Utility Functions: Generic debounce & Polyfills

items.q: How do you type an EventEmitter so events and payloads are checked?
items.a: Define an event-map type (e.g. { login: [User]; logout: [] }) and make the emitter generic over it: subscribe<K extends keyof E>(name: K, cb: (...args: E[K]) => void) and emit<K>(name: K, ...args: E[K]). Now wrong event names or payloads fail at compile time.

items.q: How can recursive/conditional types model deep transformations?
items.a: With recursive conditional types: e.g. type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }, or a Flatten type that recurses into array element types. They let the type system mirror a recursive runtime transform.

items.q: Why type the public API of a utility you implement?
items.a: So misuse (wrong argument types, event names, payloads) is caught at compile time rather than failing at runtime -- turning the implementation into a safe, self-documenting contract, which is what TS-first interviewers look for.

items.q: How would you implement a Pick utility type from scratch?
items.a:
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] } -- a mapped type iterating the selected keys K and indexing T[P] for each. The K extends keyof T constraint ensures only real keys are allowed.

 Q. What TS features power type-level programming?

 A. Mapped types ([K in keyof T]), conditional types (T extends U ? X : Y) with distributivity over unions, infer to capture types, indexed access (T[K]), template literal types, and recursion -- together letting you compute new types from existing ones.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Type-Level Utilities & the Type Challenges

items.q: What is a distributive conditional type?
items.a: When a conditional type acts on a naked type parameter that's a union, it distributes over each member (e.g. Exclude<A|B|C, B> processes each, removing B). Wrapping in a tuple ([T] extends [U]) disables distribution when you don't want it.
items.topic: Coding Challenge: Type-Level Utilities & the Type Challenges

items.q: How do you type a generic, reusable List/Table component?
items.a: Make the component generic over the item type: function List<T>({ items, renderItem }: { items: T[]; renderItem: (item: T, index: number) => React.ReactNode }). Now items and renderItem are tied to the same T, so callers get full type-checking and inference.
items.topic: Typing UI Components: Props, Generics & Events

items.q: How do you type event handlers in React with TypeScript?
items.a: Use React's built-in event types: onChange: (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => void, onClick: (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void. These type e.target and related fields correctly instead of using any.
items.topic: Typing UI Components: Props, Generics & Events

items.q: How can discriminated unions model component props?
items.a: For mutually exclusive prop sets (e.g. a button that's either a link or a submit), a union with a discriminant ({ as: 'link'; href: string } | { as: 'button'; onClick: () => void }) forces callers to provide the right props per variant, checked at compile time.
items.topic: Typing UI Components: Props, Generics & Events

items.q: What problem do branded (nominal) types solve in TypeScript?
items.a: TS is structural, so a UserId and OrderId (both string) are interchangeable, allowing accidental mix- ups. Branding adds a phantom property (string & { __brand: 'UserId' }) so the compiler treats them as distinct types, catching passing the wrong id at compile time.
items.topic: Branded Types, Template Literal Types & Nominal Typing

items.q: What are template literal types useful for?
items.a: Constructing string types from patterns and unions -- e.g. `/users/${string}`, or `${HTTPMethod} ${Path}` to type route strings, event names, or CSS values. They let the type system validate string shapes the compiler otherwise couldn't.
items.topic: Branded Types, Template Literal Types & Nominal Typing

items.q: Structural vs nominal typing - what's the difference?
items.a: Structural (TS default): compatibility is by shape, so any matching structure is assignable. Nominal: compatibility is by declared identity/name. TS simulates nominal typing with branded types when you need two same-shaped types to be incompatible.
items.topic: Branded Types, Template Literal Types & Nominal Typing

items.q: How do you type a recursive tree structure in TypeScript?
items.a: With a self-referential type: type TreeNode<T> = { value: T; children: TreeNode<T>[] }. For file/folder trees, a discriminated union ({type:'file'...} | {type:'folder'; children: Node[]}) lets you narrow on the type field to access the correct properties safely.

items.q: How do discriminated unions help with tree nodes?
items.a: A shared literal discriminant (type: 'file' | 'folder') lets TypeScript narrow a node to its variant in a switch/if, exposing only that variant's fields -- so folder-only properties like children are accessed safely and the compiler catches mistakes.

items.q: What's a caveat with deeply recursive types?
items.a: Very deep recursive conditional/mapped types can hit TypeScript's recursion limit or slow compilation. Keep recursive utility types shallow where possible, and prefer interfaces (which handle self-reference well) for plain recursive data shapes.

items.q: How does typing refs change in React 19?
items.a: ref is a normal prop now, so you declare it in your props type (e.g. ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement>) and read it directly -- forwardRef and its awkward generic signature are no longer required. This simplifies typing component APIs that expose a ref.
items.topic: Typing Modern React: use, Actions & ref-as-prop

items.q: How is useActionState typed?
items.a: It infers a tuple [state, formAction, isPending] from your action function's state type and return: useActionState(action, initialState) types state as the action's return type and formAction for use in a form's action prop, with isPending as boolean -- so the whole flow is type-checked.
items.topic: Typing Modern React: use, Actions & ref-as-prop

items.q: How is the use() hook typed?
items.a: By its argument: use(promise: Promise<T>) returns T (after suspending), and use(context: Context<T>) returns T. So the unwrapped value carries the resource's type with no manual annotation needed.
items.topic: Typing Modern React: use, Actions & ref-as-prop

items.q: What is a Lambda cold start and how do you reduce it?
items.a:
A cold start is the extra latency when Lambda spins up a new execution environment. Reduce it with smaller packages, provisioned concurrency, lighter runtimes, and keeping critical functions warm.

 Q. How does Lambda scale and what are the limits?

 A. It scales horizontally by running more concurrent environments automatically, up to your account concurrency limit; beyond that requests throttle, so set reserved/provisioned concurrency for critical functions.

items.q: How should a Lambda handle state?
items.a: Treat functions as stateless and ephemeral; persist state externally (DynamoDB, S3, RDS). The /tmp space and warm-container reuse aren't reliable for durable state.

items.q: When do you use S3 vs EBS vs EFS?
items.a: S3 for object storage (files, assets, backups) accessed via API; EBS for low-latency block storage attached to one EC2 instance; EFS for a shared POSIX file system mounted by many instances.

items.q: What makes S3 durable, and what are storage classes for?
items.a: S3 redundantly stores objects across devices and facilities for very high durability; storage classes (Standard, IA, Glacier) trade retrieval speed for lower cost based on access frequency.

items.q: Can EBS be attached to multiple instances?
items.a: Standard EBS volumes attach to one instance at a time; for shared access use EFS, or EBS Multi- Attach for specific clustered workloads.

items.q: What is a VPC and why segment it into subnets?
items.a: A VPC is an isolated virtual network. Public subnets host internet-facing resources via an internet gateway; private subnets keep databases/back-ends unexposed, reaching out through a NAT gateway -- improving security and clear traffic control.

items.q: Security group vs network ACL?
items.a: Security groups are stateful and operate at the instance level (return traffic auto-allowed); network ACLs are stateless and operate at the subnet level (must allow both directions). They layer defense-in- depth.

items.q: What is an IAM role and when do you use it over access keys?
items.a: A role grants temporary, automatically rotated credentials assumed by a service or user. Prefer roles for workloads (e.g., EC2/Lambda) over long-lived access keys to reduce leak risk and follow least privilege.

items.q: ECS vs EKS - when do you choose each?
items.a: ECS wins for simpler, AWS-native operations and faster setup; EKS fits when you need Kubernetes portability, its ecosystem/tooling, or existing platform standards -- accepting more operational overhead. A mature answer weighs business needs, not 'one is best.'

items.q: What does AWS Fargate provide?
items.a: Serverless container compute: it runs ECS or EKS tasks without you provisioning or patching EC2 worker nodes, scaling per task and billing for the resources each task uses.

items.q: What are ECS task definitions and services?
items.a: A task definition specifies containers, images, CPU/memory, ports, and env; a service maintains a desired number of tasks, integrates with a load balancer, and manages rolling or blue-green deployments and auto scaling.

items.q: How do you design a highly available, scalable web tier on AWS?
items.a: Place instances across multiple AZs, put a load balancer in front with clear health checks, and attach an Auto Scaling Group that scales on a meaningful metric. Multi-AZ gives fault isolation; the ALB removes unhealthy targets.

items.q: Latency spikes each morning but CPU stays moderate - what do you scale on?
items.a: Question the CPU metric first. Scale on the signal that tracks the bottleneck -- request rate, queue backlog, or application latency -- rather than blindly attaching a CPU threshold that won't trigger.

items.q: What's the difference between an ALB and an NLB?
items.a: ALB operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) with content/path routing and host rules; NLB operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) for ultra-low latency and high throughput, preserving source IP.

items.q: When do you choose DynamoDB over RDS?
items.a: DynamoDB for massive scale, predictable key-based access, serverless ops, and consistent low latency; RDS (relational) for complex joins, ad-hoc queries, and strong transactional/relational needs. Match the data model and access pattern.

items.q: What does Multi-AZ give an RDS database?
items.a: Synchronous standby replication in another Availability Zone with automatic failover, improving availability and durability -- distinct from read replicas, which scale reads.

items.q: Why is partition key design critical in DynamoDB?
items.a: It determines data distribution; a poor key creates hot partitions that throttle, while a well-chosen key spreads load evenly for consistent performance at scale.

items.q: SQS vs SNS - what's the difference?
items.a: SQS is a pull-based queue: consumers poll and process messages once, decoupling producers from variable consumer speed. SNS is push-based pub/sub: one message fans out to many subscribers. They're often combined (SNS to multiple SQS queues).

items.q: What problem does a dead-letter queue solve?
items.a: It captures messages that repeatedly fail processing after a set number of attempts, so poison messages don't block the queue and can be inspected and reprocessed separately.

items.q: When would you use EventBridge over SNS?
items.a: EventBridge for content-based routing of events across many AWS services and SaaS with rich rules and schemas; SNS for simpler high-throughput fan-out to subscribers. EventBridge suits event-driven orchestration.

items.q: What does CloudFront do and why use it?
items.a: It's a CDN that caches content at edge locations close to users, cutting latency and offloading the origin. It also terminates TLS, supports signed URLs/cookies, and runs edge functions for lightweight request logic.

items.q: What routing policies does Route 53 offer?
items.a: Simple, weighted (split traffic by percentage), latency-based (route to lowest-latency region), geolocation, geoproximity, and failover (to a healthy endpoint) -- enabling global availability and traffic control via DNS.

items.q: How do CloudFront and Route 53 work together?
items.a: Route 53 resolves your domain (often via an alias) to a CloudFront distribution, which then serves cached content from the nearest edge and fetches from the origin on a miss -- combining DNS routing with edge caching.

items.q: What are the pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework?
items.a: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability. They give a structured way to evaluate and improve architectures and reason about tradeoffs between competing concerns.

items.q: How do you optimize AWS costs?
items.a: Right-size resources, pick the correct pricing model (Reserved/Savings Plans for steady load, Spot for fault-tolerant batch, On-Demand for spiky), auto scale to demand, tier storage with S3 lifecycle rules, and monitor with Cost Explorer/Trusted Advisor.

items.q: When do you use Spot vs Reserved vs On-Demand?
items.a: Spot for interruptible, fault-tolerant workloads (big discount, can be reclaimed); Reserved/Savings Plans for predictable steady-state usage (committed discount); On-Demand for short-lived or unpredictable workloads where flexibility matters most.

items.q: What does CloudWatch provide?
items.a: Metrics, logs (with Logs Insights queries), alarms that fire on thresholds (notifying via SNS or triggering actions like Auto Scaling), and dashboards -- the core monitoring service for AWS resources and custom app metrics.

items.q: What problem does AWS X-Ray solve?
items.a: Distributed tracing: it follows a request across services (API Gateway, Lambda, etc.), visualizing latency and pinpointing which hop is slow or failing -- invaluable for debugging microservice performance.

items.q: How do CloudWatch alarms drive automation?
items.a: An alarm watches a metric against a threshold and, when breached, can notify via SNS or trigger actions such as scaling an Auto Scaling Group -- turning monitoring into automated response.

items.q: What does API Gateway provide in a serverless app?
items.a: A managed front door for APIs: it terminates REST/HTTP/WebSocket requests, handles authorization, rate limiting/throttling, request validation, and routes to Lambda or other backends -- so you don't run a server to expose endpoints.

items.q: When would you use Step Functions?
items.a: To orchestrate multi-step workflows as a state machine -- sequencing tasks, branching, running steps in parallel, and handling retries/errors declaratively -- instead of hand-coding coordination and error handling across Lambdas.

items.q: How do these enable event-driven architecture?
items.a: API Gateway and events (EventBridge/SQS/SNS) trigger Lambdas; Step Functions coordinate them. Each component scales independently and runs on demand, forming loosely coupled, pay-per-use event-driven systems.

items.q: What are RPO and RTO?
items.a: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (how far back a recovery point can be); RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime to restore service. They drive which DR strategy and cost are justified.

items.q: Compare the main DR strategies.
items.a: Backup & restore (cheap, slow RTO); pilot light (core infra warm, faster); warm standby (scaled- down live copy, faster still); active/active multi-site (near-zero RTO/RPO, most expensive). Pick by the RPO/RTO the business requires.

items.q: How does AWS support multi-region resilience?
items.a: Cross-region replication (S3, RDS read replicas/global databases), automated snapshots, Route 53 health-check failover routing, and IaC to recreate environments quickly in another region.

items.q: What is Amazon Bedrock and why use it?
items.a: A fully managed service exposing many foundation models (Claude, Nova, others) through one API, with security, scaling, and agent tooling -- so you build GenAI features without managing model infrastructure or hosting.

items.q: How would you architect a RAG feature on AWS?
items.a: Store/retrieve embeddings in a vector store (e.g. OpenSearch Serverless), call a Bedrock model with retrieved context, orchestrate steps with Lambda/Step Functions, and front it with API Gateway -- scaling each piece independently and paying per use.

items.q: What does Bedrock AgentCore add?
items.a: Managed building blocks for agents -- orchestration, memory, and tool/function integration -- so you can build agentic workflows on AWS without hand-rolling the coordination and state layers.

items.q: Identity-based vs resource-based policies?
items.a: Identity-based policies attach to an IAM identity (user/group/role) and say what it can do. Resource-based policies attach to a resource (e.g. S3 bucket, SQS queue), specify a principal, and say who can access that resource. Cross-account access often uses resource-based policies.
items.topic: IAM Deep Dive: Policies, Roles & Trust

items.q: How does IAM evaluate whether a request is allowed?
items.a: Deny by default. The request is allowed only if an applicable policy grants an explicit allow AND no policy has an explicit deny -- an explicit deny always overrides any allow. SCPs and permission boundaries can further constrain.
items.topic: IAM Deep Dive: Policies, Roles & Trust

items.q: Why prefer IAM roles over access keys?
items.a: Roles issue temporary, automatically rotated credentials assumed on demand (by EC2/Lambda/federated users), reducing the risk and blast radius of leaked long-lived access keys. It's a core least-privilege practice.
items.topic: IAM Deep Dive: Policies, Roles & Trust

items.q: Explain the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.
items.a: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud -- physical infrastructure, hardware, and managed- service internals; the customer is responsible for security IN the cloud -- data, IAM policies, OS/app patching on EC2, network configuration, and encryption choices. The line shifts toward AWS for more- managed services.

items.q: What are key AWS security best practices?
items.a: Least-privilege IAM with roles (not long-lived keys), encryption at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS), private subnets with tight security groups, secrets in Secrets Manager, CloudTrail/GuardDuty for audit and threat detection, and MFA on privileged accounts.

items.q: How does responsibility differ between EC2 and a managed service like Lambda?
items.a: With EC2 you patch the OS and runtime; with Lambda AWS manages the OS/runtime and you secure only your code, dependencies, IAM permissions, and data. More-managed services shift more responsibility to AWS.

items.q: Sketch a scalable, highly available web architecture on AWS.
items.a: Route 53 -> CloudFront -> ALB across multiple AZs -> auto-scaling group/ECS Fargate -> RDS Multi- AZ or DynamoDB, with ElastiCache for hot data, S3 for assets/uploads, and SQS/EventBridge for async decoupling. Add IAM least privilege, CloudWatch/X-Ray, and IaC. Justify each piece by the requirement (scale, HA, latency).

items.q: How do you add caching layers to reduce load and latency?
items.a: CloudFront edge cache for static/CDN content, ElastiCache (Redis) for hot DB reads/sessions, and HTTP caching headers. Each cuts work closer to the user; pair with sensible TTLs and invalidation to avoid serving stale data.

items.q: How do you make the data tier highly available?
items.a: RDS Multi-AZ for synchronous standby + automatic failover (and read replicas to scale reads), or DynamoDB which is multi-AZ by default; back up with snapshots and consider cross-region for DR per RPO/RTO.

items.q: Walk through how you'd approach a system design interview.
items.a: Clarify functional/non-functional requirements and scale (users, QPS, data), define the API, sketch a high-level architecture (clients, LB, services, data stores, cache, queues), then deep-dive bottlenecks -- scaling reads/writes, caching, partitioning -- justifying each tradeoff. Estimate capacity along the way.

items.q: Explain the CAP theorem and its practical implication.
items.a: Under a network partition you can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance -- and since partitions happen, you really choose between consistency and availability during one. It guides datastore choice (e.g. strongly consistent vs highly available).

items.q: SQL vs NoSQL - how do you choose in a design?
items.a: SQL for strong consistency, complex queries/joins, and transactions; NoSQL for massive scale, flexible schema, and predictable key-based access. Match to access patterns and consistency needs; many systems use both (polyglot persistence).

items.q: Compare rate-limiting algorithms (token bucket, leaky bucket, windows).
items.a: Fixed window: count per interval (simple, edge bursts). Sliding window: smooths the boundary. Token bucket: tokens refill over time, allowing controlled bursts up to capacity. Leaky bucket: processes at a steady rate, smoothing output. Token bucket is the common general-purpose choice.

items.q: Explain cache-aside vs write-through vs write-back.
items.a: Cache-aside: app loads from cache, on miss reads DB and populates cache (lazy). Write-through: writes go to cache and DB synchronously (consistent, slower writes). Write-back: write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously (fast, risk of loss). Choose by read/write mix and consistency needs.

items.q: What is the thundering-herd / cache-stampede problem?
items.a: When a popular cached key expires, many requests miss simultaneously and hit the DB at once, overloading it. Mitigate with request coalescing/locking, staggered TTLs (jitter), or serving stale-while- revalidate.

items.q: How would you design a URL shortener?
items.a: Generate a unique short key (base62 of an auto-increment id, or a hash with collision checks), store key->long-URL in a fast KV store, and redirect on lookup (301 permanent vs 302 if you need analytics). Cache hot keys, and scale the write path via the id-generation strategy. Add custom aliases and click analytics as extensions.

items.q: How do you design a scalable notification system?
items.a: An ingestion API drops events onto a queue (SQS/Kafka) to decouple producers from delivery; worker services fan out per channel (push/email/SMS) through providers, with rate limiting, retries plus a dead-letter queue for failures, deduplication, and per-user preferences/templates. Async + decoupling is the backbone.

items.q: Why use 301 vs 302 redirects in a URL shortener?
items.a: 301 (permanent) lets browsers/CDNs cache the redirect, reducing load but hiding repeat clicks from your analytics; 302 (temporary) routes every click through your service so you can count it. Choose based on whether analytics or load-reduction matters more.

items.q: How would you design a real-time chat system?
items.a: A gateway layer holds WebSocket connections and tracks which server each user is on (presence in Redis); messages are persisted to a write-optimized store (e.g. Cassandra/DynamoDB partitioned by conversation) and fanned out to recipients via pub/sub across servers, with offline users getting push notifications. Add sequence numbers for ordering and delivery...

items.q: Why WebSockets over polling for chat, and what's the fallback?
items.a: WebSockets give a persistent bidirectional connection for low-latency push, avoiding polling's overhead and delay. Fallbacks (long-polling/SSE) cover environments where WebSockets aren't available. The connection layer must scale horizontally and track presence.

items.q: How do you handle message ordering and group fan-out?
items.a: Assign per-conversation sequence numbers (or timestamps + tie-breakers) so clients order messages consistently. For groups, fan out via pub/sub to all members' connection servers; for large groups, consider fan-out-on-read to avoid write amplification.

items.q: How does consistent hashing help a distributed cache?
items.a: It maps keys and nodes onto a hash ring so each key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding/removing a node only remaps the keys between it and its neighbor -- a small fraction -- rather than rehashing everything, minimizing cache misses and data movement on scaling events.

items.q: How do you handle hot keys and cache stampedes?
items.a: Hot keys: replicate them across nodes or add a local in-process cache to spread load. Stampede (many misses when a popular key expires): use request coalescing/locking so one request refills while others wait, stagger TTLs with jitter, or serve stale-while-revalidate.

items.q: What eviction policies does a cache use and why?
items.a: LRU (evict least-recently-used -- good general default), LFU (least-frequently-used -- better when popularity is stable), and TTL-based expiry for freshness. The policy decides what to drop when memory is full, trading hit rate against recency/frequency assumptions.

items.q: How would you design a reliable distributed job queue?
items.a: A durable queue (SQS/Kafka) holds jobs; horizontally-scaled workers pull and process them. Ensure reliability with at-least-once delivery + idempotent workers, visibility timeouts to re-deliver if a worker dies, retries with exponential backoff, and a dead-letter queue for repeatedly-failing messages. Scale workers on queue depth.

items.q: Why prefer idempotent workers over exactly-once delivery?
items.a: Exactly-once is very hard in distributed systems; most queues guarantee at-least-once, so duplicates happen. Making workers idempotent (an operation repeated has the same effect -- e.g. keyed by job id) sidesteps the problem and is far simpler and more robust than chasing exactly-once.

items.q: What is a dead-letter queue and a visibility timeout?
items.a: A dead-letter queue collects messages that fail processing repeatedly so they don't block the main queue and can be inspected. A visibility timeout hides a message while a worker processes it; if the worker doesn't delete it in time (e.g. crashed), it reappears for another worker -- enabling reliable retry.

items.q: How does Twitter Snowflake generate unique IDs?
items.a: A 64-bit ID = timestamp (ms since an epoch, making IDs time-sortable) + machine/datacenter ID (uniqueness across nodes) + a sequence number (uniqueness within the same millisecond on one node). No per-ID network call, so it's fast and horizontally scalable; the leading bit is unused to keep IDs positive.

items.q: UUID vs auto-increment vs Snowflake - the tradeoffs?
items.a: UUIDv4: no coordination, but 128-bit, random (poor DB index locality), not time-sortable. DB auto- increment: simple and sortable but a central bottleneck/SPOF. Snowflake: 64-bit, time-sortable, decentralized, no per-ID network hop -- at the cost of clock-dependency and machine-ID management. Choose by sortability, size, and coordination needs.

items.q: What failure modes must a Snowflake-style generator handle?
items.a: Clock skew and backwards clock movement (can cause duplicate or out-of-order IDs -- must detect and wait or refuse), exhausting the per-ms sequence bits under extreme throughput (wait for next ms), and unique machine-ID assignment across nodes (often via a coordination service). 'No elegance survives a backwards clock.'

items.q: OT vs CRDT for collaborative editing - what's the difference?
items.a: OT transforms concurrent operations against each other so all replicas apply them consistently (Google Docs; typically server-coordinated, complex to implement correctly). CRDTs design the data so concurrent ops commute and merge automatically without central coordination (good for offline/P2P, at some metadata cost). Both aim for convergence; they differ i...

items.q: How do edits from multiple users converge consistently?
items.a: Every replica must reach the same final state regardless of operation order. OT achieves this by transforming operations relative to concurrent ones; CRDTs by using data types whose merges are commutative, associative, and idempotent. Both preserve user intent and guarantee eventual consistency across clients.

items.q: What else does a collaborative editor need beyond convergence?
items.a: Real-time transport (WebSockets), presence and live cursors, document persistence and versioning/history, access control, and a strategy for offline edits syncing on reconnect. Latency hiding (optimistic local apply) keeps typing responsive while changes propagate.

items.q: How do you efficiently find nearby drivers/places at scale?
items.a: Use a spatial index instead of computing distance to everyone: geohash encodes coordinates so nearby points share string prefixes (prefix/range queries), or a quadtree subdivides space so you only scan relevant cells. Redis geospatial commands or a geo-indexed store back fast 'within radius' lookups.

items.q: What is geohashing and why is it useful here?
items.a: Geohash maps a lat/long to a short string where shared prefixes mean geographic proximity. This turns 'find nearby' into a prefix/range query and shards naturally by region - far cheaper than pairwise distance, and easy to store/index in a KV store.

items.q: What are the scaling challenges in a ride-matching system?
items.a: A massive write volume of frequent driver location pings (favor an in-memory geo store), hot/dense areas (cell load imbalance, needs finer subdivision), real-time delivery of updates to riders (WebSockets), and reconciling rapidly-moving data with matching decisions while avoiding double- assigning a driver.

items.q: How do replication and quorums control consistency in a KV store?
items.a: Each key is replicated to N nodes. A read/write succeeds after R/W replicas respond. If W + R > N, reads and writes overlap on at least one node, giving strong consistency; smaller W/R favor lower latency and higher availability at the cost of possibly stale reads (eventual consistency). The knobs tune the CAP tradeoff.

items.q: How are conflicts from concurrent writes resolved?
items.a: With versioning: vector clocks capture causality so the system can detect concurrent (conflicting) versions and either resolve automatically or return siblings to the client; simpler systems use last- writer-wins by timestamp (which can lose data). Read-repair and anti-entropy (Merkle-tree comparison) fix replica drift over time.

items.q: How do nodes track membership and detect failures?
items.a: A gossip protocol: nodes periodically exchange state with random peers, so membership changes and failures propagate without a central coordinator. Combined with consistent hashing, this lets the cluster rebalance and route around failed nodes in a decentralized way.

items.q: How do you find the top-K frequent items in a data stream with limited memory?
items.a: Combine a Count-Min Sketch (estimates item frequencies in sublinear space using multiple hashed counter rows) with a min-heap of the current top-K. For exact results on small data, a hash-map of counts plus a size-k min-heap suffices (O(n log k)); at stream scale you accept bounded approximation for huge memory savings.

items.q: What is a Count-Min Sketch and what's its tradeoff?
items.a: A probabilistic frequency estimator: a 2D array of counters where each item increments one counter per hash function; a query takes the minimum across its counters. It uses sublinear memory and never undercounts, but can overcount (collisions) -- a small, bounded error tunable by width/depth. Great for heavy hitters at scale.

items.q: How do you compute top-K across a distributed stream?
items.a: Shard the stream by item key so each node counts a partition, compute each node's local top-K (with heaps or sketches), then merge the candidates at an aggregator to get the global top-K. Multi- stage aggregation and windowing keep it scalable; merging approximate sketches is supported by their additivity.

items.q: Why not use 2PC for distributed transactions across microservices, and what's the alternative?
items.a: 2PC (prepare then commit via a coordinator) is strongly consistent but blocking and coordinator- dependent -- it doesn't scale well and is brittle under failure across services. The Saga pattern is the common alternative: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions to undo on failure, giving eventual consistency without distributed locks.

items.q: Choreography vs orchestration Sagas - what's the difference?
items.a: Choreography: each service listens for events and emits its own, with no central controller -- decentralized and loosely coupled, but the flow is implicit and can become hard to follow. Orchestration: a central orchestrator explicitly invokes each step and handles failures/compensations -- clearer and easier to monitor, at the cost of a coordinating component.

items.q: What makes compensating transactions tricky to design?
items.a: They must semantically undo a completed step, which isn't always a simple reverse -- e.g. refunding a payment must handle fees, partial refunds, currency changes, and compliance, not just subtract the amount. Some actions aren't fully reversible, so you design for idempotency and business-correct compensation, sometimes with retries or manual handling.

items.q: What is a context window and why does it matter?
items.a: It's the maximum number of tokens (prompt plus response) the model can consider at once. Exceeding it drops earlier content, so you manage it with summarization, chunking, or retrieval.

items.q: What is tool use / function calling in an LLM?
items.a: The model decides to call a defined function with structured arguments; your code runs it and returns the result, which the model uses to continue -- letting LLMs fetch live data or take actions.

items.q: What is RAG and when would you use it?
items.a: Retrieval-Augmented Generation fetches relevant documents into the prompt so the model answers from grounded, current sources rather than memory, reducing hallucination for docs Q&A.

items.q: What is few-shot prompting and when does it help?
items.a: Including a few input/output examples in the prompt to demonstrate the desired pattern. It improves consistency and format adherence for tasks hard to specify with instructions alone.

items.q: How do you reduce hallucinations from an LLM?
items.a: Ground it with retrieved sources (RAG), instruct it to answer only from context or say it doesn't know, request citations, lower temperature, and verify high-stakes outputs externally.

items.q: What does temperature control?
items.a: The randomness of token sampling: low temperature gives focused, deterministic output (good for facts/code); high temperature gives more varied, creative output.

items.q: What is an LLM agent and how does it differ from a single prompt?
items.a: An agent runs a loop: it reasons, decides to call tools, observes results, and iterates toward a goal -- handling multi-step tasks autonomously, versus a single prompt that returns one response with no tool use or follow-up.

items.q: What problem does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve?
items.a: It standardizes how models connect to external tools and data sources, so integrations are reusable across apps and models instead of bespoke per-tool glue code.

items.q: How do you control cost and latency in an LLM app?
items.a: Pick the right model per task, cache repeated prompts/results, trim context, stream output, and batch where possible -- balancing quality against tokens and response time.

items.q: How do you evaluate an LLM feature's quality?
items.a: Build representative test sets with expected behavior, combine automated metrics with human review (and sometimes LLM-as-judge), and track them over time to catch regressions when prompts or models change.

items.q: What is prompt injection and how do you mitigate it?
items.a: An attack where malicious instructions in untrusted content try to override the system's intent. Mitigate by separating trusted instructions from untrusted data, constraining tool permissions, validating outputs, and not blindly executing instructions found in content.

items.q: When should a human stay in the loop?
items.a: For high-stakes or irreversible actions (financial, legal, destructive operations) and low-confidence outputs -- the model proposes, a human approves, with logging for auditability.

items.q: How do you get reliable structured (JSON) output from an LLM?
items.a: Define the desired schema (or a tool/function definition), instruct strict JSON with no prose, validate the output against the schema, and retry or repair on failure. Lower temperature helps determinism.

items.q: What is function/tool calling and how does it give structure?
items.a: You declare functions with typed parameters; the model returns structured arguments matching that schema instead of free text, which your code validates and executes -- a reliable bridge between language and code.

items.q: Why validate LLM output even when it looks correct?
items.a: Models can produce malformed or hallucinated fields; treating output as untrusted and validating against a schema (with retries) prevents bad data from flowing downstream.

items.q: How do you give an LLM 'memory' across turns?
items.a: Short-term by including recent conversation in the prompt; long-term by persisting facts or embeddings externally and retrieving the relevant ones (RAG) into each prompt, since the model itself is stateless between calls.

items.q: Walk through a RAG pipeline.
items.a: Chunk documents, embed each chunk into vectors, store them in a vector index; at query time embed the question, retrieve the top-k similar chunks, and put them in the prompt so the model answers from grounded sources.

items.q: Why not just put everything in a long context window?
items.a: Larger contexts cost more tokens, add latency, and can dilute the model's focus ('lost in the middle'). Retrieving only relevant chunks keeps prompts lean, cheaper, and better grounded.

items.q: How do you reduce LLM cost and latency in production?
items.a: Right-size the model per task (route simple queries to cheaper ones), cache repeated/similar prompts and static context, trim context to what's relevant, stream output to improve perceived latency, and batch requests where the workload allows.

items.q: What is prompt caching and when does it help?
items.a: Reusing a previously processed static prefix (system prompt, large context) so repeated calls skip recomputing it -- cutting cost and latency when many requests share the same large preamble.

items.q: How do you decide which model size to use?
items.a: Define a quality bar with evals, then pick the smallest/cheapest model that clears it for each task type -- routing harder cases to larger models -- balancing the cost/latency/quality triangle rather than defaulting to the biggest.

items.q: What does it mean that a model is multimodal?
items.a:
It can process more than one input type -- e.g. text plus images or PDFs -- in the same prompt, enabling tasks like reading a document, describing a chart, or extracting fields from a scanned form.

 Q. How would you build a document-data-extraction feature?

 A. Send the document (image/PDF) with an instruction and a target output schema, ask for strict structured output, validate the result, and chunk or summarize very large documents to fit the context window and control cost.

items.q: What are the trade-offs of passing large documents to an LLM?
items.a: They consume many tokens (cost and latency) and can dilute focus; manage by extracting relevant pages, chunking with retrieval, and validating outputs rather than trusting a single huge-context pass.

items.q: When do you use RAG vs fine-tuning vs just prompting?
items.a: Prompt first (cheap, fast). Use RAG when answers need current or proprietary knowledge grounded in documents. Fine-tune for consistent style/format or specialized behavior at scale. They combine -- RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behavior, prompting throughout.
items.topic: Prompting vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Choosing an Approach

items.q: Why is RAG often preferred over fine-tuning for knowledge?
items.a: Knowledge changes; RAG retrieves up-to-date documents at query time and cites sources, while fine-tuning bakes in static knowledge that ages and can't easily be updated or attributed.
items.topic: Prompting vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Choosing an Approach

items.q: What does fine-tuning do well that prompting doesn't?
items.a: Reliably enforce a consistent style, format, or narrow behavior across many calls without long prompts, and can improve quality on specialized tasks -- at the cost of data prep, training, and reduced flexibility.
items.topic: Prompting vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Choosing an Approach

items.q: What is a system prompt and what belongs in it?
items.a: Persistent, high-priority instructions that frame every turn -- the assistant's role, tone, constraints, and output format. Put stable rules there; keep per-request specifics in the user message. It steers behavior without repeating instructions each turn.

items.q: How do you guard against prompt injection in conversation design?
items.a: Keep trusted instructions (system prompt) separate from untrusted input (user content, retrieved docs), don't let content dictate actions, constrain tool permissions, and validate outputs -- treat anything from outside as data, not commands.

items.q: How do you manage long multi-turn conversations within the context window?
items.a: Summarize or trim older turns while preserving key state/decisions, or store history externally and retrieve only what's relevant -- keeping the prompt within the window without losing important context.

items.q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
items.a: An open standard for connecting LLMs to external tools and data sources in a uniform way, so a given integration (a database, an API, a file system) works across different apps and models instead of bespoke per-tool glue.
items.topic: Claude in 2026: Opus 4.x, Claude Code & MCP

items.q: What is Claude Code and where does it fit?
items.a: An agentic coding tool (CLI/IDE) for delegating coding tasks to Claude -- planning, editing files, running commands/tests -- fitting into developer and CI workflows behind human review, accelerating mechanical work.
items.topic: Claude in 2026: Opus 4.x, Claude Code & MCP

items.q: How do you choose a Claude model for a task?
items.a: Define a quality bar with evals, then pick the smallest/cheapest model that clears it per task type -- routing harder cases to larger Opus models -- balancing the cost/latency/quality triangle rather than defaulting to the biggest.
items.topic: Claude in 2026: Opus 4.x, Claude Code & MCP

items.q: How do you evaluate an LLM feature systematically?
items.a: Build a representative eval set (inputs + expected behavior or rubric), score with automated checks, human review, and/or LLM-as-judge, and track scores over time to catch regressions when prompts/models change -- treating it like a test suite for a non-deterministic system.

items.q: What is LLM-as-judge and its caveats?
items.a: Using a model to grade another model's outputs against a rubric -- scalable and cheaper than all- human review, but it can be biased or inconsistent, so validate it against human labels and use clear criteria.

items.q: Offline evals vs online monitoring - why both?
items.a: Offline evals catch regressions before release on a fixed set; online monitoring (user feedback, success metrics, sampling) catches real-world issues the eval set missed. Together they cover pre- and post-deployment quality.

items.q: What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?
items.a: An attack where malicious instructions in untrusted content (web pages, docs, user input) try to override the system prompt or exfiltrate data. Defend by separating trusted instructions from untrusted data, never executing instructions found in content, constraining tool permissions, requiring confirmation for sensitive actions, and validating outputs.

items.q: Why is the principle of least privilege critical for LLM tools?
items.a: Because a successfully injected prompt acts with whatever permissions the model's tools have. Scoping tools to the minimum (read-only where possible, no destructive/financial actions without confirmation) limits the blast radius of a successful injection.

items.q: How should you treat retrieved documents in a RAG system, security-wise?
items.a: As untrusted data, not instructions -- a poisoned document could contain injection text. Keep it clearly delimited from system instructions and never let its content trigger tool calls or override behavior.

items.q: How would you architect a document-Q&A (RAG) feature?
items.a: Chunk and embed documents into a vector store; at query time embed the question, retrieve top-k relevant chunks, build a prompt with that context plus system instructions, call the model (streaming), then validate/cite the output. Add caching, evals, and injection defenses.
items.topic: Building an AI Feature: Architecture & Tradeoffs

items.q: What tradeoffs do you weigh when designing an LLM feature?
items.a: The cost/latency/quality triangle (model size, caching, context length), grounding vs hallucination (RAG, citations), safety (prompt-injection, output validation, least-privilege tools), and where a human must stay in the loop for sensitive or irreversible actions.
items.topic: Building an AI Feature: Architecture & Tradeoffs

items.q: How do you keep an AI feature's responses grounded and trustworthy?
items.a: Ground answers in retrieved sources (RAG) and ask for citations, validate structured output against a schema, constrain scope via the system prompt, and evaluate with a test set -- so answers are sourced and checkable rather than confident guesses.
items.topic: Building an AI Feature: Architecture & Tradeoffs

items.q: How can you use an LLM effectively to prepare for technical interviews?
items.a: Generate practice problems and variations, get level-appropriate explanations, run mock interviews with feedback, and have it critique your solutions for edge cases and complexity -- using it for active recall and feedback rather than passively reading answers.
items.topic: AI-Assisted Interview Prep: Using LLMs to Study Effectively

items.q: What are the risks of relying on an LLM for interview prep?
items.a: It can give wrong complexity analysis, hallucinate APIs/methods, or sound confident while being subtly incorrect. Verify against official docs and authoritative platforms, and run the code -- never memorize an answer you can't reproduce and explain yourself.
items.topic: AI-Assisted Interview Prep: Using LLMs to Study Effectively

items.q: How do you keep AI help from undermining real learning?
items.a: Use it to test and stretch your understanding (explain-back, harder variants, find your gaps), not to hand you solutions. The interview rewards reasoning you can reproduce under pressure, which only comes from doing the work yourself.
items.topic: AI-Assisted Interview Prep: Using LLMs to Study Effectively

items.q: When do you use few-shot vs zero-shot prompting?
items.a: Zero-shot (instruction only) for simple, well-understood tasks; few-shot (a few input/output examples) when the format or behavior is hard to specify in words, or to improve consistency on edge cases. Few-shot costs tokens, so use the minimum examples that work.
items.topic: Prompt Patterns: Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought & Structured Output

items.q: What is chain-of-thought prompting and when does it help?
items.a: Prompting the model to reason step by step before answering. It improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning, math, and complex logic; for simple lookups it adds cost without benefit. You can keep the reasoning internal and surface only the final answer.
items.topic: Prompt Patterns: Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought & Structured Output

items.q: How do you reliably get structured (JSON) output?
items.a: Specify the exact schema (or use tool/function calling), instruct strict JSON with no prose, validate the result against the schema, and retry/repair on failure; lower temperature for determinism. Treat output as untrusted until validated.
items.topic: Prompt Patterns: Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought & Structured Output

items.q: How do you implement streaming responses in a chat UI?
items.a: Consume a streamed response (SSE or a ReadableStream from fetch) and append chunks to the in- progress assistant message as they arrive, re-rendering incrementally. Provide a stop button (AbortController) and handle stream errors/partial output gracefully.

items.q: What state and UX does a chat interface need?
items.a: A messages array (role+content), optimistic rendering of the user's message, a typing/loading indicator, error+retry, auto-scroll with a manual scroll-to-bottom control, and safe markdown/code rendering (sanitized). Abortable requests let users cancel long generations.

items.q: Why sanitize and constrain rendered AI output in a UI?
items.a: Model output (and any embedded tool/retrieved content) is untrusted -- rendering it as raw HTML risks XSS, and tool outputs could carry injection. Sanitize markdown/HTML and never let rendered content trigger privileged actions.

items.q: What is a vector database and why does RAG need one?
items.a: It stores embeddings (vectors representing meaning) and performs fast approximate nearest- neighbor search to find chunks semantically similar to a query. RAG needs it to retrieve the most relevant context to ground the model's answer, rather than scanning all documents linearly.

items.q: How does chunking strategy affect RAG quality?
items.a: Chunk size and overlap trade context against precision: too large dilutes relevance and wastes tokens; too small loses context. Overlap preserves continuity across boundaries. Good chunking (often semantic/section-based) is one of the biggest levers on retrieval quality.

items.q: What is hybrid search and when does it help?
items.a: Combining vector similarity with keyword search (e.g. BM25) and merging results. It helps when exact terms matter (names, codes, acronyms) that pure semantic search may miss, improving recall over either method alone.

items.q: What should you log and monitor for an LLM application?
items.a: Per-interaction: prompt, response, model, latency, token usage, and cost, with tracing across multi- step chains/agents. Plus operational metrics (latency, error rate, cost) and quality signals (user feedback, refusal/hallucination flags, retrieval relevance) to catch issues in production.

items.q: How is LLM observability different from offline evals?
items.a: Evals test on a fixed dataset before release; observability watches real production traffic -- actual prompts, costs, latencies, failures, and user feedback -- surfacing issues the eval set missed and feeding new cases back into evals. You need both.

items.q: What is drift and how do you detect it?
items.a: A degradation in quality when the model, prompt, retrieved data, or input distribution changes. Detect it by tracking quality metrics and feedback over time, sampling and re-scoring outputs (LLM-as- judge or human), and alerting when scores or error rates move.

items.q: What distinguishes an AI coding agent from autocomplete?
items.a: Autocomplete suggests next tokens; an agent takes a goal and runs a loop -- planning, editing files, executing commands and tests, reading results, and iterating -- to finish a multi-step task.

items.q: What is the agentic loop?
items.a: Plan, then act (edit or run), then observe (results, errors, tests), then refine, repeated until the goal is met or it hits a blocker -- letting the agent self-correct.

items.q: How do you use coding agents safely?
items.a: Give clear bounded goals, review the diff, run your own tests, restrict permissions and scopes, and keep a human in the loop for merges.

items.q: How do you give a coding agent good context?
items.a: Point it at the relevant files and tests, state a clear acceptance criterion, and scope the task. Narrow, well-specified tasks beat vague ones; for big repos, indicate the modules involved so it doesn't guess.

items.q: How should you review an agent's code changes?
items.a: Read the full diff, run the existing test suite plus new tests, check edge cases and security, and avoid merging changes you don't understand -- the agent accelerates work but you own correctness.

items.q: Why do smaller tasks yield better agent results?
items.a: Bounded tasks have clearer success criteria and less room for the agent to drift or accumulate errors across many steps, so verification is easier and outcomes more reliable.

items.q: Where does a coding agent like Codex fit in a team workflow?
items.a: In the CLI for quick tasks, in the IDE for inline edits and review, and in CI for automated chores (test fixes, dependency bumps, PR drafts) -- always behind human approval and a passing test suite before merge.
