items.topic: Integrating Codex: CLI, IDE & CI Workflows

items.q: How do you scope an agent's permissions safely?
items.a: Grant least privilege: limit which repos and whether it can write, require review on its branches, and isolate credentials so an automated change can't bypass checks or touch unintended systems.
items.topic: Integrating Codex: CLI, IDE & CI Workflows

items.q: How should agent output be quality-gated in CI?
items.a: Run the full test suite, linters, and security scans on the agent's branch, require passing checks plus human review, and never auto-merge changes that aren't independently verified.
items.topic: Integrating Codex: CLI, IDE & CI Workflows

items.q: What makes a good prompt for a coding agent?
items.a:
A bounded task with clear acceptance criteria, the relevant files/tests in context, and constraints stated explicitly. For complex work, ask for a plan first, then iterate in small, reviewable steps.

 Q. What are the limits of today's coding agents?

 A. They can hallucinate non-existent APIs, miss unstated constraints, and degrade on large vague tasks. They accelerate mechanical work but don't replace architectural judgment or final human review.
items.topic: Prompting Patterns & Limits of Coding Agents

items.q: How do you reduce wasted agent iterations?
items.a: Scope tasks tightly, give failing tests as the target, point at specific modules, and require a plan on ambiguous work so the agent doesn't drift across many costly steps.
items.topic: Prompting Patterns & Limits of Coding Agents

items.q: Why is test-driven prompting effective with coding agents?
items.a: Failing tests give the agent an objective, verifiable definition of done, so it iterates until they pass rather than guessing intent -- and you can trust the result because the suite proves it.

items.q: What does a spec-driven agent workflow look like?
items.a: Provide a clear spec or acceptance criteria, have the agent propose a plan, implement against the spec, and run tests/linters; you review the diff against the same criteria before merging.

items.q: How does giving tests reduce agent drift?
items.a: Tests bound the task and catch regressions immediately, so the agent self-corrects toward a concrete target instead of wandering across an under-specified problem.

items.q: How do you safely have an agent do a multi-file refactor?
items.a: Define the exact change and the affected scope, let it locate all call sites, apply consistent edits, and run the full test suite to surface breakage -- then review the complete diff before merging.

items.q: What's the risk of agent edits in a large codebase?
items.a: Inconsistent or partial changes and missed call sites that compile-break or silently change behavior. Comprehensive tests plus a human review of the aggregate diff are the guardrails.

items.q: How do you help an agent navigate a big repo?
items.a: Point it at relevant modules and entry points, share conventions and constraints, and scope the task tightly so it doesn't waste steps exploring irrelevant code or drift from the goal.

items.q: What security risks come with AI-generated code?
items.a: Subtle logic bugs, insecure patterns (injection, weak crypto, hardcoded secrets), and hallucinated or unvetted dependencies that add supply-chain risk. The fluent, confident output can mask these, so it needs rigorous review.
items.topic: Security, Review & Trust Boundaries for AI Code

items.q: How do you safely incorporate agent code into a codebase?
items.a: Run it through the same gates as any contributor: human diff review, SAST and secret scanning, dependency/license checks, and tests in CI -- with least-privilege permissions and no auto-merge of unreviewed changes.
items.topic: Security, Review & Trust Boundaries for AI Code

items.q: Why treat agent output as untrusted?
items.a: Because the model optimizes for plausible code, not guaranteed-correct or secure code; verifying via review and automated checks prevents confident-but-wrong changes from reaching production.
items.topic: Security, Review & Trust Boundaries for AI Code

items.q: How do you use an agent to debug a failing test?
items.a: Give it the failing test, the error output, and the relevant code; let it form hypotheses, make edits, and re-run the test loop until it passes -- then review its diff and reasoning to confirm the fix is correct, not a hack.

items.q: How should agent-generated tests be reviewed?
items.a: Check that assertions are meaningful (testing behavior and edge/error cases), not just lines executed for coverage. Reject tautological or coverage-padding tests; keep the ones that would catch real regressions.

items.q: Why does an agent need a runnable environment to debug well?
items.a: So it can execute tests and observe real results to verify fixes, rather than guessing from static reading -- closing the loop turns speculation into evidence-based correction.

items.q: Where do coding agents fit in a PR/review workflow?
items.a: They draft changes or PRs; a human reviews the diff, runs and reads the tests, checks security and edge cases, and owns the merge. The agent accelerates the mechanical work but doesn't replace review or accountability.
items.topic: Code Review, PR Workflows & When Not to Use an Agent

items.q: When should you NOT rely on a coding agent?
items.a: For ambiguous architectural decisions, security-critical code, and large under-specified tasks where judgment and context dominate -- supervise tightly or do it yourself. Agents excel at bounded, well- specified, mechanical work.
items.topic: Code Review, PR Workflows & When Not to Use an Agent

items.q: How should agent contributions be treated in review?
items.a: Like a capable junior's PR: read every line, don't merge what you don't understand, require passing tests and checks, and give feedback to refine -- never rubber-stamp because it looks confident.
items.topic: Code Review, PR Workflows & When Not to Use an Agent

items.q: How can a coding agent speed up onboarding to a new codebase?
items.a: Ask it to summarize structure, trace a feature's path across files, explain complex functions, and locate where changes belong -- grounded in the real code -- turning days of code archaeology into guided exploration you then verify.

items.q: What's the risk of trusting an agent's code explanation?
items.a: It can misread, over-generalize, or hallucinate behavior that isn't there. Verify against the source and by running code/tests; treat explanations as a fast first map, not authoritative documentation.

items.q: How do you get the most accurate explanations from an agent?
items.a: Give it the relevant files/context, ask specific questions (this function, this flow), and confirm key claims by reading the cited code or running it -- narrow, grounded prompts beat broad 'explain everything' asks.

items.q: What is Codex Goal Mode?
items.a: A mode (now generally available) where Codex pursues a defined objective autonomously over long horizons -- planning, acting, and course-correcting on failures -- rather than doing one-shot edits, suited to multi-step tasks with a clear success criterion.
items.topic: Codex in 2026: Goal Mode, Cloud Agents & Workflow Fit

items.q: Where does Codex fit across a 2026 workflow?
items.a: In the CLI for quick tasks, the IDE for inline edits/review, and the cloud/CI for delegated chores (test fixes, dependency bumps, PR drafts) -- always behind scoped permissions, passing tests, and human review before merge.
items.topic: Codex in 2026: Goal Mode, Cloud Agents & Workflow Fit

items.q: What makes agentic coding reliable in practice?
items.a: Bounded, well-specified goals; tests and linters as guardrails; least-privilege permissions; and mandatory human review of diffs. The agent accelerates mechanical work but doesn't own correctness or architecture.
items.topic: Codex in 2026: Goal Mode, Cloud Agents & Workflow Fit

items.q: How are coding agents used in CI/CD?
items.a: For unattended maintenance: dependency upgrades, fixing failing tests, codemods, issue triage, and PR drafts -- triggered on schedule/events, run with scoped credentials in isolation, with the output PR gated behind CI and human review before merge.

items.q: How do you keep automated agent changes safe?
items.a: Bound the task with a clear definition of done (passing tests), isolate execution with least-privilege credentials, never auto-merge, and require CI plus human review -- so the agent accelerates toil without bypassing safeguards.

items.q: What maintenance tasks suit agents best?
items.a: Mechanical, well-specified, verifiable ones: dependency bumps, lint/format fixes, test repair, and routine refactors -- where success is checkable by tests and the change is bounded.

items.q: How do you evaluate the quality of agent-generated code?
items.a: On correctness (passes tests + meets spec), security (no injection/secrets/unsafe patterns), maintainability (clear, idiomatic, consistent), and scope discipline (only the asked-for change). Read every line and run the suite -- same bar as any PR.

items.q: What are common red flags in AI-generated code?
items.a: Hallucinated or non-existent APIs, over-broad refactors beyond the task, missing edge/error cases, plausible-but-wrong logic, and inconsistent style. Confident phrasing can mask these, so verify against the source and tests.

items.q: How does reviewing agent code differ from writing it?
items.a: It shifts your effort from authoring to rigorous review -- you must understand and verify code you didn't write, which can be harder. The discipline (tests, reading every line, no unexplained merges) stays the same as human PRs.

items.q: How are AI coding tools changing technical interviews?
items.a: They shift evaluation from memorized syntax toward judgment -- how you decompose a problem, prompt effectively, verify and test output, and catch AI mistakes. Many take-homes now allow AI, so the skill tested is integrating and reviewing it, not raw recall.
items.topic: Using Agents in Live Coding & Take-Home Interviews

items.q: If allowed to use an agent in an interview, how do you use it well?
items.a: For boilerplate, scaffolding, and exploration -- but read and understand every line, run and test it, explain your choices, and correct its errors. Treat it as a fast junior whose output you own; never paste code you can't explain.
items.topic: Using Agents in Live Coding & Take-Home Interviews

items.q: What new skill do interviewers probe in the AI era?
items.a: The ability to critically review and correct AI-generated code -- spotting hallucinated APIs, security issues, and subtle bugs -- plus clear reasoning about tradeoffs that a model can't decide for you.
items.topic: Using Agents in Live Coding & Take-Home Interviews

items.q: How can an agent help you master implementation challenges?
items.a: Solve it yourself first, then have the agent review for edge cases (e.g. EventEmitter prototype-key collisions, deep-clone cycles), compare alternative approaches and their complexity, and generate test cases to validate your version -- using it as a reviewer/coach, not an answer key.
items.topic: Solving & Explaining Coding Challenges with an Agent

items.q: Why not just have the agent write the coding-challenge solution?
items.a: You learn nothing you can reproduce under interview pressure, and the generated code may hide subtle bugs you won't recognize. The point is building the understanding to write and explain it yourself.
items.topic: Solving & Explaining Coding Challenges with an Agent

items.q: How do you verify an agent's solution to a utility like deepClone?
items.a: Have it (or you) generate tests for the contract and edge cases -- cycles, Date/Map/Set, nested structures, mutation isolation -- and run them. Tests turn 'looks right' into verified behavior.
items.topic: Solving & Explaining Coding Challenges with an Agent

items.q: How do you turn a spec into reliable agent-built code?
items.a: Provide clear requirements and acceptance criteria (best as executable tests), have the agent plan then implement against them, and run the suite -- iterating until it passes. Review the diff against the spec to confirm every criterion is met and nothing extra crept in.
items.topic: Spec-to-Implementation: Driving an Agent from Requirements

items.q: Why are executable tests the best form of a spec for an agent?
items.a: They give an objective, automatically-checkable definition of done, so the agent iterates toward passing them rather than guessing intent -- and you can trust the result because the suite proves the behavior.
items.topic: Spec-to-Implementation: Driving an Agent from Requirements

items.q: How do you keep a spec-driven agent task from scope-creeping?
items.a: Bound it tightly, list explicit acceptance criteria, and review the diff against exactly those -- rejecting unrequested changes. Smaller, well-specified tasks produce more reliable, reviewable output than broad vague ones.
items.topic: Spec-to-Implementation: Driving an Agent from Requirements

items.q: How do you use an agent to prepare for machine-coding rounds?
items.a: Build the component yourself under time pressure, then have the agent review it for missed requirements (a11y, race conditions, interval cleanup), propose the follow-ups interviewers add (autoplay, keyboard nav, virtualization), and generate tests -- using it as a reviewer/coach rather than letting it write the solution.
items.topic: Practicing Machine-Coding Rounds with an Agent

items.q: What's the risk of letting an agent build practice components for you?
items.a: You won't be able to reproduce or explain the solution under interview pressure, and you miss the muscle memory of handling edge cases yourself. The agent should stress-test your understanding, not replace the practice.
items.topic: Practicing Machine-Coding Rounds with an Agent

items.q: How can an agent deepen understanding of a reference solution?
items.a: Ask it to explain why each part exists, what edge cases it handles, the complexity, and what a follow-up requirement would change -- turning a static solution into an interactive learning dialogue you verify against docs.
items.topic: Practicing Machine-Coding Rounds with an Agent

items.q: How do agents like Codex gain new capabilities via MCP?
items.a: They connect to MCP servers that expose tools and resources through a uniform open protocol -- a database query, file access, an API call -- so the same integration works across MCP-compatible agents rather than custom per-tool wiring. The agent calls the tool and incorporates the result.
items.topic: Extending Agents with MCP Tools & Custom Integrations

items.q: What safety practices apply when giving an agent tools?
items.a: Least privilege per tool (read-only when possible), confirmation gates for destructive/irreversible actions, input/output validation, and treating tool-returned data as untrusted (it can carry injected instructions). This limits the blast radius if the agent is misled.
items.topic: Extending Agents with MCP Tools & Custom Integrations

items.q: Why is a standard like MCP valuable for agent tooling?
items.a: It makes integrations reusable and composable across agents and apps -- build a connector once and any MCP-compatible agent can use it -- reducing bespoke glue and standardizing how capabilities and permissions are exposed.
items.topic: Extending Agents with MCP Tools & Custom Integrations

items.q: Why does context management matter for coding agents?
items.a: The context window is finite -- dumping a whole repo or a long history degrades quality (the model loses focus, 'lost in the middle') and inflates cost. Curating relevant files and pruning history keeps the agent accurate and runs cheaper.
items.topic: Managing Context & Token Budgets in Agentic Coding

items.q: How do you fit a large codebase into a limited context?
items.a: Retrieve only relevant files/snippets via code search or embeddings rather than including everything, summarize prior steps, keep a concise task/state note, and scope each task narrowly so the necessary context fits the window.
items.topic: Managing Context & Token Budgets in Agentic Coding

items.q: How does context size relate to agent cost?
items.a: Cost scales with tokens processed per step times the number of steps; bloated context multiplies cost across a long agent run. Tighter, relevant context lowers both cost and latency while improving answer focus.
items.topic: Managing Context & Token Budgets in Agentic Coding

items.q: Explain the CSS box model and its four areas.
items.a: An element is a box of: content (text/image), padding (space inside the border around content), border (around the padding), and margin (space outside the border between elements). Together they determine the element's rendered footprint.
items.topic: The Box Model, box-sizing & Layout Fundamentals

items.q: content-box vs border-box - what's the difference?
items.a: With content-box (default), width/height apply only to content, so padding+border add to the visible size. With border-box, width/height include padding and border, so the element keeps its declared size -- preferred in modern resets to avoid layout math surprises.
items.topic: The Box Model, box-sizing & Layout Fundamentals

items.q: What is margin collapsing?
items.a: Adjacent vertical margins (e.g. a paragraph's bottom margin and the next's top margin) combine into a single margin equal to the larger of the two, rather than summing. It applies to vertical margins of block elements in normal flow and often surprises developers.
items.topic: The Box Model, box-sizing & Layout Fundamentals

items.q: How does Flexbox differ from CSS Grid, and when use each?
items.a: Flexbox is one-dimensional (lay out along a single row or column); Grid is two-dimensional (rows and columns together). Use Flexbox for components and single-axis distribution (navbars, centering); use Grid for page-level/2D layouts. They're complementary, often combined.
items.topic: Flexbox vs CSS Grid: When to Use Each

items.q: How do you center an element with Flexbox?
items.a: On the container: display:flex; justify-content:center (main axis); align-items:center (cross axis). This solves the classic vertical+horizontal centering that was painful before Flexbox -- for a single item, the whole box centers in both directions.
items.topic: Flexbox vs CSS Grid: When to Use Each

items.q: What does grid-template-areas give you?
items.a: A way to name regions and lay them out visually in CSS -- you draw the layout shape as a string grid (e.g. "header header" "sidebar main"), making the structure self-documenting and easy to rearrange responsively by redefining the areas in a media/container query.
items.topic: Flexbox vs CSS Grid: When to Use Each

items.q: How is CSS specificity calculated?
items.a: As a tuple: inline styles (highest), then number of IDs, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then element/pseudo-element selectors. Compare left to right; higher wins. Equal specificity is resolved by source order (later wins). !important overrides normal specificity.

items.q: What problem do cascade layers (@layer) solve?
items.a: They add an explicit ordering axis above specificity: rules in a later-declared layer beat earlier layers regardless of selector specificity. This lets you structure styles (reset/base/components/utilities) so override order is intentional, ending specificity wars and reliance on !important.

items.q: What do :where() and :is() do to specificity?
items.a: :where() always contributes zero specificity -- ideal for easily-overridable defaults. :is() matches any selector in its list and takes on the specificity of its most specific argument. Both reduce selector repetition, but they differ in specificity impact.

items.q: What are container queries and how do they differ from media queries?
items.a: Media queries respond to the viewport; container queries (@container) respond to the size of a component's containing element. This makes a component adapt based on the space it's actually given, so the same component works in a sidebar or full-width without viewport-specific overrides -- true component-level responsiveness.
items.topic: Responsive Design: Media Queries, Container Queries & Fluid Type

items.q: What is mobile-first responsive design and why prefer it?
items.a: Write base styles for small screens, then add complexity with min-width media queries as space grows. It's simpler (progressive enhancement), tends to ship less CSS to mobile, and matches how most users access sites -- versus desktop-first, which patches down with max-width overrides.
items.topic: Responsive Design: Media Queries, Container Queries & Fluid Type

items.q: How does clamp() help responsive design?
items.a: clamp(min, preferred, max) sets a value that scales fluidly with the preferred (often viewport- relative) value but stays within min/max bounds -- e.g. fluid font sizes or spacing that grow with the screen without needing many breakpoints.
items.topic: Responsive Design: Media Queries, Container Queries & Fluid Type

items.q: Why use semantic HTML over generic divs?
items.a:
Semantic elements (header, nav, main, article, button, etc.) convey meaning and structure -- screen readers expose landmarks and controls, search engines understand content, and code is more maintainable. A div soup forces ARIA patches and excludes assistive-tech users.

 Q. What are the core accessibility requirements to mention?

 A. Meaningful alt text for images, associating labels with form controls, sufficient color contrast (4.5:1 for normal text), full keyboard operability with visible focus, correct heading hierarchy, and respecting preferences (reduced motion). These map to WCAG's POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust).

items.q: What is the first rule of ARIA?
items.a: Don't use ARIA if a native HTML element already provides the semantics -- e.g. use a real <button> instead of <div role='button'>, which gives focus, keyboard, and roles for free. ARIA supplements semantics only when no native element fits; misused ARIA can make things less accessible.

items.q: Explain the CSS position values.
items.a: static (normal flow, default); relative (offset from its normal position but still takes space); absolute (removed from flow, positioned relative to nearest positioned ancestor); fixed (positioned relative to the viewport, stays on scroll); sticky (relative until a scroll threshold, then sticks like fixed within its container).

items.q: Why might a high z-index not bring an element to the front?
items.a: Because z-index only orders elements within the same stacking context. If the element sits in a stacking context that's painted below another tree, no z-index value will lift it above elements in the higher context -- you must fix the contexts, not just raise the number.

items.q: What creates a new stacking context?
items.a: The root element, positioned elements (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky) with a z-index other than auto, and properties like opacity < 1, transform, filter, will-change, isolation: isolate, and others. Each forms an independent layer for z-index ordering of its descendants.

items.q: How do CSS custom properties differ from Sass/preprocessor variables?
items.a: Custom properties are live at runtime -- they cascade, inherit, can be scoped per selector, change with media queries or JS, and update the page without recompiling. Sass variables are compiled away at build time and are static. Use custom properties for dynamic theming; preprocessor variables for build-time constants.

items.q: How do you implement dark mode with CSS variables?
items.a: Define theme variables on :root (light defaults), then override the same names under a .dark / [data-theme='dark'] selector; reference them everywhere via var(). Toggle the class/attribute (often with JS) and the whole UI re-themes from one place -- no duplicated component styles.

items.q: Can you read and change custom properties from JavaScript?
items.a: Yes -- read with getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue('--x') and set with el.style.setProperty('--x', value). This enables runtime theming, user-adjustable settings, and driving animations/layout from JS, which static preprocessor variables can't do.

items.q: Why are transform and opacity the recommended properties to animate?
items.a: The browser can animate them on the GPU compositor without recalculating layout or repainting each frame, so they stay smooth. Animating width/height/top/left triggers layout and paint every frame -- the most common cause of janky animations on slower devices.

items.q: Transition vs animation - when use each?
items.a: Use a transition to smoothly animate between two states on a trigger (hover, class toggle). Use @keyframes animation for multi-step sequences, looping, or motion that runs on its own (e.g. a spinner, entrance animation) without a state change driving it.

items.q: What is will-change and how should you use it?
items.a: A hint telling the browser to promote an element to its own compositor layer ahead of an animation, reducing first-frame jank. Use it sparingly and remove it after -- over-applying it wastes memory by creating too many layers. Also honor prefers-reduced-motion for users sensitive to motion.

items.q: How does native HTML form validation work?
items.a: Constraint attributes (required, type=email, min/max, pattern, minlength) let the browser validate without JS, blocking submit and showing built-in messages. The Constraint Validation API (checkValidity, setCustomValidity, :invalid/:valid) lets you customize messages and styling while keeping native behavior.

items.q: What makes a form accessible?
items.a: Every control has an associated <label> (via for/id or wrapping), related controls are grouped with <fieldset>/<legend>, errors are conveyed with aria-invalid and linked via aria-describedby (not color alone), inputs use correct types/autocomplete, and the whole form is keyboard-operable with visible focus.

items.q: Why choose specific input types like email or number?
items.a: They give mobile users the right on-screen keyboard, enable free built-in validation and semantics, and improve autofill -- a better UX and accessibility outcome than a generic text input plus custom JS parsing.

items.q: What does repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)) do?
items.a: Creates as many equal columns as fit the container, each at least 250px and growing to share leftover space (1fr), wrapping to new rows automatically -- a responsive grid with no media queries. minmax bounds each track; auto-fit fills the row with as many as fit.
items.topic: CSS Grid Deep Dive: template-areas, fr, minmax & auto-fit

items.q: auto-fit vs auto-fill - what's the difference?
items.a: Both create as many tracks as fit. auto-fill keeps empty leftover tracks (so existing items don't stretch to fill the row), while auto-fit collapses empty tracks to zero so the actual items expand to fill the available width. Visible difference only when items are fewer than columns that fit.
items.topic: CSS Grid Deep Dive: template-areas, fr, minmax & auto-fit

items.q: When do you use grid-template-areas?
items.a: For page/section layouts where the structure should be visible and easy to rearrange -- you name regions (header/sidebar/main/footer) and 'draw' the layout as strings, then reassign areas in a media/container query to reflow. It's self-documenting versus line-number placement.
items.topic: CSS Grid Deep Dive: template-areas, fr, minmax & auto-fit

items.q: rem vs em vs px - when do you use each?
items.a: px: fixed, ignores user font settings (use sparingly). rem: relative to the root font-size -- best for typography and spacing because it honors the user's browser zoom/font preference (accessibility). em: relative to the parent's font-size -- handy for component-relative spacing, but compounds when elements nest.
items.topic: CSS Units & Modern Functions: rem/em, vh, calc(), min/max/clamp

items.q: What do calc(), min(), max(), and clamp() enable?
items.a: calc() mixes units and does math (calc(100% - 3rem)); min()/max() pick the smaller/larger of values; clamp(min, preferred, max) gives a fluid value bounded by min/max -- ideal for fluid typography and spacing that scales with the viewport without many breakpoints.
items.topic: CSS Units & Modern Functions: rem/em, vh, calc(), min/max/clamp

items.q: Why prefer rem over px for font sizes?
items.a: rem scales with the root font-size, so if a user increases their browser's default font for readability, rem-based text scales accordingly. px is fixed and ignores that preference -- an accessibility regression for low-vision users.
items.topic: CSS Units & Modern Functions: rem/em, vh, calc(), min/max/clamp

items.q: Explain the difference between INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER JOIN.
items.a: INNER returns only rows with a match in both tables. LEFT returns all left-table rows plus matches (NULLs where none). RIGHT is the mirror (all right rows). FULL OUTER returns all rows from both, NULLs where there's no match. Choose by which side's unmatched rows you need to keep.

items.q: Why can filtering a LEFT JOIN in WHERE accidentally make it an INNER JOIN?
items.a: Because unmatched right-table rows have NULLs, and a WHERE condition on a right-table column (e.g. right.status = 'x') filters those NULL rows out, leaving only matched rows. To keep the left rows, put the condition in the ON clause instead of WHERE.

items.q: What is SQL's logical query execution order?
items.a: FROM/JOIN, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT (and aliases), then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. This explains why you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE (WHERE runs before SELECT) but can in ORDER BY, and why HAVING (post-aggregation) differs from WHERE (pre-aggregation).

items.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
items.a: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping/aggregation and can't reference aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can use aggregates (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). Use WHERE to cut rows early, HAVING to filter on group-level results.
items.topic: SQL Aggregation: GROUP BY, HAVING & Aggregate Functions

items.q: What's the rule for columns in a GROUP BY query?
items.a: Every column in SELECT that isn't inside an aggregate function must appear in the GROUP BY clause; otherwise the value is ambiguous (which row's value?). Strict SQL modes reject violating queries. Aggregated columns (COUNT/SUM/etc.) don't need to be grouped.
items.topic: SQL Aggregation: GROUP BY, HAVING & Aggregate Functions

items.q: How would you find the second-highest salary?
items.a: Several ways: SELECT MAX(salary) WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary)); or SELECT DISTINCT salary ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1; or a window function DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) and filter rank = 2 (which also handles ties cleanly).
items.topic: SQL Aggregation: GROUP BY, HAVING & Aggregate Functions

items.q: What do window functions do that GROUP BY can't?
items.a: They compute across related rows (a 'window') while keeping every row in the output, instead of collapsing groups. So you get per-row results like running totals, rankings, and access to neighboring rows (LAG/LEAD) alongside the detail rows -- impossible with GROUP BY alone.

items.q: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK?
items.a: All assign ordering within a partition. ROW_NUMBER gives unique consecutive numbers (ties broken arbitrarily). RANK gives the same rank to ties but leaves gaps (1,1,3). DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank with no gaps (1,1,2). Pick by whether you need uniqueness, gapped, or dense ranking.

items.q: How do you get the top-N rows per group in SQL?
items.a: Use a window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) in a subquery/CTE, then filter WHERE rn <= N in the outer query. This is cleaner and faster than correlated subqueries or self-joins.

items.q: What is a database index and what's the tradeoff?
items.a: A structure (typically a B-tree) that lets the DB locate rows without a full scan, speeding up lookups, ranges, ORDER BY, and JOINs. The tradeoff: indexes consume storage and slow down writes (inserts/updates/deletes must maintain them), so you index selectively based on query patterns.

items.q: How does the column order of a composite index matter?
items.a: A composite index (a, b, c) serves queries filtering on a leftmost prefix -- (a), (a,b), or (a,b,c) -- but not on (b) or (c) alone. Order columns by how queries filter (most selective / most-used leading), or the index won't be used.

items.q: How do you find out why a query is slow?
items.a: Use EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the query plan: whether it's doing a full table scan vs an index scan, join strategy, and row estimates vs actual. Then add/adjust indexes, rewrite the query, or fix statistics. Avoid wrapping indexed columns in functions, which disables index use.

items.q: What are 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF?
items.a:
1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF plus no non-key column depends on only part of a composite key (no partial dependency). 3NF: 2NF plus no non-key column depends on another non- key column (no transitive dependency). Each step removes a class of redundancy/update anomaly.

 Q. Normalization vs denormalization - when denormalize?

 A. Normalize by default to avoid redundancy and anomalies (integrity). Denormalize deliberately when read performance demands it -- duplicating data to avoid expensive JOINs (analytics, read-heavy or NoSQL designs) -- accepting harder writes and consistency management. It's a measured tradeoff, not a default.
items.topic: Normalization, Schema Design & SQL vs NoSQL

items.q: How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL?
items.a: SQL for structured, related data needing complex queries/JOINs and strong ACID guarantees. NoSQL for flexible/evolving schemas, very high horizontal scale, and known access patterns (document, key- value, wide-column, graph). Match the store to data shape, query patterns, and consistency requirements -- many systems use both.
items.topic: Normalization, Schema Design & SQL vs NoSQL

items.q: What does ACID stand for?
items.a: Atomicity (all operations commit or none do), Consistency (the transaction takes the DB from one valid state to another, honoring constraints), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere observably), and Durability (committed changes survive crashes). It's the guarantee set relational databases provide for transactions.

items.q: What are the SQL isolation levels and what do they prevent?
items.a: READ UNCOMMITTED (allows dirty reads), READ COMMITTED (prevents dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (also prevents non-repeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (also prevents phantom reads -- full isolation). Higher levels remove more anomalies but reduce concurrency through more locking/contention.

items.q: Explain dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads.
items.a: Dirty read: seeing another transaction's uncommitted changes. Non-repeatable read: re-reading the same row returns different values because another transaction committed an update between reads. Phantom read: re-running a range query returns new rows that another transaction inserted. Each is blocked at progressively higher isolation levels.

items.q: What makes Neon different from traditional Postgres hosting?
items.a: It separates compute and storage, so compute autoscales and can suspend to zero when idle (serverless-friendly billing), while storage persists independently. It also offers instant copy-on-write branching and a serverless HTTP driver for edge runtimes -- standard Postgres underneath.

items.q: Why does Neon's serverless driver matter for Next.js on Vercel?
items.a: Serverless functions open many short-lived connections, quickly exhausting Postgres connection limits. Neon's HTTP/WebSocket serverless driver avoids that pooling problem and works in edge runtimes, which is why Neon natively powers Vercel Postgres and is a common Next.js choice.

items.q: What is Neon database branching used for?
items.a: Instant copy-on-write branches of your database (schema + data) -- like Git branches. Teams use them for per-PR preview environments, testing migrations against real data safely, and isolating dev/staging, then discarding the branch when done.

items.q: How is Drizzle different from Prisma?
items.a: Drizzle is a thin, SQL-first, type-safe query builder with near-zero runtime overhead and types inferred from a TypeScript-defined schema -- you write queries that look like SQL. Prisma is a higher- level ORM with its own schema language and generated client. Teams pick Drizzle for SQL transparency, edge compatibility, and a smaller footprint.
items.topic: Drizzle ORM: Type-Safe SQL for TypeScript

items.q: How do migrations work in Drizzle?
items.a: drizzle-kit generate compares your TypeScript schema to the last snapshot and emits SQL migration files for the diff; drizzle-kit migrate applies pending files in order. You can also push directly in dev (drizzle-kit push). Migrations are plain SQL you can inspect and version.
items.topic: Drizzle ORM: Type-Safe SQL for TypeScript

items.q: Why is Drizzle well-suited to edge/serverless?
items.a: It's lightweight with minimal runtime and offers drivers like drizzle-orm/neon-http that talk to Postgres over HTTP, working in edge runtimes where TCP-based clients don't. Combined with end-to- end type inference, it fits the Next.js/Vercel + Neon serverless model.
items.topic: Drizzle ORM: Type-Safe SQL for TypeScript

items.q: What does Clerk provide and why not build auth yourself?
items.a: Clerk provides complete auth and user management -- sign-in/up UI, OAuth/social, MFA, sessions, and compliant PII storage (SOC 2/HIPAA). Rolling your own means handling password security, social integrations, MFA, compliance, and user management yourself -- high effort and high risk, which is why managed auth is recommended.

items.q: How do you integrate Clerk with a Next.js App Router app?
items.a: Install @clerk/nextjs, wrap the app in <ClerkProvider>, add middleware to protect routes, use prebuilt components (<SignIn/>, <UserButton/>), and read the user on the server with auth()/currentUser() in Server Components, Route Handlers, and Actions. Set publishable and secret keys via env vars.

items.q: How do you keep your database in sync with Clerk users?
items.a: Use Clerk webhooks (verified with a signing secret) to receive user.created/updated/deleted events and upsert into your own DB -- commonly storing the Clerk user id as a key in your Neon/Drizzle tables, so app data joins to the authenticated identity.

items.q: What is Better Auth and how does it differ from Clerk?
items.a: Better Auth is an open-source, self-hosted, framework-agnostic auth library for TypeScript -- you own the data in your own database. Clerk is a managed service that hosts auth and PII for you. Better Auth gives control and avoids per-user pricing; Clerk reduces operational burden and handles compliance.

items.q: How does Better Auth store its data?
items.a: Through ORM adapters (Drizzle, Prisma) it creates and uses tables in your own database (e.g. Neon Postgres) for users, sessions, accounts, etc. You run its request handler in a framework route, so authentication data never leaves your infrastructure.

items.q: What does Better Auth's plugin system add?
items.a: Modular features beyond core email/password and social login -- such as two-factor auth, organizations/multi-tenancy, magic links, and passkeys -- enabled as plugins, so you add capabilities without adopting a heavyweight framework or external service.

items.q: What is Kinde and who is it aimed at?
items.a: A managed auth and user-management platform for startups/product teams that bundles authentication (social, passwordless, MFA), multi-tenant organizations with roles/permissions, feature flags, and built-in billing -- so a small team can ship a subscription product without integrating several separate services.
items.topic: Kinde: Auth & Billing for Product Teams

items.q: How does Kinde compare to Clerk and Auth0?
items.a: All are managed auth providers handling sign-in, sessions, and compliance. Kinde's pitch is breadth toward product needs -- auth plus roles/permissions, feature flags, and billing in one platform -- whereas Clerk focuses on polished auth/user-management UX and Auth0 on enterprise identity. Choose by which adjacent features you need bundled.
items.topic: Kinde: Auth & Billing for Product Teams

items.q: What do organizations and roles in Kinde enable?
items.a: Multi-tenancy: grouping users into organizations with role- and permission-based access control, plus feature flags/entitlements per plan. This supports B2B SaaS where each customer is an org with its own members, roles, and enabled features.
items.topic: Kinde: Auth & Billing for Product Teams

items.q: What problem does Zod solve that TypeScript types don't?
items.a: TypeScript types are erased at runtime, so they can't validate real incoming data. Zod validates at runtime AND infers the static type from the same schema (z.infer), giving one source of truth -- so untrusted input (API bodies, forms, env) is both checked at runtime and typed at compile time.

items.q: What's the difference between .parse and .safeParse?
items.a: .parse returns the typed value on success and throws a ZodError (with detailed issues) on failure. .safeParse never throws -- it returns { success: true, data } or { success: false, error }, which is better for expected validation failures like form input where you want to handle errors without try/catch.

items.q: How do you express custom rules and derive types in Zod?
items.a: Use refinements (.refine/.superRefine) with custom messages for rules the built-ins don't cover, and chain validators (.min, .email, .regex). Derive the static type with type T = z.infer<typeof schema>, keeping the runtime schema and compile-time type perfectly in sync.

items.q: What is Conform and what makes its approach distinctive?
items.a: A form-validation library built on the web platform: it leverages native form/constraint validation and progressively enhances, so forms work without JS and pair naturally with Server Actions. It validates against a schema (Zod/Valibot) on the server and wires accessible error messages -- favoring platform behavior over heavy client state.

items.q: How does Conform work with Zod and Server Actions?
items.a: You define a Zod schema, and in a Server Action parse the submitted FormData with Conform's parser against that schema; it returns typed field errors you render inline. Validation runs on the server (and can mirror on the client), keeping a single schema and supporting no-JS submission.

items.q: Why does progressive enhancement matter for forms?
items.a: A progressively-enhanced form submits and validates via the native HTML form even if JavaScript hasn't loaded or fails, then enhances with richer client UX when JS is available. This improves resilience and accessibility -- the form is never fully broken for any user.

items.q: How does Inngest differ from a traditional job queue?
items.a: You publish events (inngest.send()) rather than pushing to a queue; Inngest routes them to matching functions and orchestrates execution over HTTP. It adds durable step functions, built-in retries, delays (step.sleep), concurrency, and observability -- handling orchestration you'd otherwise build atop Redis/SQS yourself.

items.q: What are Inngest step functions and why do they matter?
items.a: A function split into steps (step.run); each step is retried independently and its result is memoized, so on failure the function resumes from the last successful step instead of re-executing prior work. This makes multi-step workflows durable and idempotent without manual checkpointing.

items.q: How do you delay work durably in Inngest?
items.a: Use step.sleep()/step.sleepUntil() -- the wait is durable and survives process restarts/redeploys (unlike a setTimeout in a serverless function that can't run that long), so you can model 'wait 3 days then send a follow-up' reliably within one function.

items.q: What is Upstash QStash and when do you use it?
items.a: An HTTP message queue + scheduler for serverless: you publish a message with a target URL and QStash calls it with retries, scheduling, and delays -- no workers/Redis. Ideal for serverless async tasks under ~1M/day (emails, webhooks, reports). For multi-step workflows use Inngest; for very high throughput, self-managed BullMQ.
items.topic: Upstash QStash: Serverless Message Queue & Scheduling

items.q: How does QStash ensure reliable delivery and security?
items.a: At-least-once delivery with automatic retries on failure, and request signing -- your endpoint verifies an incoming message is genuinely from QStash using signing keys (which rotate, with both valid during transition so deploys don't break in-flight messages). Make handlers idempotent since delivery is at-least-once.
items.topic: Upstash QStash: Serverless Message Queue & Scheduling

items.q: What are QStash's key constraints?
items.a: A ~60-second endpoint timeout (so it's not for long-running compute -- use a dedicated worker/Trigger.dev for that), and it's most cost-effective under about 1M messages/day. Local dev needs a tunnel (ngrok-style) since QStash calls a public URL.
items.topic: Upstash QStash: Serverless Message Queue & Scheduling

items.q: Why use Upstash Redis instead of self-hosted Redis in serverless?
items.a: Serverless/edge functions can't reliably hold the persistent TCP connections traditional Redis needs. Upstash exposes Redis over HTTP/REST with an edge-compatible SDK and per-request, scale-to-zero pricing -- so you get Redis caching/rate-limiting without managing clusters or connection pools.
items.topic: Upstash Redis: Serverless Redis over HTTP

items.q: How do you add rate limiting with Upstash?
items.a: Use @upstash/ratelimit backed by Upstash Redis: instantiate a limiter (e.g. sliding window, N requests per interval), then call limit(identifier) in middleware or a route handler; it returns whether the request is allowed and remaining quota. A few lines, no custom data structures or Redis ops.
items.topic: Upstash Redis: Serverless Redis over HTTP

items.q: What are common Upstash Redis use cases?
items.a: Caching (cache-aside for expensive DB queries/API calls with TTLs), session and token storage, rate limiting, and lightweight counters/leaderboards -- anywhere you need fast, shared, in-memory-style state from serverless functions.
items.topic: Upstash Redis: Serverless Redis over HTTP

items.q: Explain the cache-aside pattern with Redis.
items.a: On read, check Redis first; on a hit return it, on a miss read the database, populate Redis with a TTL, and return. On write, invalidate or update the cached key. The app manages the cache (lazy loading), so only requested data is cached and stale data expires via TTL.
items.topic: Redis Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside, TTLs & Invalidation

items.q: How do you keep a Redis cache consistent with the database?
items.a: Set sensible TTLs so stale data self-expires, invalidate or update keys on write, and choose a strategy (cache-aside vs write-through). Accept that caches are eventually consistent; for critical reads, read- through with short TTLs or explicit invalidation on mutation keeps drift small.
items.topic: Redis Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside, TTLs & Invalidation

items.q: How do you prevent a cache stampede on a hot key?
items.a: When a popular key expires, many requests miss at once and hammer the DB. Mitigate with single- flight/locking (one request refills while others wait), staggered TTLs with jitter, or serving stale-while- revalidate. This protects the database from a thundering herd.
items.topic: Redis Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside, TTLs & Invalidation

items.q: What is Arcjet and how is its approach different?
items.a: A developer-first security platform configured inside your application code (via SDK), bundling rate limiting, bot protection, a Shield WAF, email validation, PII redaction, and prompt-injection/AI-abuse protection. Because rules are in code, you apply different protections per route and use request context -- without running your own WAF or Redis infrastruc...
items.topic: Arcjet: In-Code Application Security (Bots, Rate Limits, Shield)

items.q: Why combine Arcjet bot protection with rate limiting?
items.a: Bot detection can't be 100% accurate (malicious bots impersonate users), so pairing it with rate limiting blocks abusive clients while minimizing impact on real users -- together giving stronger, layered traffic control than either alone. Arcjet's docs explicitly recommend combining them.
items.topic: Arcjet: In-Code Application Security (Bots, Rate Limits, Shield)

items.q: What does Arcjet offer for AI/LLM endpoints?
items.a: AI-abuse protection: bot blocking and rate/budget limits to stop automated clients inflating token costs or exhausting per-user budgets, plus prompt-injection detection to guard completion APIs and tool/MCP handlers -- addressing the direct financial and security harm bots cause to AI features.
items.topic: Arcjet: In-Code Application Security (Bots, Rate Limits, Shield)

items.q: What is Vitest and why is it the 2026 default for new projects?
items.a: A Vite-native test runner that reuses your Vite pipeline, giving out-of-the-box ESM/TypeScript support, very fast cold starts, and instant watch re-runs. Its Jest-compatible API makes adoption easy. For Vite-based React/TS apps it's the default; Jest stays common for Webpack and React Native.

items.q: How hard is migrating from Jest to Vitest?
items.a: Mostly mechanical: the API mirrors Jest (describe/it/expect), with vi.* replacing jest.* for mocks/spies/timers, and config moves into the Vite config. RTL component tests are largely unchanged. The main work is mock/config differences and ESM handling.

items.q: How does Vitest fit with RTL and MSW?
items.a: RTL is runner-agnostic (it renders and queries the DOM), so the same component tests run under Vitest; MSW mocks the network layer regardless of runner. Vitest provides the fast runner, RTL the rendering/queries, MSW the API mocks -- a common modern unit/integration stack.

items.q: Why has Playwright become the leading E2E tool for new projects?
items.a: Real cross-browser coverage including WebKit/Safari from one API, auto-waiting that cuts flakiness, web-first retrying assertions, built-in free parallelism/sharding, network interception, and rich failure artifacts (trace/video/screenshots). It's fast and capable without a paid cloud, which is why new E2E projects default to it.

items.q: How does Playwright reduce test flakiness?
items.a: Auto-waiting: before acting on an element it waits for it to be attached, visible, and actionable, and its assertions retry until they pass or time out -- so you rarely need manual waits/sleeps. Combined with resilient role/test-id locators, tests are far more stable than sleep-based scripts.

items.q: Playwright vs Cypress - how do you choose?
items.a: Playwright leads on multi-browser support (incl. WebKit), built-in parallelism, and execution speed, and tests run outside the browser process. Cypress offers a very polished in-browser interactive debugging UX. Pick Playwright for breadth/speed/CI scale; Cypress when its debugging experience is the priority.

items.q: What is the T3 stack and its guiding principle?
items.a: An opinionated, type-safe Next.js full-stack stack scaffolded by create-t3-app: Next.js + TypeScript + Tailwind + tRPC + Prisma/Drizzle + NextAuth/Auth.js, with Zod for validation. Its principle is end-to-end type safety ('bleed responsibly' -- add complexity only when justified), so types flow from database to API to UI.

items.q: How does tRPC provide end-to-end type safety in T3?
items.a: You define server procedures in a router; tRPC infers their input/output types and exposes them to the client without codegen or manual API types. The client calls procedures like typed functions, so a server-side change immediately surfaces as a compile error on the client -- eliminating a class of API drift bugs.

items.q: What does create-t3-app do for you?
items.a: It scaffolds a new project letting you choose pieces (Tailwind, tRPC, Prisma/Drizzle, NextAuth) and wires them with sensible, type-safe defaults and folder structure -- so you start from a coherent, production-shaped baseline instead of integrating each library yourself.

items.q: What are the three main types of machine learning?
items.a: Supervised (labeled data, learn input->output for classification/regression), unsupervised (unlabeled, find structure via clustering/dimensionality reduction), and reinforcement learning (an agent learns from rewards through trial and error). Most business ML is supervised; LLM pretraining is self-supervised (labels derived from the data itself).

items.q: What is overfitting vs underfitting, and how do you address it?
items.a: Overfitting: the model memorizes training data and fails on new data (high variance) -- mitigate with more data, regularization, simpler models, and validation. Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the pattern (high bias) -- use a richer model or better features. The goal is generalization, measured on a held-out test set.

items.q: Why split data into train/validation/test sets?
items.a: Train fits the model; validation tunes hyperparameters and selects models; test gives an unbiased final estimate of generalization. Mixing them (e.g. tuning on the test set) causes leakage and over- optimistic results that won't hold in production.

items.q: How does a neural network learn?
items.a: Forward pass: inputs flow through layers (weighted sums + activation functions) to a prediction; a loss function measures error. Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss w.r.t. each weight, and gradient descent updates weights to reduce loss, repeated over many epochs until it converges. The non-linear activations let it model complex patterns.

items.q: What is the role of activation functions?
items.a: They introduce non-linearity so the network can model complex relationships; without them, stacked layers collapse into a single linear function. ReLU is the common default (fast, mitigates vanishing gradients); sigmoid/softmax appear at outputs for probabilities. The choice affects training stability and speed.

items.q: How does deep learning differ from classical machine learning?
items.a: Deep learning uses many-layered neural networks that learn features automatically from raw data (images, text, audio), excelling at unstructured data at scale -- but needing lots of data and compute. Classical ML (trees, SVMs, linear models) often works better on smaller, structured/tabular datasets and is more interpretable.

items.q: What is the Transformer's self-attention mechanism and why does it matter?
items.a: Each token derives query, key, and value vectors; attention scores how relevant every other token is (query-key alignment) and produces a weighted blend of values. This lets the model capture long- range dependencies and context, and because it's parallelizable (unlike sequential RNNs), it scales to huge datasets -- the breakthrough behind modern LLMs.
items.topic: How LLMs Work: Transformers, Attention & Pretraining

items.q: How are LLMs trained?
items.a: Primarily self-supervised pretraining: predict the next token over massive unlabeled text, so the 'labels' come from the data itself. This teaches grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns. Models are often then fine-tuned and aligned (e.g. instruction tuning, RLHF) to follow instructions and behave helpfully and safely.
items.topic: How LLMs Work: Transformers, Attention & Pretraining

items.q: How does an LLM generate text at inference?
items.a: Autoregressively: given the context, the final layer produces a probability distribution over the vocabulary (softmax); a token is sampled (temperature/top-p control randomness), appended to the context, and the process repeats token by token until a stop condition. Each new token conditions on all previous ones.
items.topic: How LLMs Work: Transformers, Attention & Pretraining

items.q: What is a token and why don't LLMs work with words directly?
items.a:
A token is a subword unit from the tokenizer (BPE/WordPiece); models operate on tokens, not words, so a fixed vocabulary can encode any text and rare words split into pieces. Roughly ~0.75 words per token in English. Token counts drive cost, latency, and context limits.

 Q. What is the context window and what happens at its limit?

 A. The maximum tokens (prompt + response) a model can attend to at once; content beyond it is ignored. Exceeding it forces truncation, and very long contexts can cause 'lost in the middle' (degraded recall of mid-context info). Manage it by summarizing, trimming, or retrieving only relevant chunks (RAG).

items.q: Why does tokenization affect cost and prompt design?
items.a: APIs bill per token and latency grows with tokens, so verbose prompts and long outputs cost more and run slower. Knowing ~4 chars/token helps estimate usage, and concise, well-structured prompts (plus retrieval instead of dumping everything) keep you within budget and the context window.

items.q: What's the progression of prompting techniques to learn?
items.a: Zero-shot (instruction only) -> few-shot (examples) -> chain-of-thought (step-by-step reasoning) -> role/system prompting (persona + constraints) -> structured output (JSON/tool calling, validated) -> prompt chaining/decomposition (multi-step), which leads into agentic workflows where the model plans and uses tools.
items.topic: Prompt Engineering: From Zero-Shot to Agentic (Foundations)

items.q: When does chain-of-thought help and when does it not?
items.a: It improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning, math, and logic by letting the model work through intermediate steps. For simple lookups or classification it adds cost/latency without benefit. You can keep the reasoning internal and surface only the final answer.
items.topic: Prompt Engineering: From Zero-Shot to Agentic (Foundations)

items.q: What makes a prompt reliable in production?
items.a: Specificity (clear task, context, constraints), examples for hard-to-describe formats, explicit output schema with validation, and measurement via an eval set so changes are verified rather than guessed. Treat prompts like code: version, test, and monitor them.
items.topic: Prompt Engineering: From Zero-Shot to Agentic (Foundations)

items.q: What is RAG and what problem does it solve?
items.a: Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves relevant documents (via embeddings and vector search) and adds them to the prompt so the model answers from current, private, or authoritative data instead of only its training. It reduces hallucination and lets you update knowledge without retraining the model.
items.topic: RAG, AI Agents & MCP: The Application Layer

items.q: What distinguishes an AI agent from a single LLM call?
items.a: An agent runs the LLM in a loop with tools: it plans, calls APIs/functions, observes the results, and iterates toward a goal over multiple steps -- adding autonomy and the ability to act in the world, versus a one-shot prompt->response. Reliability comes from bounded goals, tool permissions, and human oversight.
items.topic: RAG, AI Agents & MCP: The Application Layer

items.q: What is MCP and why does it matter?
items.a: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting LLMs to external tools and data sources uniformly, so a given integration (a database, an API, files) is reusable across MCP-compatible models and apps rather than custom per-tool wiring -- standardizing how agents access the world.
items.topic: RAG, AI Agents & MCP: The Application Layer

items.q: What is multimodal AI?
items.a: Models that handle multiple data types -- text, images, audio, video -- by encoding each modality into a shared representation so the model reasons across them. Examples: describing or answering questions about an image, reading a chart/document, or generating images from text. It broadens AI beyond pure text understanding.

items.q: When should you fine-tune versus use prompting or RAG?
items.a: Prompt first (cheapest, most flexible); add RAG when the model needs external/current/private knowledge; fine-tune when you need consistent style/format/behavior or domain adaptation that prompting and RAG can't reliably achieve, and you have quality training data. Fine-tuning costs more and is less flexible, so it's a deliberate last resort for the right c...

items.q: What causes hallucination and how do you reduce it?
items.a: LLMs generate the most probable next tokens, not verified facts, so they can produce fluent but false content -- especially beyond their training knowledge. Reduce it by grounding answers in retrieved sources (RAG) with citations, lowering temperature, allowing 'I don't know', constraining/validating outputs, and evaluating against ground truth.

items.q: What are embeddings and how does vector search use them?
items.a: Embeddings are dense numeric vectors encoding semantic meaning, so similar texts are near each other. A vector database stores them and runs approximate-nearest-neighbor search using cosine similarity / dot product / Euclidean distance to retrieve the chunks most relevant to a query -- the retrieval step in RAG.
items.topic: Embeddings, Vector Search & Chunking for RAG

items.q: How does chunking affect RAG quality?
items.a: Chunk size and overlap trade context richness against retrieval precision: too large dilutes relevance and wastes context; too small loses meaning. A typical 10-20% overlap prevents cutting ideas mid- thought. Good chunking plus re-ranking the retrieved pieces materially improves answer quality.
items.topic: Embeddings, Vector Search & Chunking for RAG

items.q: What is hybrid search and why use it?
items.a: It combines dense semantic search (embeddings, good for synonyms/paraphrase) with sparse keyword search like BM25 (good for exact terms, IDs, proper nouns). Merging both makes retrieval more robust than either alone, especially for queries mixing concepts with specific names or codes.
items.topic: Embeddings, Vector Search & Chunking for RAG

items.q: Walk through how RLHF works and its limitations.
items.a: Collect human preference comparisons between outputs; train a reward model to predict them; optimize the LLM to maximize that reward (typically PPO). Limits: human labels are noisy/biased, feedback is costly to scale, the reward model may not capture intended values, and PPO can be unstable -- motivating simpler alternatives.
items.topic: Alignment: RLHF, DPO, RLAIF & Constitutional AI

items.q: How does DPO differ from RLHF, and why is it popular?
items.a: Direct Preference Optimization removes the separate reward model and PPO loop, optimizing the model directly on preference pairs via an implicit reward derived from them. It's simpler, more stable, and more compute-efficient, so major labs adopt it as an alternative or complement to PPO-based RLHF.
items.topic: Alignment: RLHF, DPO, RLAIF & Constitutional AI

items.q: What is Constitutional AI?
items.a: Anthropic's alignment approach where the model critiques and revises its own responses against a set of written principles (a 'constitution'), so harmful-content alignment relies less on human labelers. It pairs with RLAIF (AI-generated feedback) to scale alignment more cheaply than pure human feedback.
items.topic: Alignment: RLHF, DPO, RLAIF & Constitutional AI

items.q: What is the ReAct pattern for agents?
items.a:
ReAct interleaves Reasoning and Acting: the model thinks about what to do, takes an action (calls a tool), observes the result, and repeats -- building toward the goal over multiple steps. It makes the agent's process inspectable and lets it incorporate real tool outputs rather than guessing.

 Q. How does function/tool calling enable agents?

 A. The LLM outputs a structured JSON object specifying which function to call and with what arguments instead of free text; the system executes it and returns the result to the model. This reliable, machine-parseable hand-off is the foundation of tool use and most agent frameworks, enabling real-world actions and data access.
items.topic: Agentic AI Patterns: ReAct, Tool Use & Multi-Agent

items.q: What makes agentic systems reliable in production?
items.a: Bounding the loop (max steps/budget), scoping tool permissions and adding human-in-the-loop approval for risky actions, robust handling of tool failures/retries, idempotency, cost/latency control per step, and observability/tracing of each reasoning and tool step. Start with narrow, well-scoped tasks before broad autonomy.
items.topic: Agentic AI Patterns: ReAct, Tool Use & Multi-Agent

items.q: What is LoRA and why is it efficient?
items.a: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the pretrained weights and adds two small trainable low-rank matrices whose product approximates the weight update. You train a tiny fraction of parameters (and can keep swappable per-task adapters), drastically cutting compute/memory while retaining the base model's knowledge -- the leading PEFT method.

items.q: How does QLoRA differ from LoRA?
items.a: QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit so it fits in much less GPU memory (often ~2 GPUs vs 4 for LoRA, ~two-thirds the peak RAM), then trains LoRA adapters on top -- reaching accuracy close to LoRA. The trade-off is ~28-32% slower training from dequantization overhead. It makes fine-tuning large models feasible on modest hardware.

items.q: What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you mitigate it?
items.a: When fine-tuning on a narrow task degrades the model's general capabilities. Mitigate by mixing general data with task data, using lower learning rates and fewer epochs, parameter-efficient methods (LoRA touches less of the model), and evaluating on general benchmarks alongside the target task. Adapter approaches help by leaving base weights intact.

items.q: Why do transformers need positional encoding, and what's modern practice?
items.a: Self-attention is permutation-invariant, so without position info token order wouldn't affect output. Original transformers added fixed sinusoidal encodings; modern LLMs favor RoPE (rotary embeddings, rotating Q/K vectors) for good relative-position handling and length extension (e.g. YaRN), while ALiBi uses a linear distance bias that extrapolates to longe...

items.q: What is the KV cache and why does it matter for inference?
items.a: During autoregressive decoding, the model caches the key and value vectors of past tokens so each new token's attention reuses them instead of recomputing -- cutting compute at the cost of memory that grows with sequence length. The KV cache is the primary memory/latency bottleneck in long- context inference, which is why its management (paging, quantization)...

items.q: How do multi-query/grouped-query attention and FlashAttention help?
items.a: MQA/GQA share key/value heads across query heads, shrinking the KV cache (less memory, faster decoding) with minimal quality loss. FlashAttention restructures the attention computation to minimize GPU memory movement, speeding training/inference without changing results. Both target the efficiency limits of standard attention at scale.

items.q: How do you evaluate an LLM application?
items.a: Curate an eval set of representative cases with expected behavior; score with automated methods (exact/semantic match, embedding similarity, LLM-as-judge against a rubric) and human preference ratings. Run these as regression tests in CI on every prompt/model change, and expand the set with real production failures over time.

items.q: What RAG-specific metrics matter, and why separate them?
items.a: Measure retrieval and generation separately: faithfulness (answer grounded in retrieved context, i.e. not hallucinated), answer relevance, and context precision/recall (did retrieval surface the right chunks?). Separating them tells you whether a bad answer is a retrieval failure or a generation failure, so you fix the right component.

items.q: What do you monitor for an LLM feature in production?
items.a: Operational metrics (latency, token cost, error/timeout and refusal rates), quality signals (user thumbs, drift versus your eval baseline), and traces across multi-step chains/agents to debug. Pair with guardrails -- output schema validation, PII redaction, prompt-injection defense -- and feed surfaced failures back into the eval set.
